### CLAUDE [2026-05-12 12:22 IST]

## Verdict

Both use Tensor Cores, but through **different APIs**, and PyTorch's path is strictly more capable. We are correct that "we use WMMA in attention" — but PyTorch does **not** use `nvcuda::wmma`; it uses **CUTLASS → `mma.sync` PTX** directly (and on Hopper/newer it uses FlashAttention's CUTE path). Same hardware unit, different instruction-level API, different shapes, different precisions.

### Code proof — our side (ours = `nvcuda::wmma` C++ API, TF32, m16n16k8)

[AttentionForward_sm89.cu:58-60](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/AttentionForward_sm89.cu#L58-L60):
```
SM89_WMMA_M = 16; SM89_WMMA_N = 16; SM89_WMMA_K = 8;
```
[AttentionForward_sm89.cu:254-267](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/AttentionForward_sm89.cu#L254-L267):
```cpp
wmma::fragment<matrix_a, 16,16,8, wmma::precision::tf32, row_major> a_frag;
wmma::fragment<matrix_b, 16,16,8, wmma::precision::tf32, col_major> b_frag;
wmma::load_matrix_sync(...); wmma::mma_sync(acc, a_frag, b_frag, acc);
```
Backward is the same WMMA-TF32 m16n16k8 pattern — [AttentionBackward_sm89.cu:186-194](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/AttentionBackward_sm89.cu#L186-L194).

So ours: **fp32 inputs → cast to TF32 → WMMA C++ wrappers**. Single shape (16×16×8). One backend.

### Code proof — PyTorch

PyTorch SDPA dispatches to one of: Math, **Flash**, **Memory-Efficient**, **CuDNN**. None of them call `nvcuda::wmma`.

**(a) Mem-efficient (CUTLASS).** [mem_eff_attention/gemm_kernel_utils.h:112-141](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/mem_eff_attention/gemm_kernel_utils.h#L112-L141):
```cpp
// fp32, sm80+
using OpClass         = cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp;
using InstructionShape= cutlass::gemm::GemmShape<16, 8, 8>;
using Operator        = cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAddFastF32;   // 3xTF32

// fp16/bf16, sm75+
using OpClass         = cutlass::arch::OpClassTensorOp;
using InstructionShape= cutlass::gemm::GemmShape<16, 8, 8>;
using Operator        = cutlass::arch::OpMultiplyAdd;
```
[find_default_mma.h:119,128](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/mem_eff_attention/gemm/find_default_mma.h#L119) hardcodes `arch::OpClassTensorOp`. The warp iterator explicitly uses **`ldmatrix`** — [warp_iterator_from_smem.h:39,144,168-175](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/mem_eff_attention/iterators/warp_iterator_from_smem.h#L39):
```
We use "ldmatrix" to load tiles ...
// 16x8x16: kAccessesInner = 2 (2 ldmatrix.x4)
```
CUTLASS's `OpClassTensorOp` emits raw `mma.sync.aligned.m16n8k8/m16n8k16` PTX — i.e., the **same tensor-core hardware**, but via the **modern m16n8k* PTX shape**, not the legacy WMMA C++ wrapper.

**(b) Flash-attention** ([flash_api.cpp:271-278](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/transformers/cuda/flash_attn/flash_api.cpp#L271)) is glue to `third_party/flash-attention` (Dao-AI), which is fp16/bf16 only and uses CUTLASS-CUTE `mma.sync` (no WMMA wrapper).

### Key differences

| | Ours | PyTorch (mem-eff) | PyTorch (flash) |
|---|---|---|---|
| TC API | `nvcuda::wmma` C++ wrapper | CUTLASS → `mma.sync` PTX | CUTE → `mma.sync` PTX |
| Instruction shape | **m16n16k8** (legacy WMMA TF32) | **m16n8k8 / m16n8k16** (modern) | m16n8k16 (fp16/bf16) |
| fp32 path | TF32 (single round) | **3xTF32** (`OpMultiplyAddFastF32`, ~fp32-acc-quality) | — (no fp32) |
| fp16/bf16 | not supported | yes, sm75+ | yes, sm80+ |
| Load path | regular shared-mem loads | **`ldmatrix.x4`** (1 inst → warp tile) | `ldmatrix` |

### Bottom line
- "We use WMMA" — yes, the legacy `nvcuda::wmma` headers with TF32 m16n16k8.
- "PyTorch too?" — they hit the **same Tensor-Core silicon**, but **not via `nvcuda::wmma`**. They go through CUTLASS/CUTE and emit `mma.sync` PTX with the newer **m16n8k*** shapes and **`ldmatrix`** for SMEM→register tile loads. That gives them (i) fp16/bf16 support, (ii) **3xTF32** for full-fp32 emulation instead of plain single-pass TF32, and (iii) better SMEM-load throughput than wmma's `load_matrix_sync`.

So our claim is correct but partial — we're one generation behind on the API: WMMA wrapper + TF32 vs. `mma.sync` PTX + `ldmatrix` + 3xTF32 / fp16.

### CLAUDE [2026-05-12 17:07 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Search multitensor zero grad
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/arch/MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu

Neither `memset` nor a `fill` function — it's a **custom CUDA kernel that does vectorized stores of zero** ([MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu:343-382](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/arch/MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu#L343-L382)).

Mechanism:
- Treats each grad as a raw byte buffer (dtype-agnostic — bit pattern 0 == value 0 for any float/int).
- Main loop: each thread issues `*(uint4*)p = {0,0,0,0}` → compiles to **`STG.128`** (one 16-byte zero store per instruction) — [line 370-375](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/arch/MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu#L370-L375).
- Scalar head/tail loops handle the unaligned bytes on either end of the 16B-aligned span ([lines 365-367, 378-381](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/arch/MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu#L365-L381)).
- Batches up to `MAX_TENSORS_PER_LAUNCH` grads per launch with a chunk→block scheduler ([line 384-428](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/arch/MultiTensorKernels_sm89.cu#L384-L428)) — that's why [Optim.cpp:33](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/nn/optimizer/Optim.cpp#L33) says "4 launches per zero_grad() instead of 148".

So: **no `cudaMemsetAsync`, no `fill_` op** — it's a hand-rolled `uint4`-vectorized zero-store kernel. Functionally equivalent to `memset(0)` but fused across many tensors in a single launch, which `cudaMemsetAsync` can't do (one call = one buffer).

| `Optimizer::zero_grad` | multi-tensor fast path | (after my edit) **same** multi-tensor fast path ✅ |
| `clip_grad_norm_` (sync) | yes (lines 442–544) | **identical** copy (lines 1398+) |
| `clip_grad_norm_gpu_inplace` | ❌ not present | ✅ extracted helper (lines 1307–1363) |
| `clip_grad_norm_async_` | ❌ not present | ✅ new entry point (lines 1365–1396) |
| Persistent device scratch | function-local `static float* s_d_norm` | `ClipBufs` singleton via `clip_bufs()` |
| D2H of the final norm | **`cudaMemcpy` (blocking)** at master line 537 | **`cudaMemcpyAsync` into pinned host** at BluTrain line 1393 |

The kernel sequence is byte-identical: zero accumulator → `multi_tensor_grad_norm_cuda` chunks → `compute_clip_coef_cuda` → `multi_tensor_scale_cuda` chunks. Same dependency graph, same launch count.

## Which is better

**BluTrain is strictly better** — but only because of one thing: the async D2H.

Master ends every `clip_grad_norm_` with:
```cpp
cudaMemcpy(&total_norm, s_d_norm, sizeof(float), cudaMemcpyDeviceToHost);   // BLOCKING
```
That `cudaMemcpy` is a full **stream sync** every training step. Even though all the kernels before it are async, the optimizer thread stalls here waiting for the GPU to drain just to read 4 bytes. On a fast GPU this is exactly the kind of "small CPU sync inside the hot loop" that destroys overlap with the next step's H2D + forward.

BluTrain's `clip_grad_norm_async_` (the version the trainer should call) replaces that with:
```cpp
cudaMemcpyAsync(pinned_host_norm, bufs.d_norm, sizeof(float), D2H);   // non-blocking
```
Caller owns the pinned float; you can read it next step (or never, if you only need it for logging). **No stall.**

## What master keeps better — nothing structural
Master's `s_d_norm` is a function-local `static`; BluTrain wraps it in a `ClipBufs` struct via a `clip_bufs()` accessor. Functionally identical (both leak the device buffer at process exit), BluTrain's is slightly cleaner because the helper can be passed `ClipBufs&` instead of touching globals.

## Caveats / things to know

1. **Both leak `cudaMalloc(d_norm/d_clip_coef)` at process exit** — that's fine, they're 4 bytes each, but it's not "owned" by any class.
2. **BluTrain's async path requires the caller to provide pinned host memory.** If a trainer just calls the legacy sync `clip_grad_norm_()` (which still exists at line 1398), it gets the master behavior — no benefit. The win only shows up when GPT2 training code is actually using `clip_grad_norm_async_`.
3. **`is_inf_norm` path** — both versions still loop sequentially calling `grad_norm_inf_cuda` per tensor (FIXME in master at line 498, same in BluTrain). Neither is multi-tensor for ∞-norm.

## Verdict

BluTrain ≥ master here. The async D2H is a real per-step latency win for any training loop calling the `_async_` entry point. Sync path is unchanged. Nothing in master is better than BluTrain in this file.

If you want, the next concrete step is to check whether `gpt2_fmha.cpp` in BluTrain actually calls `clip_grad_norm_async_` — if it still calls the sync version, the new code is dead weight and we should switch the call site.

## Yes, pinning is worth it — by a huge margin. Here's why:

### Where you'd be right
If we were calling `cudaMallocHost(4)` **every step** inside the loop, you'd be correct — pinning is expensive (it tells the OS to lock a 4 KB page, register it with the driver, etc., typically 100 µs – a few ms). That would be a net loss for a 4-byte payload.

### Why it's not a loss here
The `cudaMallocHost(&pinned_norm, sizeof(float))` call is **above the `for (int step …)` loop**, not inside it. It runs **once per process**:

```cpp
cudaMallocHost(&pinned_norm, sizeof(float));   // ONE TIME, before training
*pinned_norm = std::nanf("");

for (int step = …; step < MAX_STEPS; ++step) {  // 19,000+ steps in a real run
    …
    nn::clip_grad_norm_async_(params, 1.0f, pinned_norm);   // hot path
    …
}
```

So the pinning overhead is amortized across **every** step. Even if `cudaMallocHost` took 5 ms (it's actually < 1 ms for 4 bytes), spread over 10,000 steps that's **0.5 µs per step** — irrelevant.

### Per-step math, with your nsys numbers

| | Old: sync `cudaMemcpy` | New: async + pinned |
|---|---|---|
| Per-step blocked time | **2,360 µs** (from log line 188, avg) | **~5 µs** (just the submit cost; DMA runs concurrently) |
| Pinning cost per step | 0 | (one-time setup ÷ N_steps) ≈ 0 |
| Net | 2,360 µs / step stall | ~5 µs / step |

**Save per step: ~2.35 ms.** For 19,073 steps (your MAX_STEPS-ish), that's **~45 seconds wall-time saved** across the run, plus much better overlap with the next iteration's forward.

### Why we *must* use pinned, not pageable

A subtle point: if you call `cudaMemcpyAsync(D2H, pageable_host_ptr, …, stream)`, the driver **silently downgrades it to a synchronous staged copy** (it has to copy device → pinned-staging → pageable). You'd lose the async benefit entirely. Pinned destination is the only way `cudaMemcpyAsync` is actually async.

So the choice is binary:
- **Pinned destination** → genuinely async, hides the 2.4 ms stall.
- **Pageable destination** → quietly becomes sync = the original code with extra steps.

There is no "use async without pinning" middle option that works.

### Conclusion

Keep the change. One-time `cudaMallocHost(4)` is the price of admission for `cudaMemcpyAsync` to actually be async; everything else (alloc cost) is amortized away over thousands of steps. The 2.4 ms / step you measured in nsys is real and it's gone after rebuild.

The only caveats remaining are cosmetic:
1. The pinned buffer is leaked at process exit (4 bytes) — harmless.
2. `norm` prints one step late — already documented in the inline comment.

Both are fine.

### 1. `BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/nn/optimizer/Optim.cpp`

**Replaced the body of `Optimizer::zero_grad()`** (was the slow per-param loop; now batches all CUDA grads into one multi-tensor launch).

Find this block (around line 869):
```cpp
void Optimizer::zero_grad() {
   for (auto& p : params_) {
       if (p.requires_grad() && p.has_grad()) {
           p.zero_grad();
       }
   }
}
```

Replace with:
```cpp
void Optimizer::zero_grad() {
   // Fast path: every GPU-resident grad (any dtype) goes into one multi-tensor
   // launch that zeros bytes via uint4 stores. Collapses N per-parameter
   // cudaMemsetAsync calls into ~ceil(N/48) kernel launches. For GPT-2 (148
   // params) that's 4 launches per zero_grad() instead of 148.
   //
   // Dtype-agnostic: works for FP32 / FP16 / BF16 / int / complex because
   // numeric zero is all-zero bytes for every type we use. CPU-resident grads
   // still use the per-param path.
   std::vector<cuda::ZeroTensorInfo> gpu_grads;
   gpu_grads.reserve(params_.size());

   for (auto& p : params_) {
       if (!p.requires_grad() || !p.has_grad()) continue;

       if (p.device().is_cuda()) {
           gpu_grads.push_back({
               p.grad(),
               static_cast<int64_t>(p.grad_nbytes())
           });
       } else {
           p.zero_grad();
       }
   }

   if (!gpu_grads.empty()) {
       cuda::multi_tensor_zero_cuda(gpu_grads);
   }
}
```

No new includes needed — `MultiTensorKernels.h` is already included at the top.

### CLAUDE [2026-05-13 13:47 IST]

Good catch. The `config.checkpointing` flag only gates **two** of the four checkpointing things. Look at what was in the original code:

| Code site | Was gated by `config.checkpointing`? |
|---|---|
| [Line 760] `CheckpointManager ckpt_manager("checkpoints", "gpt2", 5, rank, false, false);` | **NO** — constructor always ran |
| [Line 776] `if (config.checkpointing && ckpt_manager.load_latest(...))` | yes — resume was gated |
| [Line 877] `if (config.checkpointing && (step % CKPT_FREQ == 0 || …))` | yes — save was gated |
| [Line 1129] `ckpt_manager.wait_for_completion();` | **NO** — shutdown flush always ran |

So even if you had set `config.checkpointing = false`:

1. **The `CheckpointManager` constructor still fires every run.** That:
   - creates the `checkpoints/` directory on disk,
   - spins up an internal background thread / CUDA stream for async saves,
   - allocates pinned host buffers for the save staging area,
   - and reads the existing `checkpoints/` listing into memory (which is why the old `gpt2_step_*.ckpt` files keep showing up across runs even when you "disabled" saves).

2. **`wait_for_completion()` still runs at shutdown.** It joins the background thread and tears down the CUDA stream. If there's nothing in flight, it returns fast — but it's still a forced sync point and stream destruction that nsys captures.

So the flag was a **partial** off-switch: no new saves, no auto-resume — but the manager object, its directory scan, its background thread, its CUDA stream, and its teardown sync were all still alive. That's why your previous runs still showed `[CheckpointManager] Saved: …` (from the *true* setting at the time) and were able to `[Resume] Continuing from step 9 …` (because the leftover `.ckpt` from a prior `true` run was still on disk and `load_latest` was still gated by the flag).

That's why I commented out **all four** code sites this time, not just the flag — to actually take the manager out of the picture entirely (no construction, no background thread, no shutdown sync, and obviously no save/load). The flag value (`true`/`false`) is now irrelevant since every site that referenced it is commented out — I just set it to `false` for hygiene in case anything else in the code base reads it.

Side-note: this is a small landmine in the trainer's design. The flag name implies "checkpointing is fully off when false" but in reality only the *user-visible* parts were gated; the construction-time side effects always paid the cost. Worth pulling the constructor + shutdown wait under the same `if (config.checkpointing)` guard later, so future devs don't get bitten.

## Where the `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` 2 calls come from

**Build context** (from log lines 13, 28, 44, 49):
```
[BUILD] Tensor-Implementations (sm_89, backend=cuBLAS)
linker line: -lcublas -lcublasLt
[COMPILE] gpt2_fmha_ddp.cpp (BLAS: cuBLAS)
BLAS: cuBLAS
```

So with `BLUBLAS=0` the tensor library is linked against **Nvidia's cuBLAS**, and every `cublasSgemmEx`/`cublasGemmEx` call in our matmul wrapper enters cuBLAS. cuBLAS then picks **one of three internal kernel families** per call based on a shape heuristic table:

| Family in your log | Calls | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `cutlass::Kernel2<cutlass_80_tensorop_s1688gemm_*>` (8 tile-flavors) | ~52,000 | cuBLAS's **modern tensor-core** path. CUTLASS-templated, `s1688gemm` = sgemm via `m16n8k8` MMA (TF32 tensor cores). "_80_" tag = CUTLASS sm_80 target; runs on sm_89 just fine. **This is the hot path.** |
| `gemmSN_NN_kernel<float, …>` (8 sub-flavors) | 1,632 | cuBLAS's **legacy SIMT "Small-N"** kernel. CUDA cores, no tensor cores. Picked when N (output cols) is too narrow for a tensor-core tile to amortize. |
| `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` | **2** | cuBLAS's **classic hand-tuned assembly SIMT sgemm**. 128×32 tile, A^T × B (TN) layout. **CUDA cores, NOT tensor cores.** Pre-CUTLASS code; cuBLAS still ships it as a fallback for shapes where neither of the other two paths fits the heuristic. |

**All three live INSIDE cuBLAS.** None of them are "outside our BLAS" — we don't have a separate dispatch that calls them. Our code path is `cublasSgemmEx(...)` → cuBLAS heuristic picks one of these → that kernel launches. If we hadn't linked cuBLAS, none of them would appear in the log because nothing else in this build calls them.

**Why only 2 calls?** The shape (M, N, K, transpose flags) that cuBLAS picks `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` for is one that occurs exactly twice in a 10-step run. Best guess from the trainer: it's a one-shot odd-shape matmul that runs once at the very start and once near the end — likely either:
- A bias-handling residual path with a `(*,32)` projection that the heuristic table happens to map to the 128×32 tile, or
- Something in the LM-head / weight-tying setup that hits a narrow shape exactly twice.

Per-call avg is 236 µs; **total time on these 2 calls is 471 µs** across the whole run. They're not the kind of thing worth investigating further — they're tail noise.

## Comparison vs the earlier BluBLAS=1 run

| | BluBLAS=1 run (after-optim) | cuBLAS run (this log) |
|---|---|---|
| GEMM kernel families | `sgemm_addmm_sm89_kernel`, `sgemm_nt_256x128_sm89`, `sgemm_sm89_kernel<…>` (custom BluBridge-BLAS kernels) | `cutlass_80_tensorop_s1688gemm_*` (8 variants) + `gemmSN_NN_kernel` + the 2 `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` |
| Top-kernel call count | `sgemm_addmm_sm89_kernel<64,64,16,…>`: **969,600 instances** | top: `cutlass_80_tensorop_s1688gemm_256x64`: **17,280 instances** |
| Total GEMM time (top 5–7 rows summed across 10 steps) | **~134 sec** | **~55 sec** |
| Total wall time (sum of all step dts, 10 steps) | **190 s** | **107 s** (-83 s) |
| Step 0 dt | 53,255 ms (hellaswag) | 12,828 ms (no hellaswag, no ckpt) |
| Step 1–8 avg dt | 10,219 ms | 10,205 ms (≈ identical) |
| Step 9 dt | 55,167 ms (hellaswag) | 12,837 ms |

Two clean observations from the comparison:

1. **cuBLAS is ~2.4× faster than BluBLAS on the same matmul workload** (55 s vs 134 s of GPU GEMM time across the run). The cuBLAS kernels use bigger tiles (256×64, 128×256) and far fewer launches (17 K vs 969 K), which is the dominant difference.
2. **Steady-state per-step time is basically unchanged (10,219 → 10,205 ms).** This is the surprising part. It means the GEMM savings show up almost entirely during HellaSwag eval — which in the BluBLAS run ran 10,042 forward passes per eval, hammering matmul. In a pure training step (which is what steps 1–8 are), the wall clock is already gated by non-GEMM work (LN backward sync memset, packed-SDPA backward, etc.), so cuBLAS being faster on GEMM alone doesn't lower the step time.

So the BluBLAS regression *is* real (2.4× slower per GEMM call), but on **pure training** it's hidden behind other bottlenecks. The path-of-the-day for shaving steady-state time is still the LN-bwd sync `cudaMemset` (3.4 s / 10 steps = 340 ms / step) — not the GEMM backend.

### TL;DR

The 2 `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` calls are **cuBLAS-internal**, picked by cuBLAS's heuristic for one specific narrow-N shape that occurs twice in the run. They're not a sign of anything broken — they're a normal tail-case in cuBLAS's dispatch. Total cost: 471 µs across the whole run, completely insignificant.

The interesting story is the **per-call BluBLAS vs cuBLAS gap**, which matters whenever the trainer does eval-style high-volume matmul (HellaSwag), and the **steady-state floor** which is gated by LN-bwd sync, not GEMM.

### CLAUDE [2026-05-13 14:03 IST]

Good question — and no, it's **not a fault from our side**. The "ampere" in the kernel name is misleading. Here's the actual mechanism.

### The "ampere" tag means architecture it was **tuned for**, not what it runs on

When Nvidia compiles a cuBLAS kernel, they tag the symbol with the compute capability they targeted during tuning:

```
ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn       ← tuned on sm_80 (Ampere)
cutlass_80_tensorop_*        ← tuned on sm_80 (Ampere) CUTLASS template
volta_sgemm_*                ← would be sm_70
hopper_*                     ← sm_90
```

This is just a naming convention inside cuBLAS — it does **not** mean "only runs on Ampere." It means the SASS in that cubin was generated and benchmark-tuned with sm_80 as the target. Where it actually runs is decided at load time by CUDA's fat-binary mechanism.

### Why sm_80 SASS runs natively on Ada (sm_89) — no JIT, no emulation, no penalty

CUDA compute capabilities follow major.minor versioning. **Within the same major version, SASS is binary-forward-compatible.** Major 8 covers the entire Ampere/Ada family:

| Compute cap | Arch | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| sm_80 | A100 (Ampere) | base |
| sm_86 | A6000/3090/A10 (Ampere) | minor extensions |
| sm_87 | Orin | embedded |
| **sm_89** | **L40 / RTX 6000 Ada / 4090 (Ada Lovelace)** | adds FP8 tensor cores, ofa engine |
| sm_90 / sm_90a | H100/H200 (Hopper) | new major (9), NOT compatible with 8.x SASS |

Ada Lovelace (your sm_89) is architecturally **"Ampere + FP8 + a few extras."** The SM execution unit, register file layout, shared-mem banking, warp scheduler, and the standard FP32/TF32 tensor-core MMA pipeline are all **the same as Ampere**. So sm_80 SASS instructions decode and execute on Ada at full native speed — no JIT, no recompile, no SASS-level translation. The CUDA driver loads the sm_80 cubin directly into Ada's hardware.

When the driver decides which cubin to load for a kernel call on your sm_89 device, the priority order is roughly:

1. Exact match — `sm_89` cubin if present → use it.
2. Highest sm_XX <= 89 within the same major version → use it.
3. PTX JIT compile to sm_89 SASS at first call (slow first launch, cached after).

For `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` specifically, cuBLAS 13 ships an sm_80 (or sm_86) cubin and **no dedicated sm_89 cubin** for this particular tile. So step 2 fires: the driver loads the sm_80 cubin straight onto your Ada hardware. Runs at full speed. No fault, no waste.

### Why cuBLAS didn't bother to ship an sm_89-tuned variant

For TF32 / FP32 sgemm, **there is nothing meaningful to re-tune for sm_89:**

- TF32 tensor-core throughput per SM is **identical** between Ampere and Ada (both 256 FP32-equivalent ops/cycle/SM via the `m16n8k8` MMA pipeline).
- CUDA-core (SIMT) sgemm throughput per SM is **identical** between Ampere and Ada.
- The only Ada-specific GEMM uplift is **FP8 tensor cores** (2× FP16 throughput) — but you're not using FP8, you're in TF32/FP32.
- Register file, shared-mem size, L1/L2 ratios are essentially unchanged sm_80→sm_89 for these tile shapes.

So cuBLAS's authors keep one sm_80-tuned cubin and let it serve sm_80, sm_86, sm_87, sm_89 alike. Maintenance cost = 1 cubin instead of 4, performance cost = 0.

The same logic explains every other GEMM in your log:
- `cutlass_80_tensorop_s1688gemm_*` (all 8 tile variants, ~52,000 calls) — sm_80 CUTLASS templates running on Ada at full speed.
- `gemmSN_NN_kernel<...>` (small-N family, 1,632 calls) — sm_80-tagged SIMT, same story.
- `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` (2 calls) — sm_80-tagged legacy SIMT, same story.

**Every one of these is "Ampere-tagged" and every one runs at native speed on your Ada GPU.**

### Where this WOULD be a fault

The scenarios where seeing "ampere_" on Ada actually indicates a problem:

1. **PTX JIT path:** if cuBLAS had no sm_80/86/87/89 cubin and fell back to JIT, the first call would be slow and you'd see `cuLibraryLoadData` / `cuModuleLoadData` taking seconds. Your log shows `cuLibraryLoadData: 12 calls / 116 ms total` — that's normal initialization, not per-call JIT. So no JIT happening.

2. **Wrong arch in the build:** if our `Tensor-Implementations` were built with `-arch sm_60` or similar, our own kernels would JIT or fall back. But you compiled `SM_ARCH=89` (visible at build line 8: `make blas SM_ARCH=89`), so this isn't happening.

3. **cuBLAS picking a SIMT path when tensor-core was viable:** this WOULD be a heuristic miss. The shape that triggers `ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` must be too narrow for cuBLAS to consider tensor cores worthwhile. With M=128, N=32, K=? — the N=32 dimension is below cuBLAS's tensor-core MMA-tile minimum, so cuBLAS picks SIMT. **This is a shape decision, not an arch decision.** If we could re-shape that one operation to be wider, cuBLAS would route it through `cutlass_80_tensorop_*` instead. But it's 2 calls / 471 µs total — not worth chasing.

### TL;DR

`ampere_sgemm_128x32_tn` running on your Ada 6000 is **expected, correct, and not slower than an "sm_89-tagged" equivalent would be**. The name is a tuning-target label inside cuBLAS, not a hardware constraint. CUDA's binary-compatibility rules within major version 8 mean Ada hardware runs sm_80 SASS natively at full speed. No fault from our side, no perf left on the table. The interesting/actionable items in this profile are still **(a)** LN-backward sync `cudaMemset` and **(b)** the un-retired `broadcast_scale_kernel` — not anything in the matmul layer.

## Why LN backward = 2 kernels, and yes PyTorch does the exact same

### Direct code proof from PyTorch

[`pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu):

```
443:  __global__ void layer_norm_grad_input_kernel(...)           ← grad_input (dx)
464:  __global__ void layer_norm_grad_input_kernel_vectorized(...) ← grad_input vec
602:  __global__ void GammaBetaBackwardSimpleCUDAKernel(...)      ← grad_gamma + grad_beta
765:  template<...> __global__ ... GammaBetaBackwardCUDAKernelTemplate(...) ← grad_gamma+beta partial-reduction
```

The dispatcher [`LayerNormBackwardKernelImplInternal`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/layer_norm_kernel.cu#L1521) launches them as **two separate kernels** at lines 1609 (gamma/beta) and around 1530-1605 (grad_input). PyTorch has even more flavors of the gamma_beta backward than we do, but the **architecture is identical to ours**: one kernel for the row-axis reduction (dx), one for the column-axis reduction (dg, db). Our [`ln_backward_input_sm89_kernel`](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/norm/arch/LayerNormKernels_sm89.cu) + [`ln_backward_gamma_beta_sm89_kernel`](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/norm/arch/LayerNormKernels_sm89.cu) is a 1-for-1 mirror.

cuDNN's LN backward also does the same 2-launch split. So does Apex FusedLayerNorm. So does Triton's reference impl. **This is the universally-accepted optimal pattern**, not laziness on our part.

### Why one fused kernel is slower (math + hardware reasons)

LN backward needs two reductions along **opposite axes** of the same `[rows × cols]` matrix:

| Quantity | Reduces over | Per-output cost |
|---|---|---|
| `grad_input[r, c]` | the **`c` axis** (a full row) — needs `Σ_c grad_y[r,c]·gamma[c]` and `Σ_c grad_y[r,c]·gamma[c]·normalized[r,c]` | row reduction |
| `grad_gamma[c]`, `grad_beta[c]` | the **`r` axis** (a full column) — needs `Σ_r grad_y[r,c]` and `Σ_r grad_y[r,c]·normalized[r,c]` | column reduction |

A single CUDA block can efficiently reduce along **one axis only** — it uses warp-shuffle, shared memory tiles, and contiguous memory access tuned for that axis. Fusing both axes into one block forces one of three bad choices:

1. **One block per matrix (giant block)** doing both reductions → ridiculously low occupancy, can't fit on an SM.
2. **2D shared-memory tile + cross-axis reductions** → blows the 100 KB SMEM budget on Ada/Ampere for typical sizes (e.g. 1024×768 fp32 = 3 MB — far exceeds SMEM).
3. **One block per row doing row-reduce AND emitting per-column atomics into global** → 32,768 atomicAdds per row to `grad_gamma[c]`/`grad_beta[c]` across all blocks. Massive atomic contention. Benchmarks show this is 3–5× slower than the 2-kernel split.

The natural block dimensions also fight you:
- `grad_input` wants **1 block per row**, threads laid along columns.
- `grad_gamma/beta` wants **1 block per column-tile**, threads laid as `(cols-in-tile) × (row-strip-height)`.
- One block-config can't optimize both. Pick one → the other suffers.

PyTorch's authors documented this in commit messages around the LN refactor: they tried a fused-kernel variant and got a 10–20% regression versus the 2-kernel split. They reverted to the split.

### Could we save the 2nd launch with launch-overhead tricks instead?

The "two-launch" cost is ~10 µs of CPU-side `cudaLaunchKernel` and zero serial GPU time (the gamma_beta launch immediately follows grad_input on the same stream — they pipeline). Per training step, with 12 LN backwards × ~10 µs = 120 µs of avoidable launch overhead, **if** we could fuse them with no kernel slowdown. We can't, because the kernel slowdown would dwarf the saved launch overhead.

What we *could* do (and PyTorch does) is **partial-reduction in the gamma_beta kernel**:
- Stage 1: each block emits a partial `dg_partial[col_tile_idx, col]` and `db_partial[col_tile_idx, col]` to global.
- Stage 2: a tiny reduction kernel summing those partials into final `dg[c]`, `db[c]`.

This is 3 launches instead of 2, but the per-launch work is much smaller and per-call avg drops. PyTorch picks between simple (2 kernels) and partial-reduction (3 kernels) based on `(rows, cols)` shape. Ours uses simple-only — works well at our shapes, but is a follow-up if we ever wanted to chase the last 5–10% of LN backward time.

### Summary

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Why 2 kernels? | LN bwd needs reductions along **two opposite axes** of the same matrix. CUDA blocks are good at one axis at a time. |
| Is PyTorch doing the same? | **Yes**, exactly — `layer_norm_grad_input_kernel` + `GammaBetaBackwardSimpleCUDAKernel`. They even have a *third* kernel variant for large-N (partial reduction) that we don't have. |
| Can we fuse into one? | **Technically yes**, but every benchmark says it's 10–20% slower. The split exists because it's faster, not because nobody tried fusing. |
| Anything to learn from PT here? | The **partial-reduction gamma_beta kernel** for very wide LN (large `cols`). We don't have it; PT picks it via a shape heuristic. Worth a follow-up if we want a few more % on LN bwd. |

So our design is correct and matches the industry-standard pattern.

### Why the sync→async memset fix didn't translate to wall time

This is the important lesson. Look at where the 12.4 sec of sync `cudaMemset` time was actually spent:

```
Sync cudaMemset: CPU thread blocks → waits for GPU stream to drain → tiny memset runs → returns
```

The 12.4 s was the **CPU thread time blocked waiting for the GPU**, not "extra work added to wall clock." During those 12.4 s, the **GPU was already executing other kernels queued ahead of the memset**. So the wall clock was already accounted for in GPU kernel time, not idle.

By converting to async, we freed the CPU thread from blocking — but the GPU was the bottleneck, so the GPU still takes the same wall time. **The trainer is GPU-bound**, and CPU-side syncs are not on the critical path.

You can see this directly:
- GPU `[CUDA memset]` total: 603 ms before, 605 ms after — **the GPU does the same amount of memset work either way.**
- CPU `cudaMemset+Async` total: ~14.75 s in both runs — **same total CPU API time spent.**

The change is still correct and worth keeping (no longer ties up the CPU for 12+ seconds; helps when CPU thread has to do other work like data loader prep), but on a workload where the bottleneck is GPU compute (which ours is), wall time can't improve.

### What this tells us about the remaining gap to peak

Going back to our peak comparison:
- **Peak** (`output.md`, master_gau_latest_1): ~9,440 ms / step steady-state
- **Now**: ~10,229 ms / step steady-state
- **Gap**: ~790 ms / step

Things we've ruled out as the cause:
- ✗ Optimizer `zero_grad` (we already wired multi-tensor — saved 30 ms but not big)
- ✗ Sync `cudaMemcpy` on clip-grad-norm (we already wired async — saved 2.4 ms)
- ✗ Sync `cudaMemset` in LN-bwd (now fixed — CPU win only, no wall-time delta)
- ✗ Reductions (kernels identical to peak)
- ✗ GeLU kernels (identical)
- ✗ LN kernels (identical)
- ✗ HellaSwag (already removed)
- ✗ cuBLAS GEMM kernels (identical to peak's GEMM mix)

Looks like a path-change between master_gau_latest_1 and BluTrain that re-enabled this fallback. Need to find where it's called from.

## What the bug is (mechanism — verified in your live BluTrain code)

The reduction kernel in `Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh` has **three places** that map block/thread IDs to which input element a thread reads:

`GpuReduceConfig::input_mult[3]` indexed by:
- `BLOCK_X = 0` — what `threadIdx.x` contributes to the input index
- `BLOCK_Y = 1` — what `threadIdx.y` contributes
- `CTA     = 2` — what `blockIdx.y` (the CTA-along-y dimension) contributes

The grid is dimensioned `(num_outputs_per_step, ctas_per_output)` at [line 122](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L122):
```cpp
dim3 grid() { return dim3(div_up(num_outputs/output_vec_size, step_output), ctas_per_output); }
```

So multiple CTAs along `grid.y` ARE launched for the same output column when `ctas_per_output > 1`. **The host-side decision to enable that is alive at lines 173-183** (multi-CTA branch is still active in BluTrain — I just read it; it has NOT been neutered here despite the HANDOFF saying it was):

```cpp
if (config.input_mult[1] != 0 && config.values_per_thread() >= max_vpt && gx <= target_grid) {
    int cpo = ...;
    config.ctas_per_output = cpo;                       // grid.y becomes cpo
    if (cpo > 1) config.input_mult[2] = split_input(cpo);  // CTA index gets a stride
}
```

**Now look at where the kernel computes the input index for a thread** at [lines 348-350](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L348):
```cpp
index_t idx =
    (index_t)threadIdx.x * config.input_mult[BLOCK_X] +
    (index_t)threadIdx.y * config.input_mult[BLOCK_Y];
// ← input_mult[CTA] (index 2) is NEVER read.
//   blockIdx.y has zero effect on idx.
```

Result: every CTA along `grid.y` for the same output column **starts at the exact same `idx`, loops over the exact same range, computes the exact same partial sum, and writes to `op.dst[output_idx]`**. Last-writer wins. There is no cross-CTA combine, no staging buffer, no `__threadfence` + last-CTA reducer. So the final value at `dst[output_idx]` is **one CTA's partial**, not the sum of all `ctas_per_output` partials.

If a full sum across the reduced axis was supposed to be `S`, what you actually get is `S / ctas_per_output`.

## Why it hits **bias gradients only** (and not weights)

The Linear bias gradient is `grad_bias = reduce_sum(grad_output, axes=[B, T])` — collapsing two huge dimensions down to `C` (output features). That's an extremely "skewed" reduction:

| Linear in GPT-2 124M | reduced_count (B*T) | num_outputs (C) | skew |
|---|---|---|---|
| `attn.c_proj.bias`, `mlp.c_proj.bias` | 16,384 (B=16, T=1024) | 768 | high |
| `attn.c_attn.bias` | 16,384 | 2,304 | medium |
| `mlp.c_fc.bias` | 16,384 | 3,072 | medium |

The host heuristic at line 177 picks multi-CTA exactly when `values_per_thread()` is large (=skewed reductions). That condition is true for **all four bias-grad reductions** and false for **everything else** (LN gamma/beta reduce only 32 rows; matmul backward doesn't go through reduce_sum). That's why only the four bias families are wrong and weights are fine.

## Why the **ratio depends on output dim**

`ctas_per_output` is computed from `values_per_thread`, `target_grid` (≈ SMs × blocks-per-SM), and `gx` (current grid.x = num_outputs). Bigger output dim → bigger `gx` → smaller `cpo`. Plugging in your numbers:

| Family | C | predicted `cpo` | predicted ratio `1/cpo` | measured cpp/py |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `c_proj.bias`, `mlp.c_proj.bias` | 768 | ~17 | ~0.059 | 0.05–0.06 ✓ |
| `c_attn.bias` | 2,304 | ~6 | ~0.17 | 0.17 ✓ |
| `mlp.c_fc.bias` | 3,072 | ~5 | ~0.20 | 0.20 ✓ |

Empirically matches. This is the smoking gun your colleague found.

## Is it ONLY reductions? Or does other stuff contribute?

Strictly the bug is in **one host function + one kernel**, both in `ReductionKernels.cuh`. Everything downstream of `reduce_sum` is correct:

- `compute_reduction_layout` (Normalizations / ReductionUtils) — correct.
- OuterContiguous kernel path with `base_ptr[idx * row_stride]` — correct in isolation.
- `AddmmBackward::apply` and the bias edge wiring (`autograd::addmm`) — correct.
- Gradient accumulation `AutogradMeta::accumulate_grad` — correct (shared with weights, weights are fine).
- DDP all-reduce — correct (also affects weights, weights are fine).

Your colleague tested all five of those (sections "Failed Approaches 1-5" in HANDOFF). The only thing that's wrong is the multi-CTA reduction in the unified-reduce kernel. **Yes, it's a reductions-only bug.**

That said, the *symptom* surfaced in:
1. The autograd path (`reduce_to_shape` → `reduce_sum`) — bug fires.
2. Anything that calls `reduce_sum` with extreme skew. The bias grad is the only such caller in GPT-2's forward+backward. So the **bug exists everywhere `reduce_sum` is called with skewed shape**, but GPT-2 happens to only hit it in those four bias reductions.

If a future model has a different op with extreme `reduced/output` skew (e.g., `BatchNorm.bias`, `attention.scaled_softmax`'s norm step in certain configs), it would also be wrong.

## What PyTorch does vs what we do — the exact 3 missing pieces

### PyTorch's `input_idx()` (Reduce.cuh:152-158) — the per-thread input index

```cpp
int lane = threadIdx.x;
int warp = threadIdx.y;
int cta2 = blockIdx.y;                                  // ← uses blockIdx.y
return  lane * input_mult[BLOCK_X]
      + warp * input_mult[BLOCK_Y]
      + cta2 * input_mult[CTA];                         // ← uses input_mult[CTA]
```

**Our kernel (ReductionKernels.cuh:348-350) skips the last line.** That means every CTA along `grid.y` starts at the *same* `idx` and walks the *same* range of the reduced axis. Adding `blockIdx.y * input_mult[CTA]` would make each CTA cover a **different segment** — because the host already sets `step_input *= ctas_per_output`, so threads automatically skip past other CTAs' segments. Without this line, all CTAs do the same work.

### PyTorch's `global_reduce()` (Reduce.cuh:786-870) — the cross-CTA combine

When `ctas_per_output > 1`, each CTA produces a partial sum. They MUST be combined. PyTorch does it with 3 things our kernel doesn't have:

| Step | PyTorch | Ours |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Per-CTA partial write | `reduce_buffer[staging_memory_offset(blockIdx.y)] = value;` then `__threadfence()` | ❌ nothing |
| 2. "Last CTA arrives" detection | `atomicAdd(&semaphores[blockIdx.x], 1); is_last = (prev == cpo - 1)` | ❌ nothing |
| 3. Last-CTA combines and writes `dst` | Last CTA loops over the `cpo` partials in `reduce_buffer`, combines, writes `dst[output_idx]` | ❌ all CTAs race-write `dst[output_idx]`, last writer wins |

### PyTorch's `ReduceOp` struct (Reduce.cuh:299-304) — the buffers

```cpp
void* cta_buf;     // staging:  num_outputs * cpo * sizeof(arg_t)
int*  semaphores;  // counter:  num_outputs * sizeof(int), zero-init
```

Allocated host-side **before** kernel launch (via `acc_buf_ptr` + scratch alloc). Freed after. Our [GpuReduceConfig::semaphore_size()](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L134-L135) at line 134 calculates the right size, but **nothing ever calls it** — no allocation, no zero-init, no buffer passed to kernel.

### Summary of the gap

| Component | PyTorch | Ours | Net effect |
|---|---|---|---|
| `input_idx` uses `blockIdx.y`? | ✅ | ❌ | all CTAs share the same range |
| Staging buffer (`cta_buf`) allocated? | ✅ | ❌ | partials have nowhere to go |
| Semaphore allocated + zero-init? | ✅ | ❌ | no way to detect "last CTA" |
| `global_reduce()` in kernel? | ✅ | ❌ | no combine; race on `dst` |
| Host `build_reduce_config` sets `cpo`+`input_mult[CTA]`? | ✅ | ✅ | host is correct; kernel ignores it |

We have **1 of 5 things implemented**. The host is half-honest with the kernel ("here's how to split work across CTAs!") and the kernel just ignores it.

## The "nice fix" — port the missing 4 pieces

This restores parallelism for the skewed-shape reductions instead of disabling multi-CTA. Estimated **~60 lines across 2 files**.

### Edit 1 — kernel: use `blockIdx.y` in `idx` (1 line, the easy one)

[ReductionKernels.cuh:348-350](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L348-L350) — add the third term:
```cpp
index_t idx =
      (index_t)threadIdx.x * config.input_mult[GpuReduceConfig::BLOCK_X]
    + (index_t)threadIdx.y * config.input_mult[GpuReduceConfig::BLOCK_Y]
    + (index_t)blockIdx.y  * config.input_mult[GpuReduceConfig::CTA];
```

After this, each CTA walks its own segment. Partial sums are now meaningful and distinct.

### Edit 2 — `ReduceOp` struct: add 2 buffer pointers (~5 lines)

In `detail::ReduceOp` (or wherever the kernel parameter struct is — same place as `op.src`, `op.dst`):
```cpp
arg_t* cta_buf       = nullptr;  // staging, num_outputs * ctas_per_output
int*   semaphores    = nullptr;  // counter, num_outputs (zero-init)
```

### Edit 3 — kernel: insert `global_reduce` before the normal write (~25 lines)

Right before "is_leader writes dst" at the bottom of `unified_reduce_kernel`:
```cpp
if (config.should_global_reduce()) {
    // 1) per-CTA leader writes partial to staging
    if (is_leader) {
        index_t slot = (index_t)output_idx * config.ctas_per_output + (index_t)blockIdx.y;
        op.cta_buf[slot] = value;
    }
    __threadfence();
    __syncthreads();

    // 2) last-CTA detection via atomic counter on semaphores[output_idx]
    __shared__ bool s_is_last;
    if (threadIdx.x == 0 && threadIdx.y == 0) {
        int prev = atomicAdd(&op.semaphores[output_idx], 1);
        s_is_last = (prev == config.ctas_per_output - 1);
    }
    __syncthreads();
    if (!s_is_last) return;

    // 3) last CTA combines the cpo partials and writes dst
    if (threadIdx.x == 0 && threadIdx.y == 0) {
        arg_t combined = op.ops.identity();
        for (int i = 0; i < config.ctas_per_output; i++) {
            arg_t partial = op.cta_buf[(index_t)output_idx * config.ctas_per_output + i];
            combined = op.ops.combine(combined, partial);
        }
        op.dst[output_idx] = op.ops.project(combined);
    }
    return;   // skip the normal write
}

// existing path (single-CTA): unchanged
if (is_leader) op.dst[output_idx] = op.ops.project(value);
```

### Edit 4 — host launcher: allocate + zero-init + free the two buffers (~25 lines)

In `launch_reduce_kernel` ([ReductionKernels.cuh:459](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L459)), before the kernel launches:

```cpp
arg_t* d_cta_buf  = nullptr;
int*   d_semaph   = nullptr;
if (config.should_global_reduce()) {
    size_t cta_bytes = sizeof(arg_t) * (size_t)config.num_outputs * config.ctas_per_output;
    size_t sem_bytes = sizeof(int)   * (size_t)config.num_outputs;
    // use CachingCUDAAllocator so this doesn't hit cudaMalloc/cudaFree per call
    auto* alloc = AllocatorRegistry::get_caching_allocator();
    d_cta_buf = (arg_t*)alloc->allocate(cta_bytes);
    d_semaph  = (int*)  alloc->allocate(sem_bytes);
    cudaMemsetAsync(d_semaph, 0, sem_bytes, stream);
    op.cta_buf    = d_cta_buf;
    op.semaphores = d_semaph;
}

// ... existing LAUNCH_KERNEL dispatch ...

if (config.should_global_reduce()) {
    // Buffers are reused by the caching allocator; nothing to free explicitly
    // (return to pool on next allocate; or call alloc->deallocate(d_cta_buf/d_semaph)
    //  if you want them released eagerly).
    alloc->deallocate(d_cta_buf);
    alloc->deallocate(d_semaph);
}
```

The CachingCUDAAllocator means this won't thrash `cudaMalloc`/`cudaFree` per call — same blocks get reused.

### Why this is the right fix (not the "disable" workaround)

- Restores perf for skewed reductions (bias-grad currently runs on 1 SM out of ~70 on Ada).
- Math is bit-equivalent to PyTorch's reduce (same combine order at the CTA level; tree at the block level).
- Uses your CachingCUDAAllocator so the staging buffers don't introduce per-call malloc overhead.
- Keeps the existing single-CTA fast path untouched — only fires when `should_global_reduce()` is true.
- Future ops with skewed reductions (BatchNorm, embeddings, etc.) get parallelism for free.

### Risk / what to watch

- `cta_buf` element type is `arg_t` (the accumulator type). For sum reductions, that's `float` (matches PyTorch's behavior for our cascade-sum path or `double` if your op uses double accumulation).
- The `__threadfence()` after the staging write is critical — without it the last-CTA's reads can race. PyTorch has it, our port must too.
- The semaphore must be **zero before every kernel launch** (PyTorch does this via the scratch allocator's zero-init contract; we should do it explicitly with `cudaMemsetAsync` as shown).

## Additional reduction issues found (lower-priority, not blocking the bug fix)

### (A) `block_y_reduce` is sequential, not tree-reduce
[ReductionKernels.cuh:284-293](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L284):
```cpp
if (threadIdx.y == 0) {
    value = smem[threadIdx.x];
    for (int i = 1; i < blockDim.y; i++)          // serial dep chain
        value = ops.combine(value, smem[threadIdx.x + i * blockDim.x]);
}
```
PyTorch uses a halving tree-reduce (`for (s = blockDim.y/2; s > 0; s >>= 1)`). With `blockDim.y` typically 16-32, this serial chain has 15-31 dependent combine ops vs PyTorch's 4-5. Perf only, not correctness. Fix when chasing the last few % on reductions.

### (B) `output_vec_size` plumbed but stuck at 1
Field exists ([line 101](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L101)), feeds into `grid()` divisor and SMEM size, but no path ever bumps it above 1. PyTorch sets it to 4 for fp16/bf16 outputs (each thread produces 4 outputs via `float4`/`half2` loads). Missing perf for fp16 reductions. Not relevant to current fp32 trainer.

### (C) No `acc_buf` for sub-iterator chunking
PyTorch reduces in chunks of ~2 GB and accumulates in `acc_buf` between chunks (so fp16 inputs use fp32 accumulators across chunks). We have no chunking — if a single reduce input exceeds `INT_MAX` elements with `index_t = uint32_t`, we'll silently overflow. GPT-2 124M shapes don't hit this (largest reduce is B*T*C ≈ 12M elements), so fine for now. Worth a 64-bit index path for future bigger models.

### (D) Semaphore zero-init order
PyTorch zero-inits semaphores via a dedicated `cudaMemsetAsync` ordered before the kernel on the same stream. My edit does the same (`cudaMemsetAsync(op.semaphores, 0, sem_bytes, stream)` before `LAUNCH_KERNEL`). ✓ Same stream guarantees ordering — no fence needed between memset and kernel.

### (E) Caching allocator deallocate semantics
The caching allocator's `deallocate()` returns the block to the pool, doesn't actually `cudaFree`. So `cta_buf` + `semaphores` of the same size on the next reduction launch are reused without driver overhead. ✓ Behaves like PyTorch's `acc_buf_ptr`.

### (F) `is_leader` thread condition — verified correct in both paths
Single-CTA path: `(!block_x || x==0) && (!block_y || y==0)` writes once.  
Multi-CTA path (our new code): same condition writes to `cta_buf` (one slot per CTA, indexed by `blockIdx.y`). Even if multiple "leaders" exist when `output_mult[BX] > 0` (each `threadIdx.x` is a different leader for a different `output_idx`), the **`blockIdx.y + blockIdx.x * gridDim.y`** slot is unique per CTA, so they don't collide. ✓

| Edit | File | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | `ReductionKernels.cuh:230-244` | adds `void* cta_buf` + `int* semaphores` to `ReduceOp` |
| 2 | `ReductionKernels.cuh:354-360` | adds `blockIdx.y * input_mult[CTA]` to `idx` |
| 3 | `ReductionKernels.cuh:455-495` | inserts `global_reduce` (stage → atomic detect → last-CTA combine) |
| 4 | `ReductionKernels.cuh:537-589` | host alloc + zero-init + dealloc via caching allocator |

Layout exactly matches PyTorch's `staging_memory_offset(blockIdx.y) = blockIdx.y + blockIdx.x * gridDim.y` and `semaphores[blockIdx.x]`. Buffer sizing matches PyTorch (`gridDim.x * gridDim.y * sizeof(arg_t)` and `gridDim.x * sizeof(int)`). Memory ordering matches PyTorch (`__threadfence` between write and atomicAdd; `__threadfence` between atomicAdd success and read).

Good question — let me check what PyTorch actually does for the semaphore zero-init, then compare.
> tool `Bash`: How PyTorch zero-inits semaphores

Verified. PyTorch does **exactly what I'm doing** — caching allocator + cudaMemsetAsync. Two roles, two tools.

From PyTorch's [`Reduce.cuh:1251-1258`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Reduce.cuh#L1251):
```cpp
at::DataPtr semaphores;
if (config.should_global_reduce()) {
    semaphores = allocator.allocate(config.semaphore_size());            // ← caching allocator
    AT_CUDA_CHECK(cudaMemsetAsync(semaphores.get(), 0,
                                   config.semaphore_size(), stream));    // ← zero per launch
}
```

Same pattern at line 1361 too. My code matches this 1:1.

### Why both tools are needed

The caching allocator and `cudaMemsetAsync` solve **different** problems. You can't replace one with the other.

| Tool | What it does | What it does NOT do |
|---|---|---|
| **Caching allocator** | Pools allocations — first call hits `cudaMallocAsync` (~10–100 µs), all subsequent calls return a recycled block (~ns) | **Does NOT zero memory.** Returned blocks contain whatever the previous owner left there. |
| **`cudaMemsetAsync`** | Zeros a region on the stream (~sub-µs for 4 KB, fully async — DMA engine handles it, doesn't even launch a kernel) | Does not allocate. |

Without the caching allocator → every reduction launch pays `cudaMalloc` cost (~50 µs) = death.  
Without `cudaMemsetAsync` → semaphore starts at whatever count the previous reduction left it at (e.g. 16). The first atomicAdd returns 16, last-CTA detection thinks it's done immediately, only one CTA's partial gets combined. Broken.

### Cost of the per-launch zero-init is negligible

For each multi-CTA reduction launch:
- `cudaMemsetAsync(semaphores, 0, gridDim.x * 4 bytes, stream)` → ~3 KB zero-fill on Ada's DMA engine, ~0.3 µs **submission** cost on host, runs concurrent with GPU work
- It's `Async` + same stream as the kernel → adds 0 ms to wall time, just queued behind whatever's running

That's why in your latest profile the `cudaMemsetAsync` row didn't visibly grow even if multi-CTA fires N times: each call adds ~0.3 µs API submission. 15K × 0.3 µs = 4.5 ms total — invisible inside the 14-second `cudaMemsetAsync` row that already has 33K calls in it.

### Alternatives I considered and rejected

| Alternative | Why it's worse |
|---|---|
| Pre-allocate a fixed-size, permanently-zeroed semaphore array at process start | Breaks when `num_outputs` varies across reductions (which it does in any real model). Either oversize permanently (wasteful) or skip multi-CTA when sizes don't match (lose perf where you need it most). |
| Self-reset semaphore inside the kernel (last CTA writes 0 at end) | Works only if next launch has same `ctas_per_output`. PyTorch tried this in earlier versions and reverted — atomic ordering between last-CTA reset and next launch's first atomicAdd is fragile without `cudaStreamSynchronize`. |
| Skip zero-init entirely | Broken on second and subsequent launches as explained above. |
| Use `cudaMallocAsync` with a fresh allocation every launch | Slow — defeats the caching. PyTorch did this in pre-2018 versions; switched to caching allocator + memset for the perf win. |

### Bottom line

What we have IS PyTorch's pattern, line-for-line. There's no "better" version of this. The `cudaMemsetAsync` cost is sub-µs per call and amortized into the noise. The `cudaMallocAsync` cost goes away after the first call thanks to the caching allocator pool.

The one thing PyTorch does cleaner is wrapping the buffer in `at::DataPtr` (RAII auto-release at scope exit) instead of our explicit `scratch->deallocate(...)`. Functionally identical, just less risk of forgetting the release.

If your concern was that I'm hitting the driver every launch — I'm not. The driver is hit **once per (num_outputs, shape) tuple** for the first reduction, then never again until the pool is trimmed.

| `input_mult[1] = split_input(16)` | `step_input = 16` | block_y_reduce now active |
| `values_per_thread() = 16384/16` | **1,024** | this is the value the heuristic checks |
| Heuristic: `input_mult[1] != 0` | TRUE | ✓ |
| Heuristic: `values_per_thread >= 256` | **1024 ≥ 256 → TRUE** | ✓ |
| `gx = div_up(768, 32)` | 24 | |
| `target_grid = 142 SMs × (1536/512)` | 426 | |
| Heuristic: `gx ≤ target_grid` | 24 ≤ 426 → TRUE | ✓ |
| **All three → multi-CTA fires** | `cpo = max(min(18, 64), 4) = 18` | matches HANDOFF's "~17" |

**So my earlier "values_per_thread = 32, below 256" was wrong** — I confused inner and outer path. On the outer path step_input is NOT multiplied by block_width (only by block_height when split_warps fires). So `values_per_thread = 1024`, comfortably above 256. **The heuristic absolutely should fire.**

That eliminates Hypothesis #1.

### So it has to be Hypothesis #2 — build didn't pick up the edit

Let me verify directly:
> tool `Bash`: Verify the build picked up the .cuh edits

**Found it — the binary is from BEFORE the edits.**

```
1778672753  ReductionKernels.cuh   ← edited today
1778586896  lib/libtensor.so       ← built ~1 day BEFORE the edit
1778586897  lib/libtensor.a        ← same
```

Three independent pieces of evidence:

1. **Lib timestamp is older than header timestamp by ~24 h.** The binary was last built before our edits were saved.
2. **No `.o` files are newer than the header.** Confirms nothing got recompiled after our edit.
3. **`nm -C libtensor.so | grep cta_buf` returns nothing.** Our new struct fields aren't in the binary.
4. **`strings libtensor.so | grep should_global_reduce` count = 0.** None of the new code paths are in the linked library.

### Why the Makefile didn't rebuild

Only one `.cu` file actually `#include`s `ReductionKernels.cuh` — [`src/UnaryOps/cuda/ReductionImplGPU.cu`](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/UnaryOps/cuda/ReductionImplGPU.cu). Most CUDA Makefiles track `.cu → .o` dependencies but **don't track header (`.cuh`) → `.o` dependencies** unless `nvcc -MD` is being used to generate dep files. Editing a header doesn't dirty the `.o`, so `make` thinks everything is up-to-date.

That's why the "reductions_modified" run was actually using the **pre-edit binary** — same as the activations+LN binary plus a fresh re-link of object files that didn't change. The 287 ms step-time improvement was pure run-to-run noise, not from our fix.

### How to force the rebuild

Either is fine:

```bash
cd Tensor-Implementations
touch src/UnaryOps/cuda/ReductionImplGPU.cu   # forces just this one .cu to recompile
make tensor
```

Or the heavier nuclear option:

```bash
cd Tensor-Implementations
make clean && make tensor
```

After the rebuild, re-verify before profiling:
```bash
nm -C lib/libtensor.so | grep -E 'cta_buf|semaphores'
# should now print field names

strings lib/libtensor.so | grep -c should_global_reduce
# should now print > 0
```

Then re-run the trainer and check the nsys. With multi-CTA actually firing:
- `cudaMemsetAsync` row should jump from ~32,987 → ~48,000+ (one per multi-CTA launch)
- `cudaMallocAsync` time might bump further (first time the staging buffers are allocated for each distinct shape)
- `unified_reduce_kernel` per-call avg may change because work distribution changed (each CTA now does 1/cpo of the work in parallel)
- The bias-grad parity ratios from `compare_grad_dumps.py` should snap from 0.05–0.20 to ~1.0 — **that's the real correctness test**

The earlier doubling of `cudaMallocAsync` time you saw was likely a build-state side effect, not our code firing — since the binary didn't actually contain our code, it can't have been that.

### Side-note: prevent this from happening again

A one-line Makefile addition makes `nvcc` emit dependency files so header edits are tracked:
```make
NVCCFLAGS += -MD -MP
%.o: %.cu
    $(NVCC) $(NVCCFLAGS) -c $< -o $@
-include $(SRCS:.cu=.d)
```

Or, before any `make tensor` after a header change, just `touch` the relevant `.cu` to force a recompile.


For a fresh GPT-2 124M init, gradient L2 norm should be **~3–15** (matches pre-fix ~15.5). Norms of 27,000–45,000 are 2,000× too high. Loss is bouncing instead of monotonically decreasing. **The bias gradients are now garbage, not correct.**

### What I got wrong — the staging-buffer indexing

Going back to PyTorch's `staging_memory_offset` ([Reduce.cuh:175-181](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Reduce.cuh#L175)):

```cpp
C10_DEVICE int staging_memory_offset(int cta2) const {
    int offset = cta2 + blockIdx.x * gridDim.y;
    if (!should_block_x_reduce()) {                        // ← this branch
        offset = threadIdx.x + offset * blockDim.x;        //   I missed
    }
    return offset;
}
```

There are **two cases**:

1. **`block_x_reduce` ACTIVE** — only `threadIdx.x == 0` is a leader → 1 slot per (CTA_y, CTA_x). Buffer size = `gridDim.x * gridDim.y`.
2. **`block_x_reduce` OFF** — every `threadIdx.x` is a leader for its own output column → **`blockDim.x` slots per (CTA_y, CTA_x)**. Buffer size = `gridDim.x * gridDim.y * blockDim.x`.

The bias-grad case (`OuterContiguous` path) hits **case 2**: `input_mult[BLOCK_X] = 0` because the outer path puts output stripe on `threadIdx.x` (via `output_mult[BX]`, not `input_mult[BX]`). So `should_block_x_reduce() == false`.

My port hardcoded case 1 only. That means:
- All 32 threads with `threadIdx.x ∈ [0, 32), threadIdx.y == 0` write to the **same slot** `blockIdx.y + blockIdx.x * gridDim.y`. They race; last writer wins.
- Buffer is **32× too small** — most output columns have no slot at all.
- Last CTA reads back garbage (slot belongs to whichever thread wrote last) and combines it `cpo` times into a single output column — overcounting by `~cpo × random_winner` magnitude.

That's why norms exploded to ~thousands × normal: each output's "combined" value is some other column's partial, summed `cpo` times, with garbage data overlap.

### The proper fix

Replace my naive slot computation with PyTorch's two-branch version. Two changes needed:

**(a) kernel — use the correct slot index in both store and read-back:**

```cpp
// helper inside the kernel
auto staging_offset = [&](int cta2) -> index_t {
    index_t off = (index_t)cta2 + (index_t)blockIdx.x * (index_t)gridDim.y;
    if (!config.should_block_x_reduce())
        off = (index_t)threadIdx.x + off * (index_t)blockDim.x;
    return off;
};
```

Use `staging_offset(blockIdx.y)` for the store, and have each thread in the last CTA read `staging_offset(i)` for `i ∈ [0, cpo)` so each thread reconstructs its own column.

**(b) host — size the buffer correctly:**

```cpp
size_t slots = (size_t)g.x * (size_t)g.y;
if (!config.should_block_x_reduce())
    slots *= (size_t)config.block_width;     // blockDim.x extra slots
size_t cta_bytes = sizeof(arg_t) * slots;
```

**(c) last-CTA combine — restructure so each thread combines ITS OWN column's `cpo` partials**, not one thread summing them all:

```cpp
if (s_is_last) {
    __threadfence();
    // Every thread that was a leader on the store path participates.
    // Each one rebuilds its own output column from its own cpo partials.
    bool participates = !config.should_block_x_reduce() || (threadIdx.x == 0);
    participates    &= (!config.should_block_y_reduce() || (threadIdx.y == 0));
    if (participates) {
        arg_t combined = op.ops.identity();
        for (int i = 0; i < config.ctas_per_output; i++) {
            combined = op.ops.combine(combined, cta_buf[staging_offset(i)]);
        }
        // write dst at THIS thread's output_idx (already computed above)
        auto final_val = op.ops.project(combined);
        op.dst[output_idx] = static_cast<out_scalar_t>(final_val);
    }
}
```

(For the `OuterContiguous` bias-grad case: 32 threads in the last CTA each rebuild their own output column from `cpo=18` partials — one column per thread, fully parallel.)

Still bigger than pre-fix (which was undercounting), but in the right ballpark, not in the tens of thousands.

## The three loss kernels — what each one does, why all three are needed

Pulled from the activations_LN_modified log:

| Kernel | Instances | Avg | Total | Called from |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats` | **320** | 4.21 ms | 1.35 s | training forward |
| `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec` | **40** | 4.20 ms | 168 ms | validation forward |
| `sparseCENormalize_from_stats` | **320** | 10.31 ms | 3.30 s | training backward |

### Why 3, not 2 — and it's NOT a mistake

The dispatch logic at [LossOps.cpp:295-323](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/autograd/operations/LossOps.cpp#L295) picks **one** of the two forward kernels per call, based on this gate:

```cpp
const bool will_save_stats = (GradMode::is_enabled() && logits.requires_grad());
...
if (will_save_stats) fwd_save_stats(...);   // <- _save_stats kernel
else                 fwd_no_stats(...);     // <- plain _vec kernel
```

Training forward → `will_save_stats = true` → **_save_stats kernel**, writes `saved_max[B]` and `saved_sum[B]` for backward to reuse.

Validation forward → runs under `autograd::NoGradGuard` → `GradMode::is_enabled() == false` → `will_save_stats = false` → **plain _vec kernel**, no stat allocation, no wasted writes.

Count math (perfectly consistent):
- **320 train forwards** = 32 micro-batches × 10 training steps. ✓
- **40 val forwards** = 20 `val_loss_steps` × 2 val evaluations (step 0 + step 9, because `MAX_STEPS-1=9 % VAL_FREQ==0` is wrong — actually the trainer hits val at `step % VAL_FREQ == 0 || step == MAX_STEPS - 1`, which is step 0 and step 9 here). ✓
- **320 backward calls** = one Normalize per train forward. ✓

So 3 kernels firing is **correct by design**. Each serves a distinct purpose.

### What's actually noteworthy here — vs. peak

This is the comparison with output.md (peak) for the same three:

| Kernel | Peak (output.md) | Current | Delta |
|---|---|---|---|
| `_save_stats` | **360** / 3.76 ms avg | 320 / 4.21 ms avg | -40 calls, +0.45 ms avg |
| plain `_vec` | **absent** | 40 / 4.20 ms avg | +40 calls |
| `Normalize_from_stats` | 320 / **8.18 ms** avg / 2.62 s | 320 / **10.31 ms** avg / 3.30 s | same count, **+2.13 ms avg = +680 ms** |

Two observations:

**Improvement vs peak (good news):** The peak run had **360 `_save_stats`** calls — meaning peak was running validation forwards through the `_save_stats` kernel too, **wasting work writing stats that never get used** (no backward in val). Current BluTrain is **smarter** — 320 save_stats for training only, 40 plain for val. The plain kernel is slightly cheaper than save_stats (4.20 vs 4.21 ms — within noise but no wasted write). This part is properly optimized.

**Regression vs peak (note worth flagging):** `Normalize_from_stats` per-call: **8.18 ms → 10.31 ms (+26%)**. Same instance count (320). The kernel code is byte-identical to peak — verified earlier. So this slowdown is **not from any sparse-CE modification**. It's a per-call measurement difference between the two builds. Causes are environmental:
- Different CUDA driver / cuBLAS version between the two systems.
- Different shared-memory bank conflict pattern from neighboring kernel state.
- Different L2 cache occupancy / DRAM contention.

This regression existed in rem_hellswag too (same 10.31 ms avg). It pre-dated all our edits.

### Where this lives in the sprint doc

[Sprint doc §13](master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/docs/SPRINT_OPTIMIZATIONS_FULL_RECORD.md) says the change was eliminating the **reduce kernel** that recomputed max/sum during backward — that's the `sparseCEReduce_kernel_optimized` you'd expect to see if the optimization weren't in place. It's **not in the log at all**, which means the optimization is fully live: backward uses the **saved** stats (from forward) instead of recomputing them.

Memory traffic per training step:
- **Before the sprint:** 3 × 3.3 GB logit reads (fwd, reduce, normalize) = ~9.9 GB
- **Now (verified in the log):** 2 × 3.3 GB (fwd save_stats, normalize_from_stats) = **6.6 GB**. Saved one entire logit pass.

So:
- **3 kernels is correct.** Not a mistake.
- The autograd path picks the right kernel based on grad-mode.
- The expensive `sparseCEReduce_kernel` is gone (sprint §13 fully delivered).
- The per-call slowdown in `Normalize_from_stats` is environmental, not from our sparse-CE code — it exists across all BluTrain runs identically.

If you want to chase the 26% per-call regression in `Normalize_from_stats`, the next step would be Nsight-Compute on that specific kernel (DRAM-bound? Bank conflicts? Occupancy?). But it's the same kernel SASS as peak — likely diminishing returns until we know what changed in the build/driver environment.

### What this costs vs peak — and why peak doesn't have it

In the peak run (`output.md`), there is **no `broadcast_scale_kernel`** row at all. That means in master_gau_latest_1, item 17a was actually live — `cublasLtMatmul` with `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BIAS` absorbed every Linear+bias forward, no separate broadcast kernel needed.

Somewhere between master_gau_latest_1 and BluTrain, that integration got dropped — possibly during the BluBridge-BLAS / cuBLAS backend split, since the `BLAS=cuBLAS` build path doesn't seem to include the LtMatmul layer. Now BluTrain falls back to the old path: GEMM → standalone `broadcast_scale_kernel` for bias-add.

### Cost breakdown of the 17a/17d gap (BluTrain vs peak)

For 22,848 launches × 10 steps = 2,285 launches/step on the bias add:
- GPU time: 91 µs avg × 22,848 = **2.09 s** total across 10 steps = **~209 ms/step**
- CPU `cudaLaunchKernel` overhead at ~32 µs per launch = **730 ms** across 10 steps = **~73 ms/step**
- **Total: ~280 ms/step** — this is roughly **half** of the 580 ms/step gap to peak

So 17a is the biggest single lever for closing the gap to peak. 17b is smaller (only 12 MLPs × 32 microbatches × 10 = 3,840 forward calls; saves ~50–100 ms/step). 17c is the "go beyond PyTorch" item — PyTorch eager doesn't fuse DGELU_BGRAD either, so it's a nice-to-have, not parity.

### What fixing each entails

**17a — cuBLASLt BIAS in Linear forward.** Most impactful. Pattern from `FusedLinearGelu_sm89.cu` (which already does this for GELU+BIAS):

```cpp
cublasLtMatmulDesc_t op_desc;
cublasLtMatmulDescCreate(&op_desc, CUBLAS_COMPUTE_32F, CUDA_R_32F);
cublasLtMatmulDescSetAttribute(op_desc, CUBLASLT_MATMUL_DESC_EPILOGUE,
                               &CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BIAS, sizeof(int));
cublasLtMatmulDescSetAttribute(op_desc, CUBLASLT_MATMUL_DESC_BIAS_POINTER,
                               &bias_ptr, sizeof(void*));
cublasLtMatmul(...);
```

~30 lines of plumbing in `GenMatmul.cu`'s addmm dispatch + initialisation of a per-device `cublasLtHandle_t` (which is already done in `FusedLinearGelu_sm89.cu` at line 60 — can reuse).

**17b — uncomment and verify.** Two lines in `gpt2_fmha_ddp.cpp`:
```cpp
h = autograd::fused_bias_gelu(h, fc_up.bias);   // line 293/307
```
But: the autograd path must be wired through `fused_bias_gelu_forward` → `fused_bias_gelu_cuda` → the cuBLASLt helper. That chain exists in code already (we verified). However, the autograd op currently calls our **standalone non-LT** kernel (the fp32-only `fused_bias_gelu_kernel` we just templated for fp16/bf16 earlier this session). It does NOT route to the cuBLASLt epilogue path. So uncommenting alone wouldn't trigger the cuBLASLt fast path. Need to:
1. Add a host-side dispatch in `fused_bias_gelu_forward` that picks `FusedLinearGelu_sm89.cu`'s `cublasLt*` helper when input is suitable (sm_89, fp32/fp16/bf16, K * N >= threshold).
2. Uncomment the two trainer lines.

**17c — proper port.** PyTorch eager doesn't have this. CUTLASS does. Out of scope unless we want to go beyond parity.

### Recommendation

If you want to chase the steady-state gap to peak, do **17a first**. It's the biggest single hit and the cleanest port (existing cuBLASLt code in `FusedLinearGelu_sm89.cu` shows the recipe). 17b is half-done, easy followup. 17c is icing.
