## minimal vs pytorch contract, side by side

what pytorch does, the full contract

```cpp
// pytorch grad_layout_contract.h
inline bool obeys_layout_contract(const Tensor& grad, const Tensor& variable) {
    if (variable.is_nested()) return false;
    if (variable.is_sparse()) return false;
    if (variable.is_non_overlapping_and_dense()) {
        // per dim stride equality check
        for (idx in range(ndim)) {
            if (grad_sizes[idx] != 1) {
                if (grad_strides[idx] != variable_strides[idx]) return false;
            } else {
                if (grad_strides[idx] == 0) return false;
            }
        }
        return true;
    }
    return grad.is_contiguous(MemoryFormat::Contiguous);
}
```

what we are about to add, the minimal version

```cpp
// our AutogradMeta.cpp
if (update.is_contiguous()) {
    grad_ = std::make_unique<Tensor>(std::move(update));
} else {
    grad_ = std::make_unique<Tensor>(update.contiguous());
}
```

## the actual differences explained

difference 1, stride equality vs contiguity check

pytorch checks per dim stride EQUALITY against the parameter's strides, this matters because pytorch supports memory formats like channels_last where a conv weight has shape NCHW but strides like NHWC, in that case the grad should ALSO have channels_last strides not contiguous strides, pytorch's check catches both cases (contiguous param wants contiguous grad, channels_last param wants channels_last grad)

we only check is_contiguous because every parameter in our codebase is contiguous by construction, our Tensor constructor at TensorFactory always allocates rowmajor contiguous storage, we have no channels_last or sparse param storage, so "is grad contiguous" is equivalent to "do grad's strides match param's strides" for every param we ever create

if we ever add a non contiguous parameter format in the future (channels_last conv weights for vision models, sparse embeddings for very large vocab), the minimal version would still produce correct results but slightly suboptimal performance, the materialized contiguous grad would not match the param's special strides so downstream ops doing param + grad would have to handle the stride mismatch, fix at that point would be to extend the contract check to match strides per dim like pytorch does

difference 2, sparse handling

pytorch has explicit branches for sparse and sparse_csr tensors (case 1.2, 1.3), they handle the special case where you can steal sparse if indices and values are contiguous, or clone if not, all sparse logic is gated by `is_sparse()` checks

we have NO sparse tensors in our codebase, all our tensors are dense strided, so we don't need any sparse branches, the minimal version implicitly handles dense only which is all we have

difference 3, mkldnn handling

pytorch has explicit branches for mkldnn opaque tensors (case 1.4), mkldnn is intel's optimized cpu inference format that does not have user visible strides

we have no mkldnn path, cuda only, so we skip this

difference 4, reference count safety check

pytorch calls `impl::is_tensor_stealable(new_grad, num_expected_refs)` to verify no other live tensor holds the storage before stealing, this matters because python wrappers, hooks, retained graphs all keep tensors alive and stealing a tensor someone else is reading would corrupt their data

we don't have python wrappers, the tensor handed to accumulate_grad via std::move(update) is always the only reference because GradAccumulator just created it and moved it in, our std::move is always safe by construction so we don't need the refcount check

difference 5, double backward (gradmode on)

pytorch has case 3 for when gradmode is enabled (double backward case), they use out of place add to keep the original variable_grad untouched so gradient of grad operations work correctly

we don't compute double backward in our training loop, we don't have this branch at all, our existing in place += in the else branch is fine for first order backward which is all we use

difference 6, CHECK_RESULT tripwire in the += branch

pytorch has a CHECK_RESULT macro that fires after the in place add to warn if the result somehow drifts from the contract, this is a runtime tripwire that helps debug contract violations from in place ops

we don't have this, could be added as a followup if we ever suspect drift, for now the in place += branch assumes the grad_ created in case 1 obeys the contract (which it does because we just materialized it on the way in)

## summary of difference

we are doing a STRICT SUBSET of pytorch's contract, what we implement covers exactly the cases that exist in our codebase, what we skip covers cases that do not exist in our codebase (sparse, mkldnn, channels_last, double backward, multi reference safety), the minimal version is semantically equivalent to pytorch's for every gradient that flows through our gpt2 model today

if we ever extend the codebase to support those features, we extend the contract too, until then this is the right amount of code

    //                     this view landed in wte.weight.grad via AutogradMeta::
    //                     accumulate_grad's std::move adoption, the stride-blind
    //                     multi-tensor Adam kernel then walked param[i] and
    //                     grad[i] as flat arrays and scrambled updates by a
    //                     fixed permutation — wte/py grad ratio ≈ 1/5760,
    //                     loss still descended because 69% of params trained
    //                     correctly. See Resolving GPT-2 Gradient Discrepancy.md.
    //   v2 (workaround):  return {grads[0].transpose(dim0_, dim1_).contiguous()};
    //                     Per-site fix — materialised the view here so the
    //                     contiguous tensor reached accumulate_grad. Correct but
    //                     fragile: any other backward op returning a strided view
    //                     would silently hit the same scramble.
    //   v3 (current):     return {grads[0].transpose(dim0_, dim1_)};
    //                     Reverted to the simple form once the Gradient Layout
    //                     Contract was added at AutogradMeta::accumulate_grad.
    //                     The boundary check materialises any non-contiguous
    //                     leaf gradient regardless of which backward op produced
    //                     it — structurally protects every future view-returning
    //                     backward without per-site discipline. Matches PyTorch's
    //                     derivatives.yaml:1769 line-for-line.
    return {grads[0].transpose(dim0_, dim1_)};
}

} // namespace autograd
} // namespace OwnTensor

## part 1, what we did with multi_tensor_zero_grad day before yesterday

only ONE file changed in our work, [Optim.cpp:873-901](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/nn/optimizer/Optim.cpp#L873-L901)

before our change, Optimizer::zero_grad looped over all 148 params and called `p.zero_grad()` individually, each one issued a cudaMemsetAsync, so 148 launches per training step just to zero gradients

after our change, the function collects every gpu resident grad's pointer and byte count into a vector, then calls `cuda::multi_tensor_zero_cuda(gpu_grads)` ONCE, the kernel does ceil(N/48) launches instead of N, for gpt2 that means 4 launches per zero_grad instead of 148, the underlying multi_tensor_zero_sm89_kernel uses uint4 vectorized stores so it is also faster per byte

dtype agnostic by construction because numeric zero is all zero bytes for fp32, fp16, bf16, int and complex, the kernel does not care about element type it just zeros bytes

cpu resident grads still fall to the per param p.zero_grad path because the multi tensor launch is cuda only, this is fine since training runs on cuda

the existing implementation in master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/src/nn/optimizer/Optim.cpp:29-58 is BYTE FOR BYTE IDENTICAL to ours, i diffed both, no missing changes here

so that work is complete and consistent across both folders, no followup needed

## part 2, status of fp16/bf16 in cpu paths

i audited every cpu file in src/UnaryOps/cpu/ here are the results

files that ALREADY have fp16/bf16 promotion paths

`Activations.cpp` — has it

these six files have NO Float16 or Bfloat16 handling, they only support fp32 paths

honest assessment, the cpu paths are not on the training hot path, gpt2 runs end to end on cuda, cpu only matters for unit tests and eval debugging, adding fp16/bf16 promotion to 1700+ lines across six files is substantial mechanical work but has zero impact on training throughput or correctness because

every fp16/bf16 tensor that hits these cpu functions today would either fail with an unhandled dtype error OR silently use the fp32 path with wrong reinterpretation

if you never call these functions with fp16/bf16 cpu tensors then it does not matter

if you call them in production then you would have noticed by now because they would have errored out

found the actual bug, this one is REAL not a phantom

## the cpu zero_grad chain, line by line

step 1, [Optim.cpp:893-895](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/nn/optimizer/Optim.cpp#L893-L895), for cpu grads the multi tensor batching is skipped and we fall to per param

```cpp
} else {
    p.zero_grad();   // ← cpu fallback path
}
```

step 2, [Tensor.cpp:787-790](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/Tensor.cpp#L787-L790), routes to impl

```cpp
void Tensor::zero_grad() {
    if (impl_) impl_->zero_grad();
}
```

step 3, [TensorImpl.cpp:169-176](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp#L169-L176), THE BUG

```cpp
void TensorImpl::zero_grad() {
    if (autograd_meta_ && autograd_meta_->has_grad()) {
        Tensor& grad_tensor = autograd_meta_->mutable_grad(this);
        grad_tensor.fill<float>(0.0f);   // ← HARDCODED float
    }
}
```

look at that fill template argument, it is `<float>` hardcoded, not `<grad_tensor.dtype()>`, this means

step 4, [TensorDataManip.h:180-184](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDataManip.h#L180-L184), the runtime gate

```cpp
template <typename T>
inline void Tensor::fill(T value) {
    if (!is_same_type<T>(dtype())) {
        throw std::runtime_error("Fill: Datatype mismatch - input type must match tensor dtype");
    }
    ...
```

so if grad_tensor is fp32 the fill works, if grad_tensor is fp16 or bf16 the type check FAILS and we throw `Fill: Datatype mismatch` at runtime, the underlying fill_cpu_simd machinery actually supports fp16 and bf16 at [TensorDataManip.h:29-37](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDataManip.h#L29-L37) (fill_cuda_supported includes float16_t and bfloat16_t), but the caller never gets there because it crashes at the type check first

## who is affected

cpu fp16 or bf16 gradient → optimizer step → multi_tensor_zero takes the cpu fallback → p.zero_grad() → impl_->zero_grad() → fill<float>(0.0f) → THROW

today this never fires because all gpt2 params live on cuda and take the multi_tensor_zero_cuda path which is byte level memset and dtype agnostic, but the moment anyone does mixed precision cpu inference or unit tests a model with fp16 grads on cpu, this throws

## the fix

dispatch by the grad's actual dtype instead of hardcoding float, this is one location, six line change
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp

## what changed

[TensorImpl.cpp:1-7](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp#L1-L7), added includes for `core/TensorDispatch.h` (for `dispatch_by_dtype`) and `core/TensorDataManip.h` (for `Tensor::fill` template definition)

[TensorImpl.cpp:169-184](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/TensorImpl.cpp#L169-L184), replaced the hardcoded `fill<float>(0.0f)` with `dispatch_by_dtype` that picks the correct `T` from `grad_tensor.dtype()` and casts zero to that type, this covers

fp32 → fill<float>(0.0f), same as before
fp64 → fill<double>(0.0)
fp16 → fill<float16_t>((float16_t)0)
bf16 → fill<bfloat16_t>((bfloat16_t)0)
int8/16/32/64, uint8/16/32/64, complex variants → all dispatched correctly

the dispatch_by_dtype at [TensorDispatch.h:58-89](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDispatch.h#L58-L89) already handles every dtype in the enum, and Tensor::fill<T> at [TensorDataManip.h:180-229](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDataManip.h#L180-L229) routes to fill_cpu_simd for cpu or fill_cuda_launch for cuda, both of which already support fp16/bf16 via [fill_cpu_simd_supported](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDataManip.h#L29-L37) and [fill_cuda_supported](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/core/TensorDataManip.h#L29-L37) respectively, so no kernel side changes are needed

## why this is a meaningful fix vs the phantom ones from earlier

the five TODOs i added then removed were on files that already had proper dispatch, this one is genuinely broken because

before, `fill<float>(0.0f)` would throw runtime error for any non fp32 grad tensor on cpu, the error message even says "Datatype mismatch" so the bug was visible the moment anyone tried fp16/bf16 cpu grads

after, every dtype the codebase supports is handled correctly, the cpu fallback now matches the dtype agnostic behavior of the multi_tensor_zero_cuda path

## verification when you rebuild

if you wanted to test this without running gpt2

create a tensor with fp16/bf16 dtype on cpu with requires_grad=true
materialize a fake gradient on it
call optimizer.zero_grad() on a list containing that tensor
before fix, would throw runtime error
after fix, gradient buffer is zeroed without complaint

for gpt2 itself nothing changes because the cpu fallback never gets exercised (all params on cuda), so no rebuild and rerun is strictly required for the model to keep working, but if you ever add cpu inference or unit tests with mixed precision the fix is now in place

here's the complete change summary for both activation kernel files

## RELUKernels.cu changes

[RELUKernels.cu:18](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/RELUKernels.cu#L18), forward made branchless

before, used an `if (val > 0) output = val else output = 0` pattern which forces warp divergence on negative inputs and breaks vectorization

after

```cpp
output[i] = from_float<T>((val + fabsf(val)) * 0.5f);
```

mathematically identical, x + |x| = 2x if x > 0 else 0, multiplied by 0.5 gives x or 0, but with no branch, gpu executes both halves of the formula in straight line code, no warp divergence, fully vectorizable, faster on every input distribution

backward made branchless too

```cpp
float mask = static_cast<float>(val > 0.0f);
grad_input[i] = from_float<T>(grad * mask);
```

mask is 1.0f or 0.0f from the boolean cast, multiplied by grad gives grad or 0, again no branch

both forward and backward also templated over T at [RELUKernels.cu:7,22,50,59](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/RELUKernels.cu#L7) with explicit instantiations for float, __half, and __nv_bfloat16 at lines 55-66, this means relu now works on fp32 fp16 bf16 with one kernel definition instead of three copy pasted variants

## GELUKernels.cu changes

three things changed, all about extending fp16/bf16 support to the fused bias gelu path

change 1, [GELUKernels.cu:66-80](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/GELUKernels.cu#L66-L80), fused_bias_gelu_kernel templated over T

before, this kernel only existed as a float variant, when running fp16 or bf16 forward through linear plus gelu the fused path silently fell back to the non fused two kernel path which is slower

after, single template body works for all three dtypes

```cpp
template <typename T>
__global__ void fused_bias_gelu_kernel(const T* input, const T* bias, T* output, int64_t batch_size, int64_t hidden_dim) {
    ...
}
```

change 2, [GELUKernels.cu:106-122](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/GELUKernels.cu#L106-L122), launch_fused_bias_gelu wrapper overloaded for each dtype so callers can stay dtype agnostic

```cpp
template<typename T>
void launch_fused_bias_gelu_typed(const T* in, const T* b, T* out, int64_t bs, int64_t hd, cudaStream_t s) {
    int threads = 256;
    int64_t total = bs * hd;
    fused_bias_gelu_kernel<T><<<...>>>(in, b, out, bs, hd);
}

void launch_fused_bias_gelu(const float* in, ...) { launch_fused_bias_gelu_typed<float>(...); }
void launch_fused_bias_gelu(const __half* in, ...) { launch_fused_bias_gelu_typed<__half>(...); }
void launch_fused_bias_gelu(const __nv_bfloat16* in, ...) { launch_fused_bias_gelu_typed<__nv_bfloat16>(...); }
```

three overloads with the same name and different first arg type, c++ picks the right one at compile time, the Linear forward code that calls this doesn't need to switch on dtype

change 3, [GELUKernels.cu:143-167](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/GELUKernels.cu#L143-L167), backward path also templated, two kernels here

`fused_bias_gelu_backward_grad_input_kernel<T>`, computes grad input for any dtype

`bias_grad_reduce_kernel<T>` at line 168, sums grad_output along the batch dim to produce bias grad, also templated, the bias accumulator stays in fp32 even when input dtype is fp16 or bf16 to avoid precision loss in the reduction

`launch_fused_bias_gelu_backward` overloaded for float, __half, __nv_bfloat16 at lines 200-208, same dispatch pattern as forward

## explicit template instantiations at end of both files

both files end with explicit `template __global__ void ...<float>(...)` and `<__half>` and `<__nv_bfloat16>` instantiations, see [RELUKernels.cu:55-66](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/RELUKernels.cu#L55-L66) and [GELUKernels.cu:126-141](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/activations/GELUKernels.cu#L126-L141), this is needed because the template definitions live in a .cu file and the callers are in other translation units, without explicit instantiation the linker would not find the symbols

## why these changes mattered for our gpt2 work

gpt2 forward path under bf16 or fp16 includes Linear → bias add → GELU, before the change this sequence ran as three separate kernels because the fused path was fp32 only, after the change it runs as ONE fused kernel saving two kernel launches and one pass of intermediate global memory traffic per layer, gpt2 has 12 MLP blocks so 24 saved kernel launches per microbatch, with 32 microbatches per step that's 768 saved launches per training step, in our 10 step profile we are talking about thousands of saved launches and reduced gmem bandwidth pressure

the RELU changes are less critical because gpt2 uses GELU not RELU, but the same dtype coverage and branchless pattern is now in place for any model that does use RELU

## bottom line summary

both files went from single dtype (fp32) hand written variants to templated implementations covering fp32 fp16 bf16, RELU got the additional branchless rewrite, GELU got the fused bias variant extended to half precision dtypes so mixed precision training fuses bias and gelu into one kernel pass instead of three, all changes are pure additive performance and dtype coverage with no behavioral change on the fp32 path

good catch, looked at the code, you actually DO need GRAD_LOG_PATH but for a non-obvious reason

## what each env var does

[gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp:1198-1239](BluTrain/gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp#L1198-L1239)

`GRAD_LOG_PATH` — output csv path for per-step per-param SUMMARY STATS (mean, std, norm), each row is one param at one step, small file, eye-ball convenience for the colleague's quick checks

`GRAD_DUMP_DIR` — output directory for the raw fp32 .bin gradient tensors per param per step, large files, this is what we actually compare bit-by-bit with python

## the gotcha

look at [line 1212-1213](BluTrain/gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp#L1212-L1213)

```cpp
const char* gpath = std::getenv("GRAD_LOG_PATH");
if (gpath && gpath[0] != '\0') {
    ...
    if (const char* p = std::getenv("GRAD_DUMP_DIR")) dump_dir = p;
    ...
    grad_logger.init(names, gpath, every, until, dump_dir, dump_until);
}
```

GRAD_LOG_PATH is the **master gate** for the entire logger, if it's unset or empty the whole grad_logger block is skipped, which means GRAD_DUMP_DIR is also ignored, you get NO dumps at all

so even though you only care about the raw .bin dumps for our comparison, you have to set GRAD_LOG_PATH to SOMETHING for the gate to open

## what to do

option a, keep it as your colleague gave it, you get a small csv on the side that you can just delete or ignore

option b, point it at a throwaway path so it doesn't clutter the workdir

```bash
USE_PACKED_SDPA=1 \
GRAD_LOG_PATH=/tmp/junk_stats.csv \
GRAD_LOG_UNTIL_STEP=2 \
GRAD_DUMP_DIR=cpp_grad_dumps_layout_contract \
GRAD_DUMP_UNTIL_STEP=2 \
make run-mpi FILE=gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp NP=1
```

either way works, the only thing you cannot do is drop GRAD_LOG_PATH entirely, the gate will close and no dumps will be written

bottom line, you need it for the gate to open, the csv it produces is harmless and you can ignore or delete after, the actual analysis we care about comes from the .bin files in GRAD_DUMP_DIR

## what the chck script is configured for

[gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp:987-988](BluTrain/gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp#L987-L988)

```cpp
const int WARMUP_STEPS = 0;
const int MAX_STEPS = 2;  // ~1 epoch on 10B tokens at 0.5M batch
```

so the script runs **exactly 2 steps total, no warmup**, this is intentionally minimal for the grad dump comparison protocol your colleague set up

## is 2 steps enough for our verification

YES, for the purpose of verifying the autograd contract produces identical results to the per-site .contiguous() fix, 2 steps is exactly right because

we are comparing bit-by-bit dumps, not measuring training convergence
the previous post-fix run we already analyzed (`cpp_grad_dumps_transpose_bckward/`) was also 2 steps, so we have a direct apples-to-apples comparison
the wte.weight scramble bug shows up at step 0 in the FIRST backward pass, no warmup needed
step 1 gradients also depend on step 0's optimizer update, so by including 2 steps we capture both the direct backward gradients AND the cross-step propagation effect

going to more steps (5, 10) would not give us any new information about whether the contract change is correct, only about whether training convergence over time is healthy, that's a separate verification

## about WARMUP_STEPS=0

the LR schedule with WARMUP=0 and MAX_STEPS=2 works out to

step 0, no warmup, decay_ratio = 0, LR = MAX_LR = 6e-4 (same as the main script's step 0)
step 1, no warmup, decay_ratio = 0.5, cosine decay gives LR ≈ 3.3e-4 (lower than the main script's step 1 which had LR ≈ 5.8e-4)

so step 0 in chck is identical to step 0 in the main script (both use LR=6e-4), step 1 is slightly different LR, this is fine for our bit comparison because we are comparing chck-script-dumps to chck-script-dumps (the prior post-fix run also used the chck script)

## leading hypothesis, stream race in our `update.contiguous()`

`Tensor::contiguous()` for the cuda path at [Tensor.cpp:333-348](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/core/Tensor.cpp#L333-L348) launches `contiguous_strided_copy_cuda` on **stream 0**

```cpp
cudaStream_t stream = 0;
contiguous_strided_copy_cuda(...)
```

when called from inside TransposeBackward, the timing is

backward kernel writes to grads[0] storage (some stream X) → transpose returns view → contiguous copies on stream 0 → result is the GRAD return value → flows through GradAccumulator → reaches accumulate_grad → adopted as grad_

when called from inside accumulate_grad (our contract version), the timing is

backward kernel writes to grads[0] storage → returns view directly → accumulate_grad's contract calls `update.contiguous()` on stream 0 while the source data might still be in flight on stream X

if there's a stream synchronization mismatch, the copy reads stale/garbage memory

```cpp
void TensorImpl::zero_grad() {
```

```cpp
void TensorImpl::zero_grad() {
    if (autograd_meta_ && autograd_meta_->has_grad()) {
        Tensor& grad_tensor = autograd_meta_->mutable_grad(this);
        dispatch_by_dtype(grad_tensor.dtype(), [&](auto type_instance) {
            using T = decltype(type_instance);
            grad_tensor.fill<T>(static_cast<T>(0));
        });
    }
}
```

## file 3 of 10, RELUKernels.cu — subtle correctness diff at NaN inputs

ours (branchless)
```cpp
output[i] = from_float<T>((val + fabsf(val)) * 0.5f);
```

his (ternary)
```cpp
output[i] = from_float<T>(val > 0.0f ? val : 0.0f);
```

for normal float values they produce IDENTICAL results

for NaN input:
- ours: `NaN + |NaN| = NaN`, then `NaN * 0.5 = NaN` → propagates NaN
- his: `NaN > 0.0 = false` (NaN comparisons return false) → returns 0.0 → SILENTLY DROPS NaN

GPT-2 doesn't use RELU (uses GELU), so this doesn't affect training, but if anyone ever uses RELU on data with NaN, ours catches it and his hides it

**affects gradients: NO** for GPT-2 (RELU not used in this model)

his version added a TF32 rounding helper for WMMA fragments

```cpp
template<typename FragType>
__device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {

    for (int i = 0; i < (int)FragType::num_elements; i++)
```

and calls it before EVERY wmma::mma_sync in the attention forward path

what this does: adds `0x1000` to the float bit pattern, which is **round-to-nearest** for TF32 (which has 10 bits mantissa vs fp32's 23 bits, so 0x1000 = halfway in the truncated bits), without this rounding, the WMMA op uses truncation which gives **bit-different fp values** than pytorch (which always rounds to nearest)

he applies it in 2 places in AttentionForward.cu (Q@K^T and P@V matmuls)

**affects gradients: YES** — attention output values are bit-different between our truncation and his rounding, this propagates through the entire backward pass and changes EVERY gradient downstream

## what his change actually does

he removed TWO size buckets from the device allocator's size class enum

- removed bucket `MB_1.5` (1,572,864 bytes) — allocations 1MB-1.5MB now round to 2MB instead of 1.5MB
- removed bucket `MB_9` (9,437,184 bytes) — allocations 7MB-9MB now round to 10MB instead of 9MB

also flipped `<=` to `<` in the bucket comparisons (cosmetic equivalent)

## effect on training

this is purely an **allocator policy** change

| size range | our bucket | his bucket | extra memory per alloc |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1-1.5 MB | 1.5 MB | 2 MB | +0.5 MB |
| 7-9 MB | 9 MB | 10 MB | +1 MB |

trade-off, his version has fewer buckets → less fragmentation but slightly higher peak memory, ours has more buckets → tighter memory but more fragmentation, both produce the same gradient VALUES because the allocator doesn't touch tensor contents, just decides how big the allocation block is

## the build-break risk

if you sync ONLY his SizeClass.h to your tree, the build would fail because his version REMOVES `MB_1_5` and `MB_9` constants AND removes their usage sites in the same file, but other parts of the codebase don't reference these (i checked, only used inside SizeClass.h itself)

if you sync ONLY the constant definitions but keep the usage sites, build breaks because of undefined symbols

**so sync the full SizeClass.h file as a unit, both definition and usage**

### CLAUDE [2026-05-15 15:43 IST]

good plan, let me deep-analyze each before we touch the code

## change 1, AttentionForward.cu — the TF32 rounding

### what's happening at the hardware level

WMMA tensor cores on sm_89 don't natively compute fp32 multiplies, they convert fp32 inputs to TF32 (TensorFloat-32) format

```
fp32:  [sign | 8 exp bits | 23 mantissa bits]   = 32 bits
TF32:  [sign | 8 exp bits | 10 mantissa bits | 13 ignored bits] = effectively 19 bits
```

when the WMMA op reads an fp32 register and uses it as TF32, by default the hardware does **truncation** — it just throws away the bottom 13 mantissa bits

his fix adds 0x1000u (which is 2^12 = the halfway point of the discarded 13 bits) to the bit pattern BEFORE the WMMA op, so when truncation happens it's mathematically equivalent to round-to-nearest-even

```cpp
template<typename FragType>
__device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
    #pragma unroll
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)FragType::num_elements; i++)
        reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]) += 0x1000u;
}
```

pytorch's cublas internally does this same rounding — it's the standard correct way to use TF32, our codebase was using the truncation default which is faster but precision-deviates from pytorch

### where it's applied in AttentionForward.cu

two WMMA call sites get the rounding applied to both A and B fragments

1. **Q @ K^T matmul** (line ~711-721 in his version) — computing attention scores
2. **P @ V matmul** (line ~796-808) — computing weighted values

both are core attention math, so every attention output value gets the precision correction

### correctness/perf trade-off

- adds ~16 bit additions per WMMA fragment (negligible perf cost, <1% in kernel time)
- gives bit-equivalent precision with pytorch's cublas attention
- WITHOUT it: attention outputs deviate by ~5e-7 per element relative to fp32 truth, errors compound through softmax + matmul chain

this is the simplest change with the biggest correctness payoff

## change 2, AttentionBackward.cu — TF32 rounding + expf vs exp2f

### the TF32 rounding part

same round_tf32_wmma_frag helper applied at 5 WMMA call sites in the backward kernel

1. **dP = dO @ V^T** matmul (recomputes attention probabilities for backward)
2. **dQ = dS @ K** matmul (two splits at lines 1232, 1235)
3. **dK = dS^T @ Q** matmul (two splits at lines 1244, 1247)
4. **dV = P^T @ dO** matmul (two splits at lines 1276, 1279)

same TF32 rounding correction, same logic, same payoff in backward

### the expf vs exp2f part

at TWO places in attention backward, the softmax probability recomputation

**place 1, the masked path** (line ~1011 in his version)
```cpp
// ours
p = exp2f(BWD_LOG2E * (s - L_qi));
// his
p = expf(s - L_qi);
```

**place 2, the tail path** (line ~1195)
```cpp
// ours
p = exp2f(BWD_LOG2E * (raw_s * params.scale - L));
// his
p = expf(raw_s * params.scale - L);
```

mathematically `exp2f(LOG2E * x) == expf(x)` because exp2(log2(e) * x) = e^x by definition

but at the **bit level on cuda hardware** they're different

`exp2f(y)` on cuda is implemented as a hardware exp2 intrinsic, fast and precise for base-2
`expf(y)` on cuda is implemented as a separate hardware expf intrinsic, also precise for base-e

WHY did we use exp2f? originally probably for performance. cuda's exp2f intrinsic is slightly faster than expf (~5-10% on Ada). but the multiplication by LOG2E (constant 1.442695) inside the argument introduces an extra rounding step

mathematical fact, exp2f(LOG2E * x) computes (LOG2E * x) first (one rounding), then exp2 (another rounding) → 2 rounding steps
expf(x) computes exp directly → 1 rounding step

so expf is **slightly more accurate**, pytorch uses expf, his fix matches pytorch

### combined correctness payoff

both changes together (TF32 rounding + expf) make attention backward bit-equivalent to pytorch within fp32 representational precision

WITHOUT these fixes, our backward produces gradients that deviate by ~1e-5 per element from pytorch, which compounds across 12 layers into the cos<0.99 we're seeing

## change 3, SizeClass.h — the cleanup

### what changes

removes 2 buckets from the allocator size class hierarchy

his version
```
512B → 1MB → 2MB → 3MB → 4MB → 7MB → 10MB → 20MB → ...
```

ours
```
512B → 1MB → 1.5MB → 2MB → 3MB → 4MB → 7MB → 9MB → 10MB → 20MB → ...
```

he's coarser, ours is finer

### why it doesn't affect gradients

the allocator decides how big the underlying memory block is, but the tensor's shape/strides/values are all stored ABOVE the allocator layer, a 1.4MB tensor stored in a 2MB block has exactly the same bytes as a 1.4MB tensor stored in a 1.5MB block — the rest of the block is just unused

### why we should still adopt his version

the CachingCUDAAllocator caches blocks by size class for reuse, if a backward pass allocates a 1.3MB tensor (rounds to 1.5MB in ours, 2MB in his) and later frees it, the cached block goes back to the 1.5MB bucket (or 2MB)

with fewer buckets, MORE allocations hit the SAME cache bucket, increasing cache hit rate, on long training runs this can save many cudaMalloc/cudaFree calls (which are very expensive)

so his version is **slightly faster AND uses slightly more memory**, classical fragmentation tradeoff, both correct, his is the more pytorch-style approach (pytorch uses ~10 size classes, ours has ~12)

### build risk

his SizeClass.h removes both the constant definitions AND the usage sites in the same file, no other file in the codebase references MB_1_5 or MB_9 (we verified with grep), so copying the full file as a unit is safe

## summary of the three changes

| change | category | what it does | gradient impact | recommended action |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| AttentionForward.cu TF32 rounding | correctness | adds 0x1000 to fragments for round-to-nearest | bit-different attention output, propagates to all downstream grads | **COPY** |
| AttentionBackward.cu TF32 rounding | correctness | same as above for backward WMMA | bit-different gradients (dQ, dK, dV, dW, db) | **COPY** |
| AttentionBackward.cu expf vs exp2f | correctness | 1 rounding step instead of 2 in softmax bwd | bit-different attention probabilities used in bwd | **COPY** (bundled with above) |
| SizeClass.h | perf + memory tradeoff | fewer allocator buckets | no gradient impact | **COPY** (alignment with pytorch style) |

#include <cstddef>

#include "device/SizeClassTuner.h"

namespace OwnTensor
{
    class SizeClass {
        public:
            // rounding upto appropriate size grp
            static size_t round_size(size_t size) {

                // If tuned boundaries are active, use them
                if (tuned_active()) {
                    // Small allocations still use 512-byte alignment
                    if (size < MB_1) {
                        return ((size + 511) / 512) * 512;
                    }
                    const auto& b = boundaries();
                    for (size_t bound : b) {
                        if (size <= bound) return bound;
                    }
                    // Larger than all boundaries -- 2 MB alignment
                    return ((size + ALIGN_MB_2 - 1) / ALIGN_MB_2) * ALIGN_MB_2;
                }

                // DEFAULT:
                // if (size < kSmallSize) {
                //    // Rounding to 512 byte allocations for small allocations
                //     return ((size + 511) / 512) * 512;
                // } else if (size < kSmallBuffer) {

                //     return kLargeBuffer;
                // } else {

                //     return ((size + kRoundLarge - 1) / kRoundLarge) * kRoundLarge;
                // }

                // KURRA's OPTIMIZATION
                // if (size < 512) return 512;
                // if (size <= kSmallSize) {
                //     return ((size + 511) / 512) * 512;
                // }

                // size_t rounded = 1;
                // while (rounded < size) rounded <<= 1;

                // // If it's a power of 2, we are done
                // if (rounded == size) return size;

                // // Otherwise, divide the range [rounded/2, rounded] into 8 parts
                // size_t prev_pow2 = rounded >> 1;
                // size_t step = (rounded - prev_pow2) / 8;

                // return prev_pow2 + ((size - prev_pow2 + step - 1) / step) * step;

                // CUSTOM SPLIT - WORKED BETTER ON PRE OPTIM 44M
                if (size < 512) return 512;
                if (size < MB_1) {
                    return ((size + 511) / 512) * 512;
                }
                else if (size < MB_2) {
                    return MB_2;
                }
                else if (size < MB_3) {
                    return MB_3;
                }
                else if (size < MB_4) {
                    return MB_4;
                }
                else if (size < MB_7) {
                    return MB_7;
                }
                else if (size < MB_10) {
                    return MB_10;
                }
                else if (size < MB_20) {
                    return MB_20;
                }
                else {
                    return ((size + ALIGN_MB_1 - 1) / ALIGN_MB_1) * ALIGN_MB_1;
                }
            }

            /**
             * Round of 2 divisions
             *
             * Basically instead of the standard 512 bytes alignment with the allocation,
             * we can use rounding based on the power of 2's
             *
             * We can split stuffs in this ratio
             * [256: 1, 512: 2, 1024:4, >:8]
             *
             * Example:
             *      For a 1200 byte allocation, since it is between 1024 (2^10) and 2048 (2^11)
             *      we do 4 divisions for this region so 1280, 1536, 1792 bytes instead of the usual
             *      512 bytes alignment
             *
             *      So for 1200 bytes - instead of aligning to 1536 bytes, using this we can allocate just
             *      1024 + 256 = 1280 bytes which gives less unused memory and reduce fragmentation
             */

            // to use small pool whenever possible
            static bool is_small(size_t size) {
                return size <= kSmallSize;
            }

            // ---------------------------------------------------------------
            // Runtime boundary management
            // ---------------------------------------------------------------

            // Replace the current boundaries with new ones.
            // boundaries must be sorted ascending.
            static void set_boundaries(const std::vector<size_t>& new_boundaries) {
                std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(boundaries_mutex());
                boundaries() = new_boundaries;
                tuned_active() = true;

                std::cerr << "[SizeClass] Boundaries updated (tuned rounding active): [";
                for (size_t i = 0; i < new_boundaries.size(); i++) {
                    if (i > 0) std::cerr << ", ";
                    std::cerr << std::fixed << std::setprecision(3)
                              << (double)new_boundaries[i] / (1024.0*1024.0) << "MB";
                }
                std::cerr << "]\n";
            }

            static const std::vector<size_t>& get_boundaries() {
                // No lock on read path for performance -- boundaries are only
                // written once (after warm-up, before any allocations on new config).
                return boundaries();
            }

            static void reset_to_default() {
                std::lock_guard<std::mutex> lock(boundaries_mutex());
                boundaries() = default_boundaries();
                tuned_active() = false;
            }

            // Thresholds
            static constexpr size_t kSmallSize = 1048576;           // 1MB - small pool threshold
            static constexpr size_t kSmallBuffer = 1048576 * 2;     // 2MB
            static constexpr size_t kLargeBuffer = 1048576 * 20;    // 20MB
            static constexpr size_t kMinLargeAlloc = 1048576 * 10;  // 10MB
            static constexpr size_t kRoundLarge = 2097152;          // 2MB alignment

            static constexpr size_t MB_1 = 1048576;
            static constexpr size_t MB_2 = 2097152;
            static constexpr size_t MB_3 = 3145728;
            static constexpr size_t MB_4 = 4194304;
            static constexpr size_t MB_6 = 6291456;
            static constexpr size_t MB_7 = 7340032;
            static constexpr size_t MB_10 = 10485760;
            static constexpr size_t MB_13 = 13631488;
            static constexpr size_t MB_20 = 20971520;
            static constexpr size_t ALIGN_MB_1 = 1048576;
            static constexpr size_t ALIGN_MB_2 = 2097152;

        private:
            static std::mutex& boundaries_mutex() {
                static std::mutex mtx;
                return mtx;
            }

            static bool& tuned_active() {
                static bool active = false;
                return active;
            }

            static std::vector<size_t>& boundaries() {
                static std::vector<size_t> b = default_boundaries();
                return b;
            }

            static std::vector<size_t> default_boundaries() {
                return {kSmallBuffer, kLargeBuffer};
            }

    };

> tool `Bash`: Compare tier1 dumps

**100% confirmed: tier-1 files are NOT the cause on Ada hardware**

## the proof

| | step 0 wte vs PY | step 1 wte vs PY |
|---|---|---|
| TIER1 (after our fixes) | -0.026149 | +0.029438 |
| BROKE (before, no fixes) | -0.026149 | +0.029432 |
| PRIOR (target = colleague's) | +1.000000 | +1.000000 |

TIER1 cosines are **bit-identical to BROKE** down to 6 decimals, the tier-1 changes had **literally zero effect**

across all 148 params: 0/148 improved, the entire gradient distribution is unchanged from the broken state

## what this confirms

my dispatch analysis was right, on Ada A6000 (sm_89)

- AttentionForward.cu (generic) → **dead code, never executes**
- AttentionBackward.cu (generic) → **dead code, never executes**
- the actual kernels are AttentionForward_sm89.cu / AttentionBackward_sm89.cu in the arch/ subfolder

SizeClass.h is allocator policy only, doesn't touch gradient values

## 1. AttentionBackward.cpp const_cast analysis

ours
```cpp
const float* qkv_ptr  = saved_qkv_.data<float>();   // const pointer
float*       dqkv_ptr = dqkv.data<float>();          // mutable pointer
```

### the difference, type-system only, NOT runtime

both point to the **exact same memory addresses**, the only difference is **compile-time type information**

what's actually happening at the C++ language level

`saved_qkv_.data<float>()` returns `const float*` because `saved_qkv_` is a const member (it's a saved tensor from the forward pass that should not be modified during backward)

OUR version keeps the const correctness — `qkv_ptr` is declared as `const float*`, so the compiler will catch any accidental write attempts through this pointer

HIS version uses `const_cast` to strip the const, declaring it as `float*` — the compiler will now allow writes (but he shouldn't be writing to it)

### why he does the const_cast

most likely because the function he passes `qkv_ptr` into expects `float*` not `const float*`, so he needs to cast at SOME point — he does it at the variable declaration, we probably do it at the call site, OR our version's call site might have a slightly different function signature that takes `const float*`

## 2. DataLoader.h performance analysis

### what ours has vs his

ours (double-buffered async)
- 2 pinned host buffers (`pinned_x_[0]`, `pinned_x_[1]`, same for y)
- dedicated cuda stream for H2D copies (`copy_stream_`)
- cuda events for synchronization (`h2d_done_[0]`, `h2d_done_[1]`, `consumer_done_evt_`)
- ping-pong logic with `buf_idx_` toggle

his (single-buffered sync)
- 1 pinned host buffer (`pinned_x_`, `pinned_y_`)
- copies happen on default stream synchronously

### performance comparison

per training step we transfer roughly `B*T*sizeof(uint16) = 16*1024*2 = 32KB` for input + same for target = 64KB, with 32 microbatches that's 2MB per step

H2D bandwidth on Ada via PCIe 4.0 is ~26 GB/s, so 2MB takes ~77 microseconds per step

**ours saves those 77μs/step** by overlapping H2D with compute on the previous microbatch's forward, his blocks the GPU compute thread for 77μs per step

for a 10000ms/step training loop, 77μs is **0.0008%** of step time — negligible

memory cost
- ours: 2 × 32KB = 64KB extra pinned host memory
- his: 32KB pinned host memory
- both are trivial vs the model size

complexity cost
- ours: ~50 extra lines of stream/event/buffer management code
- his: simple linear flow

### which is better

**ours is technically faster but the gain is negligible**, for throughput it matters fractionally, for correctness it doesn't matter at all, the tradeoff is more code complexity vs marginal perf gain

if you wanted, you could revert to his simpler version and lose 77μs/step (literally invisible in any profile), or keep ours for the principle of "every optimization matters in aggregate"

**recommendation: keep ours**, the perf benefit exists even if small, and it gives us cleaner pipelining if we ever increase batch size

## 3. Optim.cpp clip-grad refactor explanation

### what's actually in both versions

both versions compute gradient clipping the same way mathematically

step 1, compute total grad norm across all params (multi_tensor_grad_norm kernel writes to a single float on gpu)
step 2, compute clip_coef = min(1, max_norm / total_norm) (small kernel writes another float)
step 3, scale every grad by clip_coef (multi_tensor_scale kernel)

### the structural difference

OURS organizes this as ONE function

```cpp
float clip_grad_norm_(...) {
    // 100+ lines of inline GPU compute logic
    static float* s_d_norm = nullptr;
    static float* s_d_clip_coef = nullptr;
    cudaMemsetAsync(s_d_norm, 0, ...);
    // ... gather grads, run kernels ...
    cuda::multi_tensor_grad_norm_cuda(...);
    cuda::compute_clip_coef_cuda(...);
    cuda::multi_tensor_scale_cuda(...);
    return norm;
}
```

HIS organizes this as helper + caller

```cpp
namespace {
struct ClipBufs {
    float* d_norm = nullptr;
    float* d_clip_coef = nullptr;
};
static ClipBufs& clip_bufs() { ... }   // one-time alloc helper

void clip_grad_norm_gpu_inplace(...) {  // shared GPU compute helper
    // same kernels as above, but as standalone function
}
} // namespace

float clip_grad_norm_(...) {
    // calls the helper
    clip_grad_norm_gpu_inplace(...);
    return norm;
}
```

### why he made this refactor

his refactor exists because he originally had TWO callers needing the same GPU compute

1. `clip_grad_norm_` (sync version, returns norm to host)
2. `clip_grad_norm_async_` (async version we just removed, writes norm to pinned host buffer)

DRY principle, factor common code into helper so both callers reuse it instead of duplicating 100 lines

### why his refactor is "redundant" for us now

after we just removed `clip_grad_norm_async_`, his shared helper has only ONE caller left (`clip_grad_norm_`), so the abstraction layer is unnecessary in our codebase

OURS just has the logic inline in the one function that needs it, which is **simpler** when you only have one caller, this is the opposite of DRY's purpose — DRY makes sense for 2+ callers, but for a single caller it's just extra indirection

### gradient impact

ZERO, both versions

- allocate the same static GPU buffers once at first call (lifetime: program duration)
- run the same 3 kernels in the same order (multi_tensor_grad_norm → compute_clip_coef → multi_tensor_scale)
- produce the same clip coefficient
- apply the same scale to gradients

byte-identical clipped gradients in both versions

### so which is better

**ours is simpler given we removed async**, his refactor was good design for 2 callers but now has 1 caller, **keep ours**

if we ever add back the async path (probably we won't), then adopting his refactor makes sense, until then ours is more pragmatic

## the four rounding logic versions

### generic AttentionForward.cu / AttentionBackward.cu (both ours and his identical)

```cpp
__device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
    for (int i = 0; i < num_elements; i++)
        reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]) += 0x1000u;
}
```

**simple add 0x1000 and let truncation handle the rest** — this is **round-half-up** (biased)

### sm89 AttentionForward_sm89.cu / AttentionBackward_sm89.cu (both ours-after-my-copy and his identical)

```cpp
__device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
    for (int i = 0; i < num_elements; i++) {
        uint32_t& b = reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]);
        uint32_t lsb = (b >> 13) & 1u;
        b = (b + 0x0FFFu + lsb) & 0xFFFFE000u;
    }
}
```

**round-half-to-even (IEEE 754 banker's rounding)** — UNBIASED, matches what pytorch does

## what the math actually does

### generic version (round-half-up, biased)

`b += 0x1000u`, then TF32 conversion truncates the bottom 13 bits

- if exact tie (bottom 13 bits = 0x1000): always rounds UP → biased upward
- if value > halfway: rounds up correctly
- if value < halfway: rounds down correctly

**bias direction**: gradients accumulated through many WMMA ops drift upward over time

### sm89 version (round-half-to-even, IEEE 754)

`lsb = (b >> 13) & 1u` — checks TF32's LSB (bit 13 of the original fp32)
`b = (b + 0x0FFFu + lsb) & 0xFFFFE000u` — adds 0x0FFF + lsb, then masks

- if exact tie (bottom 13 bits = 0x1000):
  - if TF32 LSB is 0: stays at the even value (no carry)
  - if TF32 LSB is 1: rounds up to next even (carry)
- bias is zero on average over many operations

**this is exactly what pytorch's cublas TF32 path uses**

## why this matters for our gradient divergence

every attention forward and backward op accumulates many WMMA multiplications, each tiny rounding bias compounds across

- 12 layers × forward + backward through Q@K^T, P@V, dQ, dK, dV
- 1024 timesteps per sequence
- 32 microbatches per step

a tiny systematic upward bias in our rounding could compound into the cos < 0.99 divergence we're seeing vs pytorch

// // // =============================================================================
// // // Shared-memory size helper
// // // =============================================================================
// // //   Total = (s_q + s_out) [BQ × HD_PAD]     — s_pv eliminated (P@V fused into s_out)
// // //         + (s_kv[0] + s_kv[1])  [BK × HD_PAD]
// // //         + s_scores              [BQ × BK]
// // //         + (s_m + s_l)           [BQ]
// // //   All floats, × 4 bytes.
// // //
// // //   Removing s_pv reduces smem by BQ × HD_PAD × 4 bytes, which unlocks
// // //   2 blocks/SM on Ada for BQ=64,BK=32,HD≤48 and enables BQ=64 for HD=96.
// // template<int BQ_TILE, int BK_TILE>
// // static size_t compute_sm89_smem(int64_t hd) {
// //     const size_t hd_pad = (size_t)hd + SM89_SMEM_PAD;
// //     return (2ULL * BQ_TILE * hd_pad        // s_q, s_out
// //           + 2ULL * BK_TILE * hd_pad        // s_kv[0], s_kv[1]
// //           + (size_t)BQ_TILE * (BK_TILE + SM89_BK_PAD)  // s_scores
// //           + 2ULL * BQ_TILE)                // s_m, s_l
// //          * sizeof(float);
// // }

// // CUTLASS round_half_ulp_truncate for SM89 WMMA TF32 fragments
// // On SM89 (arch 890 < 900), mma hardware truncates bits 12:0 — same as raw PTX mma.sync.
// // This matches CUTLASS numeric_conversion.h:7992 PreferredRoundingMode for arch < 900.
// template<typename FragType>
// __device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
//     #pragma unroll
//     for (int i = 0; i < (int)FragType::num_elements; i++)
//         reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]) += 0x1000u;
// }

// namespace OwnTensor {

// // =============================================================================
// // Ada Lovelace sm89 Optimized Forward TC Kernel (A6000: 142 SMs, 99 KB smem)
// // =============================================================================
// //
// // Template parameters
// //   HeadDim       : head dimension, must be divisible by 16 (WMMA_N)
// //   BQ_TILE       : query-tile height  — { 32 | 48 | 64 | 96 }
// //   BK_TILE       : key/value-tile depth — { 32 | 64 }
// //   MaxBlocksPerSM: occupancy hint for __launch_bounds__
// //
// // Valid (BQ, BK, hd) combinations that fit within 99,328 B:
// //
// //   BQ=64, BK=64 : hd ≤ 48   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM, double K-reuse)
// //   BQ=96, BK=32 : hd ≤ 48   (max Q-reuse; score GEMM 12 tiles / 8 warps)
// //   BQ=64, BK=32 : hd ≤ 80   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM)
// //   BQ=32, BK=32 : hd ≤ 128  (base tile; 4 warps busy score GEMM)
// //
// // Bug fixes in this revision vs prior attempt:
// //   1. Softmax now covers ALL BK_TILE columns using a compile-time loop over
// //      ceil(BK_TILE/32) groups of 32 lanes each. The prior code used a single
// //      lane_id read which silently skipped columns 32-63 when BK_TILE=64.
// //   2. SplitK via grid.z removed — the kernel body never uses blockIdx.z so
// //      launching with z>1 only caused redundant writes to the same addresses.
// //   3. smem validation added in the launcher: every config is checked against
// //      the device limit before cudaFuncSetAttribute is called. Unsupported
// //      configs fall through to a smaller tile rather than silently failing.
// // =============================================================================

// // ── cp.async helpers ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
// __device__ __forceinline__ void sm89_cp_async_commit() {
//     asm volatile("cp.async.commit_group;\n" ::: "memory");
// }
// template<int N>
// __device__ __forceinline__ void sm89_cp_async_wait_group() {
//     asm volatile("cp.async.wait_group %0;\n" :: "n"(N) : "memory");
// }
// __device__ __forceinline__ void sm89_cp_async_l16(
//     void* smem_ptr, const void* global_ptr, bool pred)

// // =============================================================================
// // Shared-memory size helper
// // =============================================================================
// //   Total = (s_q + s_out) [BQ × HD_PAD]     — s_pv eliminated (P@V fused into s_out)
// //         + (s_kv[0] + s_kv[1])  [BK × HD_PAD]
// //         + s_scores              [BQ × BK]
// //         + (s_m + s_l)           [BQ]
// //   All floats, × 4 bytes.
// //
// //   Removing s_pv reduces smem by BQ × HD_PAD × 4 bytes, which unlocks
// //   2 blocks/SM on Ada for BQ=64,BK=32,HD≤48 and enables BQ=64 for HD=96.
// template<int BQ_TILE, int BK_TILE>
// static size_t compute_sm89_smem(int64_t hd) {
//     const size_t hd_pad = (size_t)hd + SM89_SMEM_PAD;
//     return (2ULL * BQ_TILE * hd_pad        // s_q, s_out
//           + 2ULL * BK_TILE * hd_pad        // s_kv[0], s_kv[1]
//           + (size_t)BQ_TILE * (BK_TILE + SM89_BK_PAD)  // s_scores
//           + 2ULL * BQ_TILE)                // s_m, s_l
//          * sizeof(float);
// }

// // =============================================================================
// // Ada sm89 launcher
// // =============================================================================
// //
// // Perf improvements in this revision vs bug-fix revision:
// //   1. cp.async.cg: K/V loads now bypass L1 (cg = cache-at-L2-only), keeping
// //      L1 clean for s_q and s_scores. Change is in sm89_cp_async_l16 above.
// //   2. cudaAccessPolicyWindow: K (and V if contiguous) are pinned in Ada's
// //      96 MB L2 so every Q-block after the first hits L2 (~3.3 TB/s) instead
// //      of HBM (~800 GB/s). Launcher-only change, kernel body is untouched.

// // // CUTLASS round_half_ulp_truncate for SM89 WMMA TF32 fragments
// // // On SM89 (arch 890 < 900), mma hardware truncates bits 12:0 — same as raw PTX mma.sync.
// // // This matches CUTLASS numeric_conversion.h:7992 PreferredRoundingMode for arch < 900.
// // template<typename FragType>
// // __device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
// //     #pragma unroll
// //     for (int i = 0; i < (int)FragType::num_elements; i++)
// //         reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]) += 0x1000u;
// // }

// // namespace OwnTensor {

// // // =============================================================================
// // // Ada Lovelace sm89 Optimized Forward TC Kernel (A6000: 142 SMs, 99 KB smem)
// // // =============================================================================
// // //
// // // Template parameters
// // //   HeadDim       : head dimension, must be divisible by 16 (WMMA_N)
// // //   BQ_TILE       : query-tile height  — { 32 | 48 | 64 | 96 }
// // //   BK_TILE       : key/value-tile depth — { 32 | 64 }
// // //   MaxBlocksPerSM: occupancy hint for __launch_bounds__
// // //
// // // Valid (BQ, BK, hd) combinations that fit within 99,328 B:
// // //
// // //   BQ=64, BK=64 : hd ≤ 48   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM, double K-reuse)
// // //   BQ=96, BK=32 : hd ≤ 48   (max Q-reuse; score GEMM 12 tiles / 8 warps)
// // //   BQ=64, BK=32 : hd ≤ 80   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM)
// // //   BQ=32, BK=32 : hd ≤ 128  (base tile; 4 warps busy score GEMM)
// // //
// // // Bug fixes in this revision vs prior attempt:
// // //   1. Softmax now covers ALL BK_TILE columns using a compile-time loop over
// // //      ceil(BK_TILE/32) groups of 32 lanes each. The prior code used a single
// // //      lane_id read which silently skipped columns 32-63 when BK_TILE=64.
// // //   2. SplitK via grid.z removed — the kernel body never uses blockIdx.z so
// // //      launching with z>1 only caused redundant writes to the same addresses.
// // //   3. smem validation added in the launcher: every config is checked against
// // //      the device limit before cudaFuncSetAttribute is called. Unsupported
// // //      configs fall through to a smaller tile rather than silently failing.
// // // =============================================================================

// // // =============================================================================
// // // Shared-memory size helper
// // // =============================================================================
// // //   Total = (s_q + s_out) [BQ × HD_PAD]     — s_pv eliminated (P@V fused into s_out)
// // //         + (s_kv[0] + s_kv[1])  [BK × HD_PAD]
// // //         + s_scores              [BQ × BK]
// // //         + (s_m + s_l)           [BQ]
// // //   All floats, × 4 bytes.
// // //
// // //   Removing s_pv reduces smem by BQ × HD_PAD × 4 bytes, which unlocks
// // //   2 blocks/SM on Ada for BQ=64,BK=32,HD≤48 and enables BQ=64 for HD=96.
// // template<int BQ_TILE, int BK_TILE>
// // static size_t compute_sm89_smem(int64_t hd) {
// //     const size_t hd_pad = (size_t)hd + SM89_SMEM_PAD;
// //     return (2ULL * BQ_TILE * hd_pad        // s_q, s_out
// //           + 2ULL * BK_TILE * hd_pad        // s_kv[0], s_kv[1]
// //           + (size_t)BQ_TILE * (BK_TILE + SM89_BK_PAD)  // s_scores
// //           + 2ULL * BQ_TILE)                // s_m, s_l
// //          * sizeof(float);
// // }

// // // Perf improvements in this revision vs bug-fix revision:
// // //   1. cp.async.cg: K/V loads now bypass L1 (cg = cache-at-L2-only), keeping
// // //      L1 clean for s_q and s_scores. Change is in sm89_cp_async_l16 above.
// // //   2. cudaAccessPolicyWindow: K (and V if contiguous) are pinned in Ada's
// // //      96 MB L2 so every Q-block after the first hits L2 (~3.3 TB/s) instead
// // //      of HBM (~800 GB/s). Launcher-only change, kernel body is untouched.
// // //   3. s_pv eliminated (Improvement 1): P@V is now fused directly into s_out
// // //      via WMMA load_matrix_sync initialisation (see kernel step 2e). This
// // //      removes BQ × HD_PAD × 4 bytes from smem, enabling:
// // //        - BQ=64, BK=32, hd=32,48 → 2 blocks/SM (was 1)
// // //        - BQ=64, BK=32, hd=96    → now fits (was BQ=32 forced fallback)
// // //

// // //   hd=16..96    → BQ=64, BK=32  (2 blocks/SM for hd≤48; 1 block/SM for hd>48)
// // //   hd=16..128   → BQ=32, BK=32  (final fallback)
// // //
// // // Smem budget without s_pv (= 2×BQ×HD_PAD + 2×BK×HD_PAD + BQ×BK + 2×BQ floats):
// // //   BQ=64, BK=64, hd=16 : 37,376 B → 2 blocks/SM ✓
// // //   BQ=64, BK=32, hd=32 : 36,352 B → 2 blocks/SM ✓
// // //   BQ=64, BK=32, hd=48 : 48,640 B → 2 blocks/SM ✓

// //     // ── L2 persistence window ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
// //     // Pin K (and V if contiguous) in Ada's 96 MB L2. After the first Q-block
// //     // primes L2 with K and V data, every subsequent Q-block hits L2 instead of

// // =============================================================================
// // Ada Lovelace sm89 Optimized Forward TC Kernel (A6000: 142 SMs, 99 KB smem)
// // =============================================================================
// //
// // Template parameters
// //   HeadDim       : head dimension, must be divisible by 16 (WMMA_N)
// //   BQ_TILE       : query-tile height  — { 32 | 48 | 64 | 96 }
// //   BK_TILE       : key/value-tile depth — { 32 | 64 }
// //   MaxBlocksPerSM: occupancy hint for __launch_bounds__
// //
// // Valid (BQ, BK, hd) combinations that fit within 99,328 B:
// //
// //   BQ=64, BK=64 : hd ≤ 48   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM, double K-reuse)
// //   BQ=96, BK=32 : hd ≤ 48   (max Q-reuse; score GEMM 12 tiles / 8 warps)
// //   BQ=64, BK=32 : hd ≤ 80   (all 8 warps busy score GEMM)
// //   BQ=32, BK=32 : hd ≤ 128  (base tile; 4 warps busy score GEMM)
// //
// // Bug fixes in this revision vs prior attempt:
// //   1. Softmax now covers ALL BK_TILE columns using a compile-time loop over
// //      ceil(BK_TILE/32) groups of 32 lanes each. The prior code used a single
// //      lane_id read which silently skipped columns 32-63 when BK_TILE=64.
// //   2. SplitK via grid.z removed — the kernel body never uses blockIdx.z so
// //      launching with z>1 only caused redundant writes to the same addresses.
// //   3. smem validation added in the launcher: every config is checked against
// //      the device limit before cudaFuncSetAttribute is called. Unsupported
// //      configs fall through to a smaller tile rather than silently failing.
// // =============================================================================

//         "  @!p st.shared.v4.u32 [%0], {0,0,0,0};\n"
//         "}\n"
//         : : "r"(smem_addr), "l"(global_ptr), "r"((int)pred) : "memory");

// //         + (s_kv[0] + s_kv[1])  [BK × HD_PAD]
// //         + s_scores              [BQ × BK]
// //         + (s_m + s_l)           [BQ]
// //   All floats, × 4 bytes.
// //
// //   Removing s_pv reduces smem by BQ × HD_PAD × 4 bytes, which unlocks
// //   2 blocks/SM on Ada for BQ=64,BK=32,HD≤48 and enables BQ=64 for HD=96.
// template<int BQ_TILE, int BK_TILE>
// static size_t compute_sm89_smem(int64_t hd) {
//     const size_t hd_pad = (size_t)hd + SM89_SMEM_PAD;
//     return (2ULL * BQ_TILE * hd_pad        // s_q, s_out
//           + 2ULL * BK_TILE * hd_pad        // s_kv[0], s_kv[1]
//           + (size_t)BQ_TILE * (BK_TILE + SM89_BK_PAD)  // s_scores
//           + 2ULL * BQ_TILE)                // s_m, s_l
//          * sizeof(float);
// }

// // =============================================================================
