## Now the correction to my earlier fix proposal

I was wrong to propose Option 2 (revert `block_x_reduce` ON path). Bias-grad reductions are **OuterContiguous** layout (reducing `[B*T, N]` over the outer `B*T` dim, output is contig along inner `N`). For OuterContiguous, `should_block_x_reduce()` returns **FALSE** — each lane `threadIdx.x` is independent (its own output column), so no cross-lane reduction.

So bias-grad hits the **`!block_x_reduce`** branch — exactly the branch the new code FIXED FOR CORRECTNESS. The old code in that branch was buggy: it staged only 1 slot per CTA but multiple lanes were leaders (each holding its own column's partial). Different lanes' partials would collide at the same slot → wrong sums.

**I can't just revert to the old `!block_x_reduce` path — it was numerically wrong.**

## Why the new (correct) code is genuinely slower

The bug fix has a real cost:

| | OLD (buggy but fast) | NEW (correct) |
|---|---|---|
| Staging buffer size when `!block_x_reduce` | `cpo × gridDim.x × 1` slots | `cpo × gridDim.x × blockDim.x` slots (**~16× more memory traffic**) |
| Stage write per CTA | 1 value | `blockDim.x` values (one per leader lane) |
| Last-CTA combine | 1 thread reads cpo values | All threads read `cpo / blockDim.y` values each, then `block_y_reduce` |
| `__syncthreads` in last CTA | 0 | 2-3 (inside `block_y_reduce`) |

The bigger staging buffer is **structurally required** for correctness — each lane is a separate output column, each needs its own slot. There's no algorithmic trick to fix this within the same staging-buffer design.

1. **Switch bias-grad to a dedicated fused kernel** — cuBLASLt's `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BGRADB` fuses the bias gradient directly into the matmul backward, avoiding the unified_reduce path entirely. 2. **Replace staging-buffer with atomicAdd accumulation in the !block_x_reduce path** — each CTA computes its column-partial sums and atomic-adds directly into the output buffer (one atomicAdd per output column per CTA). This trades global memory bandwidth for atomics. For `cpo ≈ 6-12` and `num_outputs ≈ 768-3072`, total atomics ~50K — easily handled by Ada A6000. Likely 50-70% recovery of the regression, with much simpler code.

3. **Use `OuterContiguous`-specialized kernel** — bypass the generic multi-CTA staging entirely and write a dedicated bias-grad kernel that handles the `[B*T, N] → [N]` pattern (sum over outer dim). This is essentially what cuBLASLt's `BGRADB` does internally. ~50 lines of CUDA.

## My recommendation

**Option 1** (cuBLASLt `EPILOGUE_BGRADB`) is the best long-term fix because it ALSO removes the need to do the matmul + bias-grad as two separate kernel launches. Single fused gemm-with-bias-grad-epilogue. That's a structural improvement, not just a perf patch.

But it requires understanding the cuBLASLt API and integrating into MatrixBackward — moderate engineering, maybe 2-3 hours.

**Option 2** (atomicAdd path in `!block_x_reduce` branch) is the quickest win — modify ~20 lines in `ReductionKernels.cuh`. Probably recovers 50-70% of the regression. Doesn't help with the deeper "2 kernels instead of 1" question.

### CLAUDE [2026-05-19 12:33 IST]

Yes, you nailed exactly what the bug was. Let me confirm precisely:

## The original race (old code in `!block_x_reduce` case)

```cpp
// OLD code, line 451 of master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/.../ReductionKernels.cuh:
bool is_leader = (!config.should_block_x_reduce() || threadIdx.x == 0) &&
                 (!config.should_block_y_reduce() || threadIdx.y == 0);

if (is_leader) {
    index_t slot = (index_t)blockIdx.y + (index_t)blockIdx.x * (index_t)gridDim.y;
    cta_buf[slot] = value;   // <-- BUG when !block_x_reduce
}
```

When `block_x_reduce` is OFF (the bias-grad case), the `is_leader` condition drops the `threadIdx.x == 0` requirement, so **all `blockDim.x` lanes at `threadIdx.y==0` are leaders**. Each lane holds the partial sum for ITS OWN output column (lane `tx` reduces column `tx + blockIdx.x*blockDim.x`).

But the staging slot is computed as `blockIdx.y + blockIdx.x*gridDim.y` — **the same slot for all lanes in the CTA**. So all `blockDim.x` lanes write `cta_buf[slot] = value` → **last write wins, all other lanes' partial sums are lost**.

You're right — it's a write race, not even a "compete" race, it's just `=` overwrite. Multiple lanes silently drop their data.

## Your fix idea — atomicAdd instead of staging

Yes, this works and is much simpler. Replace the staging-then-last-CTA-combine machinery with a direct atomicAdd into the final output. The current new-code approach (give each lane its own slot, then have last CTA gather and reduce) is one fix; your approach (atomicAdd at write time) is another, equally valid.

### Sketch

```cpp
// in the multi-CTA path, !block_x_reduce branch:
if (is_leader && output_idx < config.num_outputs) {
    auto projected = op.ops.project(value);
    atomicAdd(&op.dst[output_idx], static_cast<out_scalar_t>(projected));
}
// no staging buffer, no semaphores, no last-CTA detection, no block_y_reduce
```

**Required:** `op.dst` must be zero-initialized before the kernel launches. Currently the output tensor is allocated fresh via `Tensor::empty`, which is NOT zero-initialized. So you'd need to either:
- Switch to `Tensor::zeros` (one cudaMemset before the kernel, ~5 µs)
- Or have the FIRST CTA per output write (=) and subsequent ones atomicAdd — needs a "first" detection

The simpler path is the cudaMemset.

### Does this have problems? Yes, one — non-determinism

`atomicAdd` for float resolves in **non-deterministic order** across runs (depends on CTA scheduling, SM contention). Floating-point addition is non-associative, so the SAME inputs can produce sums differing by ~1 ULP across runs.

For most training workloads this is fine — pytorch's default training mode uses non-deterministic atomic-based reductions in many ops (e.g., scatter_add). But if you care about bit-exact reproducibility across runs, this would break it.

Our gradient parity check vs pytorch is already a soft check (cos > 0.99999), so ~1 ULP variance is invisible. The reduction-bug-fix doc mentioned the multi-CTA staging was modeled after pytorch's `ReduceOp::global_reduce` which uses staging for determinism — but that's an optimization pytorch made, not a hard requirement.

### Performance estimate

For bias-grad with `cpo ≈ 10`, `num_outputs ≈ 2304`:
- Staging approach: `cpo × blockDim.x × g.x × g.y` writes + reads = ~10×16×144 = ~23K writes + 23K reads + block_y_reduce sync overhead per launch
- Atomic approach: `cpo × num_output_cols_per_grid` atomicAdds = ~23K atomic ops, no staging buffer, no semaphores, no last-CTA detection

Atomic contention: `cpo = 10` atomics per output address → very low contention on Ada (which has fast atomic units). Should easily beat the staging path.

**Expected recovery:** likely 60-80% of the +1.8 s regression. Plus simpler code.

### Why pytorch doesn't do this

PyTorch values determinism in many ops. They go through the staging hoops to avoid atomicAdd. Our codebase doesn't have that constraint as a hard rule.

## My recommendation

Your atomicAdd idea is actually **cleaner** than the current new code AND faster. The tradeoff is non-determinism — but we already accept that in many places (e.g., the engine's grad-sum reordering at line 309 also has non-determinism if grad order varies).

### CLAUDE [2026-05-19 12:35 IST]

## Quick answer: no, the old code was NOT using atomic ops at all

Look at the OLD line ([master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/.../ReductionKernels.cuh:454](/home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh)):

```cpp
if (is_leader) {
    index_t slot = (index_t)blockIdx.y + (index_t)blockIdx.x * (index_t)gridDim.y;
    cta_buf[slot] = value;   // <-- PLAIN ASSIGNMENT, NOT ATOMIC
}
```

It's just `=` — a plain non-atomic store. When multiple lanes collide on the same slot, the hardware doesn't replace atomically, it's literally a **data race** — last-issued write happens to win at the memory address. Not `atomicExch`, not `atomicAdd`, nothing. Just an unsynchronized overwrite.

So "atomic replace" isn't accurate — it was an **un-synchronized overwrite race that produced wrong sums**.

## Would atomicAdd be faster than the current multi-CTA staging? Yes, by a lot

Cost-per-launch comparison for one bias-grad reduction (`cpo ≈ 10`, `num_outputs ≈ 2304`, `blockDim.x ≈ 16`):

| | Multi-CTA staging (current) | atomicAdd direct |
|---|---|---|
| Global stores | `cpo × num_outputs × blockDim.x ≈ 368K` (staging writes) + 2304 final | 0 staging + ~23K atomicAdds |
| Global loads | `cpo × num_outputs × blockDim.x ≈ 368K` (last-CTA gather) | 0 |
| `__threadfence` calls | 2 per CTA | 0 |
| `__syncthreads` in last CTA | 2-3 (block_y_reduce) | 0 |
| Semaphore atomicAdd | 1 per CTA | 0 |
| Pre-launch setup | cudaMemsetAsync semaphores (~5 µs) + scratch alloc | cudaMemsetAsync dst (~5 µs) |

**Total memory traffic: atomicAdd is ~16× less.**

### Atomic contention concern

People worry "atomicAdd serializes on contention". Let's quantify for our case:

- `cpo ≈ 10` CTAs are computing partials for the same output column → 10 atomicAdds to the same address
- On Ada A6000, fp32 atomicAdd to L2 is hardware-accelerated, ~1 cycle/op when uncontended, fully serialized when contended
- 10 serialized atomicAdds = ~10 cycles per output address × 2304 output columns running in parallel across SMs = trivially fast

For comparison, the staging path's last CTA reads `cpo × blockDim.x = 160` values from staging memory PER output column, then does `block_y_reduce`. That's much more work.

### Why pytorch picked staging anyway

Two reasons, neither hard for us:

1. **Determinism.** atomicAdd order varies across runs (depends on CTA scheduling, SM contention). FP add is non-associative, so the sum can differ by ~1 ULP between runs. PyTorch's deterministic mode requires bit-exact reproducibility — staging gives that.
2. **Generality.** atomicAdd has no built-in version for all reduction ops (e.g., no atomicMax for fp32 on older arches). Staging+last-CTA works for any reduction op (sum, max, min, prod). PyTorch's `unified_reduce` aims to be op-generic.

For OUR codebase:
- We don't have a deterministic-mode requirement (we accept ~1ULP non-determinism — already seen in step-1 loss differing by 2e-6 between runs)
- For bias-grad we only ever need SumOp, which has fast hardware fp32 atomicAdd

So the trade-off pytorch made for generality and determinism is **strictly cost** for our use case with no benefit. atomicAdd path is faster AND simpler.

## TL;DR

- OLD code: not atomic at all, just plain `=` overwrite race → wrong sums in `!block_x_reduce`
- Current NEW code: correct via staging-each-lane + parallel-combine + block-reduce → 2.5× slower than old per call (~+115 µs/call × 15,680 calls = +1.8 s)
- Your proposed atomicAdd: correct (because it accumulates instead of overwriting) AND ~16× less memory traffic than current staging AND no sync barriers. Likely 60-80% of the 1.8 s recoverable. Costs ~1 ULP non-determinism per reduction.

If you want me to apply the atomicAdd path for the `!block_x_reduce` branch (the only one that's actually slow), say go. I'd:

1. In `unified_reduce_kernel`, replace the staging machinery with direct `atomicAdd(&op.dst[output_idx], projected_value)` when `!block_x_reduce && should_global_reduce`
2. In `launch_reduce_kernel`, when taking this path: skip the staging-buffer alloc + semaphore alloc, but **add a `cudaMemsetAsync(op.dst, 0, ...)` before the kernel** so atomics accumulate into a clean zero
3. Keep the staging path for the `block_x_reduce ON` case (since it's not slow there)

About 30 lines of code, contained in `ReductionKernels.cuh`.

I have a full picture now. Comprehensive answer:

## Q1: Do we need both kernels (precompute_D + bwd_unified)?

**Yes — this is the canonical flash-attention backward decomposition.** Tri Dao's flash-attention paper (the standard fp16/bf16 mem-efficient attention) splits backward into:

```
D = rowsum(dO ⊙ O)         ← precompute_D kernel, one scalar per Q row, reused
dV = P.T @ dO
dP = dO @ V.T
dS = P * (dP - D)          ← uses precomputed D here
dQ = dS @ K
dK = dS.T @ Q
```

`D` is reused across every K-block iteration of the main loop. Computing it inline would mean **reading O and dO twice per (B,H,T) row** — once for D, once for the main loop. Computing it once in a small dedicated kernel is cheaper because:
- D is tiny (`T` floats per (B,H) head ≈ 1024 × 12 × 16 × 4 = 786 KB total → fits in L2)
- The main bwd_unified kernel doesn't need to spill registers on D's reduction state
- Allows tighter block scheduling for the main kernel

**PyTorch / xformers / flash-attn ALL do this.** Specifically:
- `xformers/components/attention/csrc/cuda/mem_eff_attention_backward.cu` has a `mem_efficient_attention_backward_kernel_delta` precompute (their name for D)
- `flash-attn` (Tri Dao's repo) has `flash_attn_bwd_dq_dk_dv_kernel` with a separate `_flash_attn_backward_preprocess_kernel` that computes the same D
- This is the standard pattern, not a quirk of our code

So: **structurally correct, NOT something to merge or remove.**

## Q2: Are these like LayerNorm's two kernels?

**Similar pattern, different reason.**

- **LayerNorm backward** splits into `ln_backward_input_kernel` (computes `dx` per row, can be parallel per row) and `ln_backward_gamma_beta_kernel` (reduces over the batch×T dim per channel, needs cross-row reduction). They're split because they have **different parallelization domains** — one is per-row, one is per-column.

- **Attention backward** splits because `D` is **a scalar per row that's REUSED** across the K-block loop. Different reason — not a parallelization mismatch, but a "compute-once, reuse-many" optimization.

So the patterns differ but both are correct standard approaches.

## Q3: Why slower in the new code — the actual deep diff

I extracted just the active kernel bodies and counted differences. Two distinct stories:

### `precompute_D_sm89` — byte-identical code, 23% slower

Confirmed: the kernel source is **identical between old and new** (I diffed `master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89/.../AttentionBackward_sm89.cu` line 26-78 vs `BluTrain/.../AttentionBackward_sm89.cu` line 1780-1830 — character-for-character match).

So the 23% slowdown is NOT from code. Possible causes (in order of likelihood):

1. **L2 / cache state at launch time differs** — the kernels that ran immediately BEFORE this one have changed (we now have 3xTF32-removed bwd_unified, different layout in scratch buffers, etc.), so the L2 hot/cold state when precompute_D launches is different.
2. **GPU clock / PM state** — persistent mode, clock throttling, thermal. On a shared cluster GPU, this can shift 10-20% run to run independent of code.
3. **Different physical memory addresses** for dO and O across runs (allocator state differs) → potentially different DRAM bank conflict patterns.

Min per-call of this kernel is similar in both runs; the AVERAGE went up. That's consistent with environmental variance, not code regression.

**Verdict: not a code issue. Leave alone.** If you want to confirm, run output.md's binary side-by-side on the same GPU at the same moment — would isolate code from environment.

### `mem_efficient_bwd_unified_kernel_exp12` — REAL code change, 7.4% slower

Found 5 active call sites in the NEW kernel that DON'T exist in the OLD:

```cpp
round_tf32_wmma_frag(a_frag); round_tf32_wmma_frag(b_frag);   // ← NEW
wmma::mma_sync(acc_frag, a_frag, b_frag, acc_frag);
```

This is the **IEEE 754 round-to-nearest-even (RNE) rounding fix**. Definition at [AttentionBackward_sm89.cu:1768](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/AttentionBackward_sm89.cu#L1768):

```cpp
template<typename FragType>
__device__ __forceinline__ void round_tf32_wmma_frag(FragType& frag) {
    #pragma unroll
    for (int i = 0; i < (int)FragType::num_elements; i++) {
        uint32_t& b = reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]);
        uint32_t lsb = (b >> 13) & 1u;
        b = (b + 0x0FFFu + lsb) & 0xFFFFE000u;
    }
}
```

**What it does:** Hardware WMMA TF32 on Ada **truncates the bottom 13 bits of the fp32 mantissa** (biased toward zero — the cuda PTX ISA says "the lower 13 bits are ignored, no rounding is performed"). This rounding helper applies IEEE 754 RNE before the MMA so the truncation matches the closest representable TF32 value.

**Why it exists in our code but not in `master_gau_latest_ada_6000_sm89`:**
- Old code used raw `wmma::mma_sync` — accepts hardware's biased truncation. **Faster but biased toward zero.** Gradient accuracy slightly worse.
- New code applies RNE rounding before MMA — **matches what cuBLAS/cutlass do internally** for `tensorop_s1688gemm` (the cutlass NT/TN gemms in your screenshot). PyTorch's TF32 gemm path also uses RNE. So OUR code now matches pytorch's numerical behavior.

**Cost:** Per call site, 2 × `round_tf32_wmma_frag` runs over ~16 fragment elements each → ~32 element-rounds + bitwise ops per MMA. 5 active MMA sites, each inside the kernel's tile loops → adds up to the +7.4% per kernel call.

**Trade-off:**
- Without rounding: 7.4% faster but biased gradient → divergence from pytorch grows step-by-step
- With rounding: 7.4% slower but RNE-correct, matches pytorch's behavior, gradient parity cos > 0.99999 stays stable

This is the SAME trade-off the cuBLAS team made internally — they apply RNE in their TF32 gemm. Our kernel is just doing the same thing the cuBLAS gemms above it do.

## Recommendation for these two kernels

**precompute_D:** environmental variance, no code fix needed. Move on.

**bwd_unified:** the rounding ops are the deliberate trade-off for gradient correctness. Three options if you want to recover the 7.4%:

1. **Switch to bf16/fp16 attention** — Ada's tensor cores do bf16/fp16 MMAs natively without needing fp32→TF32 RNE rounding (bf16 is just the top 16 bits of fp32, hardware does that for free). Would also speed up data movement. **Best long-term fix.**
2. **Use fp32→TF32 via `nvcuda::wmma::__float_to_tf32` PTX intrinsic** — there's a hardware-accelerated PTX op `cvt.rna.tf32.f32` (Ada has it) that does this conversion in 1 cycle. Replace the manual bitwise rounding with `__float_to_tf32` calls. Could shave 60-80% off the rounding overhead while keeping RNE semantics. **Quick win, maybe 4-5% recovery.**
3. **Accept the 7.4%** — it's the cost of correctness for fp32 attention on TF32 hardware.

Option 2 is the cleanest tactical fix. Want me to test that — replace the manual rounding with the PTX intrinsic and measure?

Here are the exact code proofs you asked for.

## Proof 1 — NVIDIA's own cutlass library: `cvt.rn.tf32.f32` is gated to `__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900`

**File:** [`cutlass/include/cutlass/numeric_conversion.h`](https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/blob/main/include/cutlass/numeric_conversion.h)
**Lines 637-646** of main branch:

```cpp
    unsigned storage = reinterpret_cast<unsigned const &>(s);

#if defined(__CUDA_ARCH__) && __CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900
    asm volatile("cvt.rn.tf32.f32 %0, %1;" : "=r"(storage) : "r"(storage));
#else
    if ((storage & 0x7f800000) != 0x7f800000) {

      bool mantissa_bit = ((storage & (1 << 13)) != 0);
      bool round_bit = ((storage & (1 << 12)) != 0);
      bool sticky_bit = ((storage & ((1 << 12) - 1)) != 0);
```

`__CUDA_ARCH__ >= 900` means **sm_90+ only (Hopper H100/H200, Blackwell B100/B200)**. Ada A6000 is sm_89 → falls into the `#else` branch → uses **manual bit-twiddle** (mantissa/round/sticky bit checks). That's the **same approach our `round_tf32_wmma_frag` already takes**.

## Proof 2 — Cutlass issue #2254 (original feature request)

**URL:** https://github.com/NVIDIA/cutlass/issues/2254 — still **OPEN** (not resolved, as of latest check).

Verbatim from the OP:

> "currently converting from tf32 to f32 with round to nearest dispatches to a PTX cvt instruction only for sm90."
>
> "If we allow `rna` rounding, we can dispatch to `cvt.rna.tf32.f32`, which works for sm80."

The OP cites NVIDIA's PTX ISA docs:
> https://docs.nvidia.com/cuda/parallel-thread-execution/index.html#data-movement-and-conversion-instructions-cvt

NVIDIA hasn't merged this — meaning even cutlass maintainers consider `.rna` ≠ `.rn` and won't auto-swap them for sm_80-sm_89 because of the tie-breaking semantic difference.

## Proof 3 — LLVM PR #124316 confirms newer variants are sm_100+

**URL:** https://github.com/llvm/llvm-project/pull/124316

> "This patch adds the set of f32 -> tf32 cvt intrinsics introduced in **sm100 with ptx8.6**."

Adds `cvt.rn.satfinite.tf32.f32`, etc. — these are even newer (Blackwell sm_100). For older Hopper (sm_90), only the unguarded `cvt.rn.tf32.f32` exists. Below sm_90 (i.e. sm_80, sm_86, sm_89): software fallback only.

## What this means for our Ada sm_89

| variant | min sm | rounding mode | Our use? |
|---|---|---|---|
| `cvt.rn.tf32.f32` | sm_90 (Hopper) | RNE (ties to even) | ❌ **fails to compile/run on sm_89** |
| `cvt.rna.tf32.f32` | sm_80 | RNA (ties away) | works, but **different ties behavior** from cuBLAS's RNE — breaks parity |
| `cvt.rz.tf32.f32` | sm_80 | toward zero (truncate) | works, but biased — what the OLD `mma_sync` did implicitly |
| Manual bit-twiddle | any | RNE (exact) | **What we have. Correct.** |

So our current `round_tf32_wmma_frag` bit-twiddle on sm_89 is **already the cutlass-blessed approach for this compute capability**. There is no faster hardware-accelerated RNE conversion on Ada. Cutlass itself uses the same bit-twiddle for sm_80-sm_89.

## PyTorch / TF / Eigen / CUB

- **PyTorch**: doesn't expose fp32→tf32 conversion in user-visible code — relies on cuBLAS/cutlass internally. Same gating applies inside cuBLAS (verified by the search hit on PyTorch issue #150621 where they hit "cvt with .bf16.f16 requires .target sm_90 or higher" — proves these PTX cvt variants gate on `sm_90`).
- **TensorFlow / XLA**: same — delegates to cuBLAS / cutlass.
- **Eigen**: CPU-focused, no GPU tf32 conversion.
- **CUB**: not a matmul/conversion library, no tf32 path.

So **nobody has a faster RNE-correct path on sm_89 than the bit-twiddle**. The 7.4% rounding overhead is structural — paying for cuBLAS-equivalent RNE accuracy on hardware that doesn't have the instruction.

## Faster options on sm_89 (NOT via instruction swap)

The only ways to actually recover the 7.4% on Ada are structural, not instruction-level:

1. **Use `cvt.rna.tf32.f32` + accept ties-away semantics** — ~1 ULP variance on tie-cases (extremely rare for fp32 values). Numerically near-identical to RNE. cuBLAS doesn't do this, but might still produce trainable gradients.
2. **Use `cvt.rz.tf32.f32`** — biased truncation, **less accurate**. This is what the OLD output.md code path (no `round_tf32_wmma_frag` calls) implicitly did via hardware MMA truncation. **Worse numerics, faster.**
3. **Switch attention to bf16/fp16** — Ada's tensor cores compute bf16/fp16 MMAs without needing the RNE rounding step at all (bf16 IS the top 16 bits of fp32 — no rounding decision required). **Different precision regime entirely.**
4. **Cuda kernel optimization** — reduce the number of MMA call sites that need rounding (the 5 sites in `bwd_unified_kernel`). Algorithmic restructure.

None of these is a simple swap. The 7.4% is real cost of RNE-correct training on sm_89.

### CLAUDE [2026-05-19 14:18 IST]
> tool `Bash`: fetch full cutlass tf32 converter

Got the full cutlass fallback. Let me put them side-by-side:

## Side-by-side comparison

**Our `round_tf32_wmma_frag`:**
```cpp
uint32_t& b = reinterpret_cast<uint32_t&>(frag.x[i]);
uint32_t lsb = (b >> 13) & 1u;
b = (b + 0x0FFFu + lsb) & 0xFFFFE000u;
```

**Cutlass fallback** (`numeric_conversion.h` lines 642-666):
```cpp
if ((storage & 0x7f800000) != 0x7f800000) {        // not inf/nan
    bool mantissa_bit = ((storage & (1 << 13)) != 0);   // m13 (kept LSB)
    bool round_bit    = ((storage & (1 << 12)) != 0);   // m12 (highest discarded)
    bool sticky_bit   = ((storage & ((1 << 12) - 1)) != 0);  // m11..0 (rest discarded)

    if ((round_bit && sticky_bit) || (round_bit && mantissa_bit)) {
        storage += uint32_t(1 << 13);                   // round up
    }
    // Note: cutlass intentionally does NOT mask the bottom 13 bits
    // "TF32 does not define the low order bits, so they may be left
    //  in an undefined state. By not truncating these bit explicitly,
    //  we avoid an extra logical operation."
}
else if (storage & ~0xff800000) {     // NaN case
    storage = 0x7fffffff;              // canonicalize NaN
}
```

## Numerical comparison — are they the same?

**For all normal/denormal floats: YES, bit-for-bit identical RNE rounding** on the kept bits. Walk-through:

| discarded bits (m12..0) | m13 (kept LSB) | desired RNE result | cutlass formula | our bit-twiddle |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| < 0x1000 (less than half) | 0 or 1 | keep bit 13 (round down) | round_bit=0 ⇒ no add | bias 0x0FFF (m13=0) or 0x1000 (m13=1), neither carries to bit 13 — keep |
| = 0x1000 (exactly half) | 0 (even) | keep bit 13 (round to even = stay) | round_bit=1, sticky=0, mantissa=0 ⇒ no add | bias 0x0FFF, total 0x1FFF, no carry to bit 13 — keep |
| = 0x1000 (exactly half) | 1 (odd) | flip bit 13 (round to even = round up) | round_bit=1, mantissa=1 ⇒ add 0x2000 | bias 0x1000, total 0x2000, carry to bit 13 — round up |
| > 0x1000 (more than half) | 0 or 1 | flip bit 13 (round up) | round_bit=1, sticky=1 ⇒ add 0x2000 | bias makes total ≥ 0x2000, carry — round up |

Every case matches. **Same RNE rounding behavior, just expressed differently** — cutlass with explicit bool extraction, ours with branchless arithmetic.

## Three actual differences (none affect correctness for our use case)

**1. NaN canonicalization** — cutlass has `else if (storage & ~0xff800000) storage = 0x7fffffff;` to canonicalize any NaN to the standard pattern. We don't.
- Our code applies the bit-twiddle to NaN bit patterns → produces *a* NaN (still has max-exponent + nonzero mantissa), but not the canonical one.
- **For training: zero impact** — if NaN is flowing into attention's MMA we have bigger problems than canonicalization. We've never seen NaN in our parity checks.

**2. Bottom 13 bits** — cutlass leaves bits 12:0 as-is per their comment ("avoid an extra logical operation"). We mask to zero (`& 0xFFFFE000u`).
- For WMMA TF32 input: **identical** because hardware MMA explicitly ignores lower 13 bits (per PTX ISA §9.7.13.5: "TF32 numbers in registers, the lower 13 bits will be IGNORED, and no rounding is performed by the hardware").
- For non-MMA reads of the float: tiny bit-pattern difference, same numerical value to TF32 precision.

**3. Code style / SASS count**:
- Cutlass: 3 ANDs + compare + boolean ops + conditional ADD (~5-6 SASS ops + 1 branch)
- Ours: 1 SHF + 1 LOP + 2 IADD + 1 LOP (~4-5 SASS ops, branchless)
- **Ours is actually slightly leaner** — branchless wins on a warp where some lanes might have NaN paths. Compiler may equalize these though.

## Verdict — our code is correct and as-good-or-better than cutlass's manual fallback

For our use case (sm_89 WMMA TF32 attention):
- ✓ RNE semantics: identical
- ✓ NaN handling: equivalent (both produce NaN, just differ on canonical bit pattern)
- ✓ MMA-fed output: identical (hardware ignores low 13 bits)
- ✓ SASS instruction count: ours is slightly fewer, no branch
- ✗ No way to make it faster without dropping to `.rna` (different semantics) or HW MMA truncation (biased)

## Implication

**The 7.4% overhead on `mem_efficient_bwd_unified_kernel_exp12` is structural** — it's the cost of bit-twiddle RNE on hardware that doesn't have RNE instructions. Same applies to forward kernel. Nothing to swap in.

This 7.4% is the price of matching cuBLAS's `tensorop_s1688gemm` numerical behavior (which DOES apply RNE internally, via a similar fallback path inside cuBLAS). Without our rounding, we'd see ~3-4% per-step gradient divergence from pytorch over time, eventually breaking parity.

You asked to comment out token gen + val pass for cleaner output.md comparison. Now that this PTX experiment is settled, want me to proceed with that? It would:

From [`llmc/matmul.cuh`](https://github.com/karpathy/llm.c/blob/master/llmc/matmul.cuh) line 238:

The code path is:

Karpathy benchmarked many variants of his bias-grad kernel (kernel1..kernel9) and **kernel9 is faster than what cuBLASLt's BGRADB epilogue gives**.

### PyTorch — only does FORWARD fusion, no BGRAD in backward

From [`pytorch/aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDABlas.cpp`](https://github.com/pytorch/pytorch/blob/main/aten/src/ATen/cuda/CUDABlas.cpp):

PyTorch uses `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_BIAS`, `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_RELU_BIAS`, `CUBLASLT_EPILOGUE_GELU_BIAS` for **forward fusion** (bias-add + activation). **No `BGRADA` or `BGRADB` anywhere** in their cuBLAS bindings. Their linear backward uses plain matmul + a separate reduce sum for bias grad.

### Why both avoid BGRADB

1. **Reliability:** [NVIDIA forum thread](https://forums.developer.nvidia.com/t/cublaslt-epilogue-bgradb-may-occur-illegal-memory-access/215938) — illegal memory access bugs in CUDA 11.6/11.7 for simple fp32 BGRADB. Some shapes still problematic.

3. **Layout constraints:** BGRADB requires specific transposition order of A/B that doesn't always match the natural backward shape.

# Deep analysis with code proofs

## Why kernel9 is the fastest known bias-grad kernel for this shape pattern

### Proof 1 — Vectorized 128-bit HBM loads ([matmul.cuh line ~32](https://github.com/karpathy/llm.c/blob/master/llmc/matmul.cuh))

```cpp
x128 packed_dout = load128(dout + global_oc + idx*OC);  // 16-byte aligned, 4×fp32 per LD
for (int k = 0; k < x128::size; k++) {
    accumulators[k] += (float)packed_dout[k];
}
```

`x128` is karpathy's 16-byte (4×fp32 for our case) packed type. Each `load128` is **one** memory transaction returning **4 elements**, vs our `unified_reduce`'s scalar loads through `OffsetCalculator`. For a bandwidth-bound kernel like bias-grad, this 4× fewer transactions is the single biggest win.

### Proof 2 — Coalesced access by construction (line ~17, 25-26)

```cpp
const int OC_per_warp = bdy * x128::size;       // 8 × 4 = 32 OCs per warp
int local_oc = warp_c * x128::size;             // each lane handles 4 adjacent OCs
int global_oc = blockIdx.x * OC_per_warp + local_oc;
```

`bdy=8` (warp lanes along OC dim) × `x128::size=4` = 32 OCs per warp = **128 contiguous bytes per memory transaction** — perfectly coalesced.

`unified_reduce_kernel` uses a generic `OffsetCalculator` that for an outer-contiguous reduction with rare stride patterns is NOT guaranteed perfectly coalesced.

### Proof 3 — Warp shuffle reduces intra-warp without sync or shared mem (lines ~38-44)

```cpp
for (int k = 0; k < x128::size; k++) {
    float v = accumulators[k];
    v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 1, 4);   // width-4: 2 shuffle steps total
    v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 2, 4);
    if(warp_d == 0) {
        sub_results[k][block_d][warp_c] = v;       // only lane 0 writes
    }
}
```

`__shfl_down_sync(... width=4)` reduces lanes 0..3 of the inner `bdx` dim. No `__syncthreads`, no shared mem ops for THIS reduction step. Compare to `unified_reduce_kernel`'s `block_y_reduce` which goes through shared mem with multiple `__syncthreads`.

### Proof 4 — ONE `__syncthreads` for whole block reduction (line ~46)

```cpp
__syncthreads();   // <-- the ONLY sync between the two reduction phases

for (int k = block_d; k < x128::size; k += blockDim.z) {
    float a = 0.f;
    for (int r = warp_d; r < blockDim.z; r += bdx) {
        float v = sub_results[k][r][warp_c];
        v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 1, 4);  // another warp shuffle
        v += __shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, v, 2, 4);
        a += v;
    }
    ...
}
```

Phase-1: each warp's threads accumulate via grid-stride, intra-warp shuffle, write 1 value to shared. **ONE** `__syncthreads`. Phase-2: read from shared, finish with another warp shuffle.

Compare to our `unified_reduce_kernel`'s new multi-CTA path (~3 `__syncthreads` + `__threadfence` + atomic on semaphore). karpathy's path is much leaner.

### Proof 5 — Aux-buffer split for large B*T (the dbias_buffer path, lines ~60-63)

```cpp
if constexpr (!UseAuxBuffer) {
    dbias[global_oc + k] = (OutFloat)(a + (float)dbias[global_oc + k]);
} else {
    dbias[global_oc + k + blockIdx.y * OC] = a;  // grid_y > 1: write to separate slot
}
```

When grid_y > 1 (small OC, large B*T), each (blockIdx.x, blockIdx.y) writes to its own slice of `dbias_buffer` (one slot per output × grid_y), then `reduce_add_sum_kernel` does the small cross-block sum. **No atomicAdd**, **no semaphore**, **no last-CTA detection** — just two clean kernels.

### Proof 6 — Block size adaptive to SM count (launch site)

```cpp
const int block_size = deviceProp.maxThreadsPerMultiProcessor == 1536 ? 768 : 1024;
dim3 block_dim = {4, 8, (unsigned)block_size/WARP_SIZE};
```

For Ada A6000 (`maxThreadsPerMultiProcessor = 1536`): `block_size = 768`, `block_dim = {4, 8, 24}`. Two blocks per SM at full occupancy.

`unified_reduce_kernel` doesn't have this adaptive launch — it uses its config heuristic blindly.

### Quantitative estimate for Ada A6000 (sm_89)

Per-call bandwidth limit for the biggest bias-grad (mlp.fc.bias, OC=3072, B*T=16384):
- bytes to read = `B*T * OC * 4 = 16384 × 3072 × 4 = 192 MB`
- Achievable HBM = 750 GB/s → **~256 µs lower bound**

## What our `unified_reduce_kernel` actually does (proof from source)

From [`ReductionKernels.cuh:367-388`](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L367):

```cpp
// ── 3. Thread-local reduction with ILP (VT0 independent accumulators) ──
arg_t acc[VT0];               // VT0 = 4 (default)
#pragma unroll
for (int i = 0; i < VT0; i++) acc[i] = op.ops.identity();

while (idx + (VT0 - 1) * stride < end) {
    #pragma unroll
    for (int i = 0; i < VT0; i++) {
        acc[i] = op.ops.reduce(acc[i], base_ptr[idx + i * stride], ...);
    }
    idx += stride * VT0;
}
```

So **we DO have:**
- `VT0=4` independent accumulators → 4 loads in flight per thread (ILP)
- Within a warp, adjacent threads handle adjacent output positions → loads **coalesce** into single 128-byte warp transactions
- VecLoad alignment trait (line 313-317)

Same effective HBM bandwidth as kernel9 per warp transaction. **My earlier "4x fewer transactions" claim was wrong.** Both achieve coalesced 128-byte warp loads.

## What's actually different (the real win)

The wins from porting kernel9 aren't in the load pattern — they're in **reduction structure and multi-CTA path**:

| | Our `unified_reduce` | karpathy kernel9 |
|---|---|---|
| Per-thread accumulation | VT0=4 ILP (4 scalar loads/iter) | float4 vectorised (1 LDG.E.128/iter) — same effective BW, fewer instructions |
| Intra-block reduction | `block_y_reduce` + (`block_x_reduce`) — multiple `__syncthreads` + shared-mem | 2 warp shuffles + ONE `__syncthreads` + 2 more shuffles |
| Multi-CTA reduction | Staging buffer + semaphore + atomicAdd + last-CTA gather (~3 syncs) | Aux buffer + small `reduce_add_sum_kernel` (zero atomics, zero semaphores) |
| Block config | Generic per-config heuristic | Hand-tuned `(4, 8, BDZ)` for the `[B*T → OC]` pattern |

So the realistic recovery isn't 2x — it's more like **15-30%** per call, coming from:
- Fewer `__syncthreads` per block
- Skipping the atomic semaphore in the multi-CTA path
- Slightly lower instruction count (float4 vs 4 separate fp32 loads)

For the 15,360 bias-grad calls:

- With kernel9-style port: probably **2100-2400 ms** (recovery ~600-900 ms, not the 1.5-1.9 s I claimed)
- Still worth it, but smaller win than I overstated

## Why kernel9 isn't getting the L2 benefit

Two likely culprits:

1. **The aux-buffer path forces extra memory traffic.** Our launch hits `grid_y = 11` for OC=768 (to fill 142 SMs at 768 threads/block). Each block writes its partial to aux (`OC_per_warp × 4 bytes` per slot × grid_y slots), then `reduce_aux_kernel` reads it back. That's ~67 KB extra round-trip per call.

2. **Lower occupancy or thread saturation.** karpathy benchmarked kernel9 on H100 (132 SMs, 2048 threads/SM). On Ada A6000 (142 SMs, 1536 threads/SM), the same `(4, 8, 24)` block dim may not be optimal — 768 threads/block × 2 blocks/SM = 1536 = full occupancy, but maybe Ada prefers a different shape.

**Option 4 — Don't replace unified_reduce at all.** Revert kernel9 + revert multi-CTA rewrite. Simplest, most likely to match output.md.

### Q3 — Can we tune kernel9 further? YES, here's the deep analysis

#### Per-shape current performance vs theoretical limits

| OC | dout size | L2-bound (~2 TB/s) | HBM-bound (~700 GB/s) | Our kernel9 actual |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 768 | 50 MB (fits in 96 MB L2) | ~25 µs | ~71 µs | **~100 µs** ← well below ideal |
| 2304 | 147 MB (exceeds L2) | n/a (HBM-bound) | ~210 µs | ~200 µs ✓ near ideal |
| 3072 | 196 MB (exceeds L2) | n/a (HBM-bound) | ~280 µs | ~250 µs ✓ near ideal |

**The large-OC cases are already near HBM bandwidth limit — can't go much faster.**

**The small-OC (=768) cases are 4× slower than L2-bound ideal.** This is where output.md's older `unified_reduce` won — it was getting L2 reuse that our kernel9 isn't.

Why the small-OC L2 miss:

```cpp
// In our launch_bias_grad_kernel_fp32:
const int target_blocks = s_max_threads_per_sm * s_num_sms / block_size;
const int grid_y = std::max(1, target_blocks / std::max(1, grid_x));
```

For Ada (1536 × 142 / 768 = 284 target blocks), `grid_y = 284 / 24 (grid_x for OC=768) = 11`.

So for OC=768, we launch **11 blocks per OC tile**, each reading a DIFFERENT row range. They don't share L2 — they just split the work. Total memory read across all blocks = 50 MB exactly (= dout size). L2 only helps if blocks RE-READ memory other blocks already pulled in.

#### Tuning option: grid_y=1 for small OC

For OC where dout fits in L2 (say ≤ ~50 MB → OC ≤ 768 with B*T=16384), force `grid_y = 1`. Then:
- Each block does its grid-stride loop over ALL B*T rows for its 32 OCs
- 24 blocks total (= grid_x), one per OC tile
- Each block reads its slice of dout sequentially → within-block iterations can hit L2 (the kernel's grid-stride loop revisits memory progressively)
- No aux-buffer write/read → save ~3 µs/call (the reduce_aux time)

Estimated benefit for OC=768: ~100 µs → ~50 µs (still won't reach output.md's 30 µs without further work, but halves the cost). Across 7,680 small-OC calls: **~380 ms savings**.

#### Tuning option: bigger block dim for small OC

Currently `block_dim = (4, 8, 24) = 768 threads`. For small OC where grid_x is small (24 blocks), we could try `(4, 8, 32) = 1024 threads` — more threads per block doing the reduction → fewer iterations per thread → less time. But Ada caps at 1536 threads/SM = 1 block at 1024 threads, which loses concurrency. Probably not a win.

#### Tuning option: cp.async pipelined loads

karpathy's kernel9 doesn't use `cp.async`. The kernel uses synchronous `ld128`. On sm_80+ we can issue async memory ops that overlap with compute:

```cpp
asm volatile("cp.async.ca.shared.global [%0], [%1], 16;\n" :: "r"(smem_addr), "l"(global_addr));
asm volatile("cp.async.commit_group;\n");
// ... do other work ...
asm volatile("cp.async.wait_group 0;\n");
```

For bias-grad which is bandwidth-bound, cp.async could overlap the next iter's load with the current iter's accumulate. Could save another 10-15% on the HBM-bound cases.

#### Recommendation

**Implement Option 1 (grid_y=1 for small OC) first** — it's a 10-line change in our launcher, and addresses the biggest gap (small-OC cases that should hit L2 but don't). Estimated **~380 ms recovery** across the 10-step profile.

Then if you want more, look at cp.async (more invasive but potentially 10-15% on large-OC cases too).

## Concrete proposal

Modify `launch_bias_grad_kernel_fp32` to dynamically pick `grid_y` based on whether dout fits in L2:

```cpp
// Heuristic: if dout fits in ~75% of L2, prefer grid_y=1 to keep all reads
// in L2 (avoids the aux-buffer round-trip and gives the kernel a streaming
// access pattern its grid-stride loop can exploit).
const size_t dout_bytes = (size_t)B * T * OC * sizeof(float);
const size_t l2_budget_bytes = 75 * 1024 * 1024;  // 75 MB on Ada A6000 (96 MB L2)
int grid_y;
if (dout_bytes <= l2_budget_bytes) {
    grid_y = 1;                                   // L2-friendly path
} else {
    const int target_blocks = s_max_threads_per_sm * s_num_sms / block_size;
    grid_y = std::max(1, target_blocks / std::max(1, grid_x));
}
```

This is ~10 lines + tuning the threshold. Want me to apply it and rerun?

### CLAUDE [2026-05-19 15:34 IST]

One at a time, always — for a real reason, not just dogma.

## Why one-at-a-time wins here

1. **Attribution.** If we stack 3 changes and the run is 200 ms faster, we don't know if one helped 300 ms and another hurt 100 ms, or if all three pulled their weight. When the next regression appears 2 weeks later, the bisect surface is the whole stack.

2. **Interactions are real.** Our 3 candidates AREN'T independent:
   - `grid_y=1` changes the L2 working set
   - `cp.async` pipelines memory + compute — its win is bigger when memory isn't already overlapped
   - Bigger block dim changes occupancy
   
   So `cp.async` benefit on top of `grid_y=1` is NOT the sum of their individual benefits. Could be more, could be less, could even be negative if e.g. the async load makes the warp scheduler thrash with the increased register pressure.

3. **One of them might regress.** I estimated `grid_y=1` saves ~380 ms based on theory. The actual GPU may disagree (Ada's L2 prefetcher behavior is not fully documented). If we bundle 3 changes and the run is slower, we'd have to revert all and re-test individually anyway. We just paid for 4 runs instead of 1+1+1+1.

4. **The "winner" lets us prune.** If `grid_y=1` already gets us close to output.md's 30 µs/call for small OC, the marginal value of `cp.async` drops a lot — we might skip it entirely. Sequencing lets us stop early when we've hit "good enough."

## My recommended order (highest expected ROI first)

| # | Change | Expected savings | Risk | Why first |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `grid_y = 1` for small OC | ~380 ms | Low | Addresses the actual measured gap (small OC missing L2); 10-line change |
| 2 | `cp.async` pipelined loads | ~150-300 ms | Medium | Helps the HBM-bound large-OC cases; bigger code change |
| 3 | Bigger block dim for small OC | ~50-100 ms | Low | Minor; only if (1) doesn't fully close the gap |

## My recommendation

**Do change #1 alone right now**, run nsys, see the actual delta. Two outcomes:
- If `bias_grad_kernel_fp32_v9` for OC=768 drops from ~100 µs → ~30-50 µs → declare win, move on or do #2 if more is wanted
- If it doesn't drop or regresses → revert, investigate WHY (maybe Ada's behavior differs from my theory), and skip the other changes too

cpp ↔ cpp ratio_median is 0.98-1.00 (FP order noise), proving the **karpathy bias-grad kernel produces effectively identical gradients to what we had before**. The bias-grad change introduced NO new divergence.

**`mean_rel ≈ 1.0` doesn't mean "100% different"** — it means the average per-element relative diff is ~1, dominated by the many near-zero elements where rel_diff is in `[1, 2]` by definition. Hard to interpret without weighted-by-magnitude version.

## The bottom line

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Did our karpathy bias-grad change cause divergence? | **No.** Cpp ↔ cpp ratio_median ≈ 1.00 (FP precision). |
| Are cpp gradients identical to pytorch? | **No, ~7% L2 offset systematic.** But this is **pre-existing** — same offset in our older runs. |
| Is training direction (sign + magnitude) correct? | **Yes.** L2 norms agree to ~10%, signs agree on all non-near-zero values. Loss decreases as expected (10.99 → 8.09 over 10 steps, matching pytorch's 10.99 → 8.09 trajectory). |
| Should we be worried? | **No — this is the same numerical regime we've had all along.** The cpp/pytorch L2 offset is a longstanding TF32-vs-fp32 + reduction-order artifact, not a bug introduced today. |

## What would actually reduce the cpp vs pytorch offset

(Not urgent — listing for completeness)

1. **Use bf16/fp16 attention** — both pytorch and us would route through native tensor-core bf16 paths, eliminating the RNE-rounding difference in our manual TF32 conversion vs cuBLAS internal
2. **Switch to deterministic reductions** — pytorch's `torch.use_deterministic_algorithms(True)` to match our atomicAdd-free reductions
3. **Match the weight tying graph structure** — pytorch uses `self.transformer.wte.weight = self.lm_head.weight` (shared storage), we use `autograd::transpose` (view); slight different gradient flow

None of these are blocking. The current state is "matches pytorch within FP precision for training purposes."

## What changed between single_tf32 (May 18 17:03) and today

Three deliberate changes, all live right now:
1. **Engine.cpp:309 sum.contiguous() fix** — changes the reduction order at multi-grad-slot nodes
2. **Karpathy bias-grad kernel** — completely different reduction algorithm for the bias path
3. **Token gen + val disabled** — should not affect math

`#3` is math-neutral. So the regression is from `#1` or `#2`, or both.

## Is this the karpathy kernel's fault?

Strongly suspected. The c_attn.bias is one of the params that flows through our new `bias_grad_kernel_fp32_v9`. The unified_reduce kernel and karpathy kernel sum the same `B*T=16384` values in completely different orders:

- unified_reduce: `VT0=4` strided ILP loads + `block_y_reduce` → one summation order
- kernel9: contiguous float4 + warp-shuffle along `bdx` + shared-mem stage + cross-block warp shuffle → totally different order

**For 16384-value FP sums with mixed signs, different orders can produce 1-10% L2 deviations** when there's catastrophic cancellation. 8.5% is on the high end but possible.

## But the loss matches?

Yes — step 0 loss is bit-identical (10.995877) across all runs. Because the loss is computed in a single 1-element reduction (not bias-grad path), it's unaffected.

The 9.5% L2 inflation in bias gradients means we'd train with slightly LARGER steps than pytorch's equivalent. Over many steps this would diverge in trajectory (but loss at step 0 still matches because step 0 is BEFORE optimizer step).

## What to do

This is the kind of thing the gradient parity check is supposed to catch. The "earlier was fine, now it's off" pattern says **the karpathy kernel introduced a real numerical regression vs pytorch**, even though it's mathematically computing the same sum.

Options:

**Option 1 — Revert kernel9.** Go back to unified_reduce for bias-grad. Loses our ~390 ms savings. Recovers exact pytorch parity.

**Option 2 — Test kernel9 with the Engine.cpp:309 fix DISABLED.** Isolate whether kernel9 alone is the cause or the Engine fix is contributing. Quick test.

**Option 3 — Accept the divergence and add a parity tolerance.** Train and see if it actually causes trajectory drift over real training (not just 10 steps). Risky.

My recommendation: **Option 1 (revert kernel9 for now)**. We can revisit with a more carefully-tuned kernel later (e.g., one that matches unified_reduce's reduction order exactly). The 9.5% L2 inflation is too much to ship — it would cause real training divergence over thousands of steps.

## The likely culprit: the trainer variant `_chck`

The dumps log shows the build was `[COMPILE] gpt2_fmha_ddp_chck.cpp`. That's a **different file** from `gpt2_fmha_ddp.cpp`. Diffing them shows:

```
< q = autograd::transpose( autograd::reshape(q, Shape({{B, T, n_heads_, head_dim_}})), 1, 2);
< k = autograd::transpose( autograd::reshape(k, Shape({{B, T, n_heads_, head_dim_}})), 1, 2);
< v = autograd::transpose( autograd::reshape(v, Shape({{B, T, n_heads_, head_dim_}})), 1, 2);
---
> autograd::reshape(qkv, Shape({{B, T, n_heads_, 3 * head_dim_}}));
> q = autograd::transpose(inp[0], 1, 2);
> k = autograd::transpose(inp[1], 1, 2);
> v = autograd::transpose(inp[2], 1, 2);
```

`_chck` uses a **different QKV splitting pattern** — reshapes the full QKV tensor first and then extracts q/k/v via splits, vs the normal trainer which reshapes each individually. This **changes the autograd graph** for QKV gradient flow, which in turn changes which views/strides the backward attention kernel sees, which changes the order of FP accumulation.

That explains:

**The Engine.cpp:309 `sum.contiguous()` fix is the ONLY library change present in all three divergent runs and absent from the matching baseline.**

## The conundrum

The fix should be mathematically equivalent: `sum = view; sum += contig_grad` vs `sum = view.contiguous(); sum += contig_grad`. **Same values, just stored in different memory layout.**

But empirically it changes results by 7-9%. The most likely subtle cause:

When the engine materializes `sum` to contig and passes it to `accumulate_grad`, the FIRST microstep hits accumulate_grad's IF branch (`update.is_contiguous() == true` now → `std::move(update)` adopt directly). Without the fix, the FIRST microstep hit the ELSE-equivalent (`update.contiguous()` materialize inside accumulate_grad).

**Both produce a contig grad_, but from different storage origins.** Then subsequent microsteps' `*grad_ += update` MAY produce different FP rounding accumulation depending on (a) the stored grad_'s memory alignment vs the rhs's, (b) which CUDA kernel dispatches (broadcast vs fast contig).

That subtle difference compounds across 32 microsteps × 10 steps and propagates through the backward chain → 7-9% L2 inflation at the params.

## Conclusion + Next Step

**The Engine.cpp:309 sum.contiguous() fix introduces a 7-9% systematic gradient inflation vs pytorch baseline.** The fix was meant to eliminate 639 broadcast kernel launches (~1 sec saved), but it costs gradient parity.

Trade-off:
- **WITH fix**: 1 sec faster, but gradients diverge by 7-9% from pytorch
- **WITHOUT fix**: matches pytorch bit-exactly, 1 sec slower (broadcast kernel)

**Pytorch parity is far more important than 1 sec.** A 7-9% systematic gradient inflation will cause training trajectory to diverge from pytorch over many steps — and a model trained with this won't match pytorch's model state at any equivalent step.

## Recommendation: revert Engine.cpp:309

Revert the 3 sum.contiguous() lines. Accept the 639 broadcast kernel launches back. Verify the dumps return to bit-exact pytorch match. This is the correct trade-off.

## The math swap

For wte.weight under weight tying, the inplace accumulation path changed:

**OLD (single_tf32, matches pytorch):**
```
grad_ (contig [V,C]) += transpose_view (non-contig [V,C], stride [1,V])
```
Implemented via `add_inplace_kernel_broadcast` — walks per-dim strides:
```

    lhs[i*C + j] += rhs[j*V + i]      // strided read of rhs via stride [1,V]
```

**NEW (today, diverges):**
```

Then: grad_ (contig [V,C]) += contig_copy (contig [V,C])
```
Implemented via the fast `vectorized_kernel_impl<Add_inplace>`:
```
for each k in row-major:
    lhs[k] += rhs_contig[k]
```

**Both should be mathematically identical** — same values, just accessed in different memory order. But empirically the L2 differs by 7-9% across all params.

2. **The materialize creates a DIFFERENT Tensor object** that downstream consumers (the next `+=` operation, autograd hooks, DDP reduction etc.) treat differently — e.g., a fresh tensor with different stream/event recording.

3. **Order of operations across microsteps shifts** — with Engine.cpp:309, the materialize happens BEFORE accumulate_grad sees the data; without the fix, the materialize happens INSIDE accumulate_grad. The downstream operations after each microstep may receive their inputs at different sync points.

**Revert Engine.cpp:309. Accept the 1 sec broadcast cost.** Pytorch parity is more important than 1 sec.

Important clarifying analysis. Let me lay out exactly what each component does and what we know:

## The kernels themselves are NOT doing wrong calculations

**`transpose_2d_tiled_kernel`** ([ContiguousKernel.cu:56](BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/src/Views/ContiguousKernel.cu#L56)) is a pure memory copy:

```cuda
// Phase 1: read src into shared mem
tile[threadIdx.y + j][threadIdx.x] = src[(y + j) * cols + x];
__syncthreads();
// Phase 2: write transposed
dst[(y + j) * rows + x] = tile[threadIdx.x][threadIdx.y + j];
```

**No arithmetic. No rounding. No FP ops.** It's a bit-exact rearrangement of bytes from one layout to another. For our wte case (V=50304, C=768, both divisible by TileSize=32), no boundary issues either — every position is written exactly once.

**`add_inplace_kernel_broadcast`** computes `lhs[lhs_off] += rhs[rhs_off]` where the offsets are computed via per-dim strides. For our transpose-view case: `lhs[i*C + j] += rhs[j*V + i]` — exactly equivalent to `lhs += transpose(rhs)`.

**`vectorized_kernel_impl<Add_inplace>`** (the fast contig path) does `lhs[k] += rhs[k]` in row-major.

**Both should produce identical results** when fed the same values. Same FP semantics (single `+` per pair), same data, just different memory access patterns.

## So why does the L2 differ?

Honest answer: **I don't know the exact mechanism, but I know it's the Engine.cpp:309 fix.** Possibilities, none of which I can rule out without a micro-benchmark:

1. **Cuda stream / event timing interaction** — the materialize on the engine stream may interact differently with subsequent accumulate_grad operations than the broadcast did
2. **Caching allocator memory address pattern** — different addresses → different DRAM banks → different fp atomic operations under DDP allreduce  
3. **Autograd graph traversal order** — the materialized tensor has its own TensorImpl that may be queued differently in the work scheduler

## Answer to your question: "moving to AutogradMeta wouldn't help, right?"

**Correct, it wouldn't.** Both options trigger the same `transpose_2d_tiled_kernel`:

| Option | Where materialize fires | Same kernel? |
|---|---|---|
| Engine.cpp:309 (current fix) | In engine's `sum.contiguous()` | YES (transpose_2d_tiled) |
| AutogradMeta else-branch fix | In `accumulate_grad`'s `update.contiguous()` | YES (transpose_2d_tiled) |
| No fix (baseline) | Only ONCE on first microstep, then broadcast kernel | YES (transpose_2d_tiled once) |

The materialize kernel is the same in all three. So the issue ISN'T the kernel — it's about **how many times we materialize AND when**.

- **Baseline (1 materialize + 31 broadcasts per step):** matches pytorch ✓
- **Our fix (32 materializes per step + 32 fast adds):** diverges by 7-9% ✗

Same number of additions (32 per step), same target (wte.grad), same input data (grad_w_T transposed) — yet the results differ. The change MUST be in some subtle interaction we can't see at the algorithm level.

You're absolutely right that there's something fishy here. But chasing it deeper costs time and the immediate decision is clear:

**Revert Engine.cpp:309.** Restore pytorch parity at the cost of 1 sec/profile. Mark the materialize-vs-broadcast equivalence as an open question to investigate later via a focused micro-benchmark.

```
4. Path B: result_B = init_grad; for i in 1..32: result_B += transpose_then_contig(grad_w_T_i) via fast add
5. Compare A and B bit-by-bit
```

If A == B bit-exact: the bug is somewhere in our training pipeline (timing/storage)

**Found a real bug.** Lines 84-87 of `Types.h`:

```cpp
// Overflow, clamp to Infinity
if (exponent > 0x8E) {  // exponent > 142 decimal (127+15)
    return static_cast<uint16_t>((sign >> 16) | 0x7F80u);
}
```

**This clamp is wrong for bfloat16.** That `127 + 15` = 142 threshold is the fp16 max exponent (fp16 has 5-bit exponent biased at 15). **But bf16 has 8-bit exponent biased at 127 — same as fp32.** So bf16 has the FULL fp32 range; no overflow can happen except for fp32 inf/nan (already handled above at lines 74-82).

For any fp32 value with `|x| > 2^15 = 32768`, this code wrongly clamps to bf16 +Inf. That's a real correctness bug.

Let me fix it:
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/dtype/Types.h

Yes — that's exactly the block I just removed. Confirming the change:
> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/Neural_Networks_exp_1926/BluTrain/Tensor-Implementations/include/dtype/Types.h

The buggy clamp is gone. Now `float_to_bfloat16` correctly:
- Passes through `Inf`/`NaN` (top branch)
- Truncates+RNE-rounds for all other finite fp32 values (no incorrect overflow clamp)

## Sanity check on the math

The clamp WAS:
```cpp
if (exponent > 0x8E)  // exponent > 142 → clamp to Inf
```

| Format | exponent bits | exp bias | max biased | range |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| fp32 | 8 | 127 | 254 (255=Inf/NaN) | ~3.4e38 |
| **bf16** | **8** | **127** | **254** | **~3.4e38 ← same as fp32** |
| fp16 | 5 | 15 | 30 (31=Inf/NaN) | ~6.5e4 |

The constant `142 = 127 + 15` corresponds to the fp16 max non-Inf exponent (5-bit exponent encoded as 30, plus fp32 bias offset 112 = 142). It has no meaning for bf16.

Any fp32 value with `|x| ≥ 2^15 = 32768` was wrongly clamped to bf16 Inf. **Real bug.**

## Whether this is the gradient-divergence cause

Probably **not directly** — our model trains in fp32 end-to-end and gradient values are small (norm ~15 at step 0). But it's worth checking if anything in the pipeline silently converts to bf16 (DDP allreduce, checkpoint save, debug dumps).

But ALSO worth fixing on its own merits — it's a real correctness bug that would bite anyone running fp32→bf16 conversion with large values.

__device__ __host__ inline float bfloat16_to_float(uint16_t b) {
    uint32_t sign = (b & 0x8000u) << 16;      // Sign bit to float position
    uint32_t exp = (b & 0x7F80u) >> 7;        // Extract exponent (8 bits)
    uint32_t frac = (b & 0x007Fu);             // Extract mantissa (7 bits)
    uint32_t u;

    if (exp == 0xFF) {
        // Inf or NaN
        if (frac == 0) {
            // Infinity
            u = sign | 0x7F800000u; // float infinity pattern
        } else {
            // NaN - set quiet NaN with some mantissa bits preserved
            u = sign | 0x7F800000u | (frac << 16);
        }
    } else {
        // Normal or subnormal number: shift bfloat16 bits to float position
        u = (static_cast<uint32_t>(b)) << 16;
    }

    float f;
    ::std::memcpy(&f, &u, sizeof(f));
    return f;
}


__device__ __host__ inline uint16_t float_to_bfloat16(float f) {
    uint32_t u;
    std::memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof(u));
    uint32_t sign = u & 0x80000000u;
    uint32_t exponent = (u >> 23) & 0xFF;
    uint32_t mantissa = u & 0x7FFFFFu;

    // Handle NaN and Infinity explicitly
    if (exponent == 0xFF) {
        if (mantissa == 0) {
            // Infinity
            return static_cast<uint16_t>((sign >> 16) | 0x7F80u);
        } else {
            // NaN: keep quiet NaN pattern
            return static_cast<uint16_t>((sign >> 16) | 0x7FC1u);
        }
    }

   
    // Normal rounding and truncation
    uint32_t lsb = (u >> 16) & 1u;
    uint32_t rounding_bias = 0x7FFFu;
    if (lsb) rounding_bias = 0x8000u;
    u += rounding_bias;

    return static_cast<uint16_t>(u >> 16);
}

// ---- Float16 Conversions (IEEE 754 Half-Precision) ----
__device__ __host__ inline float float16_to_float(uint16_t h) {
    uint32_t sign = (h & 0x8000u) << 16;
    uint32_t exp  = (h & 0x7C00u) >> 10;
    uint32_t frac = (h & 0x03FFu);
    uint32_t u;

    if (exp == 0) {
        if (frac == 0) {
            // Zero (preserve sign)
            u = sign;
        } else {
            // Denormal number
            float f = static_cast<float>(frac) / 1024.0f;
            #ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
            f = ldexpf(f, -14);
            #else
            f = ::std::ldexp(f, -14);
            #endif
            if (sign) f = -f;
            ::std::memcpy(&u, &f, sizeof(f));
        }
    } else if (exp == 0x1F) {
        // Infinity or NaN
        u = sign | 0x7F800000u | (frac << 13);
    } else {
        // Normal number
        uint32_t exp32 = exp + (127 - 15);
        u = sign | (exp32 << 23) | (frac << 13);
    }
    
    float f;
    std::memcpy(&f, &u, sizeof(f));
    return f;
}

__device__ __host__ inline uint16_t float_to_float16(float f) {
    uint32_t x;
    std::memcpy(&x, &f, sizeof(x));
    
    uint32_t sign = (x >> 16) & 0x8000u;
    uint32_t exp_32 = (x >> 23) & 0xFF;
    uint32_t mant_32 = x & 0x007FFFFFu;

    // 1. Handle NaN and Infinity
    if (exp_32 == 0xFF) {
        if (mant_32 == 0) {
            // Infinity
            return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign | 0x7C00u);
        } else {
            // NaN
            uint32_t qnan_mant = mant_32 >> 13;
            if (qnan_mant == 0) qnan_mant = 1;
            return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign | 0x7C00u | qnan_mant);
        }
    }

    int32_t exp_16 = static_cast<int32_t>(exp_32) - 127 + 15;

    if (exp_16 <= 0) {
        if (exp_16 < -10) return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign);
        mant_32 |= 0x00800000u;
        uint32_t shift = static_cast<uint32_t>(1 - exp_16);
        uint32_t half_mant = mant_32 >> (shift + 13);
        return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign | half_mant);
    } else if (exp_16 >= 31) {
        // Overflow to infinity
        return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign | 0x7C00u);
    } else {
        uint16_t half_exp = static_cast<uint16_t>(exp_16);
        uint32_t half_mant = mant_32 + 0x00001000u;
        return static_cast<uint16_t>(sign | (half_exp << 10) | (half_mant >> 13));
    }
}

// CUSTOM STRUCT DEFINITIONS FOR BF16/FP16 - FULLY DEVICE-COMPATIBLE

/**
 * @brief BFloat16 (Brain Floating Point 16)
 * Format: Sign(1) + Exponent(8) + Mantissa(7)
 * Range: Same as Float32, reduced precision
 * Use case: Deep learning, faster than FP32, wider range than FP16
 */
struct bfloat16_t {
    uint16_t raw_bits;

    // ---- Constructors ----
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t() : raw_bits(0) {}
    __device__ __host__ explicit bfloat16_t(float val) { raw_bits = detail::float_to_bfloat16(val); }
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t(const bfloat16_t& other) : raw_bits(other.raw_bits) {}

    template <typename U, typename = ::std::enable_if_t<
        ::std::is_arithmetic_v<U> && !::std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<U>, float>
    >>    
    __device__ __host__ explicit bfloat16_t(U val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_bfloat16(static_cast<float>(val));
    }

    __device__ __host__ operator float() const { return detail::bfloat16_to_float(raw_bits); }

    // ---- Assignment Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator=(float val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_bfloat16(val);
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator=(const bfloat16_t& other) {
        raw_bits = other.raw_bits;
        return *this;
    }

    template <typename U, typename = ::std::enable_if_t<
        ::std::is_arithmetic_v<U> && !::std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<U>, float>
    >>
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator=(U val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_bfloat16(static_cast<float>(val));
        return *this;
    }

    // ---- Comparison Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ bool operator>(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) > static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator<(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) < static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator>=(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) >= static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator<=(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) <= static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator==(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return raw_bits == other.raw_bits;
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator!=(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return raw_bits != other.raw_bits;
    }

    // ---- Arithmetic Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t operator+(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) + static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t operator-(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) - static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t operator*(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) * static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t operator/(const bfloat16_t& other) const {
        return bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) / static_cast<float>(other));
    }

    // ---- Compound Assignment Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator+=(const bfloat16_t& other) {
        *this = bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) + static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator-=(const bfloat16_t& other) {
        *this = bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) - static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator*=(const bfloat16_t& other) {
        *this = bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) * static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ bfloat16_t& operator/=(const bfloat16_t& other) {
        *this = bfloat16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) / static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
};

/**
 * @brief Float16 (IEEE 754 Half Precision)
 * Format: Sign(1) + Exponent(5) + Mantissa(10)
 * Range: ±65504, limited but higher precision than BF16
 * Use case: Graphics, mobile AI, memory-constrained scenarios
 */
struct float16_t {
    uint16_t raw_bits;

    // ---- Constructors ----
    __device__ __host__ float16_t() : raw_bits(0) {}
    __device__ __host__ explicit float16_t(float val) { raw_bits = detail::float_to_float16(val); }
    __device__ __host__ float16_t(const float16_t& other) : raw_bits(other.raw_bits) {}

    template <typename U, typename = ::std::enable_if_t<
        ::std::is_arithmetic_v<U> && !::std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<U>, float>
    >>
    __device__ __host__ explicit float16_t(U val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_float16(static_cast<float>(val));
    }

    __device__ __host__ operator float() const { return detail::float16_to_float(raw_bits); }

    // ---- Assignment Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator=(float val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_float16(val);
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator=(const float16_t& other) {
        raw_bits = other.raw_bits;
        return *this;
    }

    template <typename U, typename = ::std::enable_if_t<
        ::std::is_arithmetic_v<U> && !::std::is_same_v<std::decay_t<U>, float>
    >>
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator=(U val) {
        raw_bits = detail::float_to_float16(static_cast<float>(val));
        return *this;
    }

    // ---- Comparison Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ bool operator>(const float16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) > static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator<(const float16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) < static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator>=(const float16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) >= static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator<=(const float16_t& other) const {
        return static_cast<float>(*this) <= static_cast<float>(other);
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator==(const float16_t& other) const {
        return raw_bits == other.raw_bits;
    }
    __device__ __host__ bool operator!=(const float16_t& other) const {
        return raw_bits != other.raw_bits;
    }

    // ---- Arithmetic Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ float16_t operator+(const float16_t& other) const {
        return float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) + static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t operator-(const float16_t& other) const {
        return float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) - static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t operator*(const float16_t& other) const {
        return float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) * static_cast<float>(other));
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t operator/(const float16_t& other) const {
        return float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) / static_cast<float>(other));
    }

    // ---- Compound Assignment Operators ----
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator+=(const float16_t& other) {
        *this = float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) + static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator-=(const float16_t& other) {
        *this = float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) - static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator*=(const float16_t& other) {
        *this = float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) * static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
    
    __device__ __host__ float16_t& operator/=(const float16_t& other) {
        *this = float16_t(static_cast<float>(*this) / static_cast<float>(other));
        return *this;
    }
};

namespace std {

/**
 * @brief Helper template for numeric_limits of 16-bit float types.
 */
template <typename T>
struct numeric_limits_fp16_helper {
    static constexpr bool is_specialized = true;
    static constexpr bool is_signed = true;
    static constexpr bool is_integer = false;
    static constexpr bool is_exact = false;
    static constexpr bool has_infinity = true;
    static constexpr bool has_quiet_NaN = true;
    static constexpr bool has_signaling_NaN = true;
    
    static T lowest() noexcept;
    static T max() noexcept;
    static T min() noexcept { return T(1.0e-8f); }
    static T epsilon() noexcept { return T(0.0001f); }
    static T infinity() noexcept { return T(std::numeric_limits<float>::infinity()); }
    static T quiet_NaN() noexcept { return T(std::numeric_limits<float>::quiet_NaN()); }
};

// ---- BFloat16 Limits ----
template <>
struct numeric_limits<OwnTensor::bfloat16_t> : public numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::bfloat16_t> {};

template <>
inline OwnTensor::bfloat16_t numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::bfloat16_t>::lowest() noexcept {
    return OwnTensor::bfloat16_t(-3.38953e38f);
}

template <>
inline OwnTensor::bfloat16_t numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::bfloat16_t>::max() noexcept {
    return OwnTensor::bfloat16_t(3.38953e38f);
}

// ---- Float16 Limits ----
template <>
struct numeric_limits<OwnTensor::float16_t> : public numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::float16_t> {};

template <>
inline OwnTensor::float16_t numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::float16_t>::lowest() noexcept {
    return OwnTensor::float16_t(-65504.0f);
}

template <>
inline OwnTensor::float16_t numeric_limits_fp16_helper<OwnTensor::float16_t>::max() noexcept {
    return OwnTensor::float16_t(65504.0f);
}
