        }
        MPI_Barrier(MPI_COMM_WORLD);
        MPI_Finalize();
        return 0;
    }
    */

    // Load HellaSwag val once. Every rank loads (file is small, ~10 MB) so the
    // eval loop can shard examples by index without a separate broadcast.
    // If the binary is missing the eval is skipped with a warning instead of
    // aborting training.
    std::vector<hellaswag::Example> hellaswag_examples;
    try {
        hellaswag_examples = hellaswag::load_binary("hellaswag/hellaswag_val.bin");
        if (is_master)
            std::cout << "loaded " << hellaswag_examples.size()
                      << " HellaSwag val examples" << std::endl;
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        if (is_master)
            std::cerr << "[WARN] HellaSwag eval disabled: " << e.what()
                      << "\n[WARN] Run: python prep_hellaswag.py" << std::endl;
    }

    std::cout << "\nStarting training..." << std::endl;



    CheckpointManager ckpt_manager("checkpoints", "gpt2", 5, rank, false, false);


    
    // No interval-based auto-saves: the val block below does an explicit
    // `.save()` matching gpt2.py's structure (save lives in the val block,
    // before the optimizer step). This guarantees `gpt2_step_N.ckpt` and the
    // step-N eval reflect the SAME model state.

    int start_step = 0;
    float latest_loss = 0.0f;

    // Auto-resume if checkpoint exists. With the new save semantics
    // (checkpoint at step N == model state BEFORE iteration N's training),
    // resuming means: skip N*GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS batches consumed by steps 0..N-1
    // and start the loop at step N. No `start_step++`.
    if (config.checkpointing && ckpt_manager.load_latest(model, optimizer, start_step, latest_loss)) {
        std::cout << "[Resume] Continuing from step " << start_step << " with loss " << latest_loss << std::endl;
        size_t batches_to_skip = static_cast<size_t>(start_step) * GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS;
        if (batches_to_skip > 0) {
            std::cout << "[Resume] Skipping " << batches_to_skip << " batches..." << std::endl;
            train_loader.skip_batches(batches_to_skip);
        }
    }
        
    // Create CSV log file (master only — avoid multi-rank truncation races)
    std::ofstream log_file;
    if(is_master && config.if_log) {
        log_file.open("may20_final_check_1gpu_sample_check.csv");
        log_file << "step,loss,val_loss,hellaswag_acc,lr,grad_norm,dt_ms,tok_per_sec,elapsed_min\n";
        log_file << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6);
        log_file.flush();  // ensure header survives if training is killed mid-step
    }


    float val_loss_accum_log = -1.0f;     // -1 indicates no validation this step
    float hellaswag_acc_log = -1.0f;      // -1 indicates no hellaswag eval this step

    // Pre-allocate training loop tensors (avoids per-step allocation)
    Tensor grad_scale = Tensor::full(Shape{{1}}, TensorOptions().with_device(device),
                                        1.0f / static_cast<float>(GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS));
    Tensor loss_accum_gpu = Tensor::zeros(Shape{{1}}, TensorOptions().with_device(device));

    // Target loss tracking state
    bool train_loss_reached = false;
    bool val_loss_reached = false;
    auto training_start = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

    for (int step = start_step; step < MAX_STEPS; ++step) {
        auto t0 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();

        // PrecLogger: select this step (or no-op) before any forward/backward.
        // Param values are dumped here (pre-step state, matches the PyTorch
        // hook timing of dumping params before the step's forward).
        prec::Logger::instance().begin_step(step);
        if (prec::Logger::instance().active()) {
            for (const auto& kv : named_params) {
                prec::Logger::instance().dump_param(kv.first, kv.second);
            }
        }
        
        // Validation every VAL_FREQ steps
        if (step % VAL_FREQ == 0 || step == MAX_STEPS - 1) {
            autograd::NoGradGuard no_grad;  // No backward graph needed for validation
            val_loader.reset();
            float val_loss_accum = 0.0f;
            int val_loss_steps = 20;

            for (int val_step = 0; val_step < val_loss_steps; ++val_step) {
                Batch batch = val_loader.next_batch();

                Tensor logits = model.forward(batch.input);
                Tensor loss = autograd::sparse_cross_entropy_loss(logits, batch.target);
                
                Tensor loss_cpu = loss.to_cpu();
                val_loss_accum += loss_cpu.data<float>()[0] / static_cast<float>(val_loss_steps);
            }
            
            // Average validation loss across all ranks (skip the collective on single-GPU)
            float global_val_loss = val_loss_accum;
            if (world_size > 1) {
                MPI_Allreduce(&val_loss_accum, &global_val_loss, 1, MPI_FLOAT, MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
                global_val_loss /= world_size;
            }

            if(is_master) std::cout << "validation loss: " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4) << global_val_loss << std::endl;
            val_loss_accum_log = global_val_loss;

            // Check if target val loss reached
            if (!val_loss_reached && global_val_loss <= TARGET_VAL_LOSS && is_master) {
                val_loss_reached = true;
                auto now = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
                double elapsed_min = std::chrono::duration<double>(now - training_start).count() / 60.0;
                std::cout << ">>> TARGET VAL LOSS " << TARGET_VAL_LOSS
                            << " reached at step " << step
                            << " | val_loss=" << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << global_val_loss
                            << " | elapsed=" << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << elapsed_min << " min"
                            << std::endl;
                if(config.if_log) log_file << "# TARGET_VAL_LOSS=" << TARGET_VAL_LOSS
                            << " reached at step " << step
                            << " val_loss=" << global_val_loss
                            << " elapsed_min=" << elapsed_min << "\n";
                if(config.if_log) log_file.flush();
            }

            // HellaSwag eval (matches gpt2.py:507-538). Sharded across ranks
            // by example index, counts MPI-allreduced, master logs accuracy.
            // Stash into hellaswag_acc_log so this step's CSV row carries the
            // value; non-eval steps write -1 in that column.
            // edits: Gautam_Reddy_1926 — BENCHMARK MODE: disabled HellaSwag to get
            //   clean training-only throughput numbers. val_loss stays as canary.
            //   Re-enable by removing the `false &&` once optimization work is done.
            if (false && !hellaswag_examples.empty()) {
                double hella_acc = hellaswag::evaluate(
                    model, device, rank, world_size,
                    hellaswag_examples, is_master, step);
                hellaswag_acc_log = static_cast<float>(hella_acc);
            }

            // Checkpoint save (matches gpt2.py:494-505 — save lives inside
            // the val block, BEFORE the iteration's optimizer.step()). This
            // way gpt2_step_N.ckpt is the same model state the eval at step
            // N just measured: load it back, re-run hellaswag.py, get the
            // same accuracy reported above.
            if (config.checkpointing && (step % CKPT_FREQ == 0 || step == MAX_STEPS - 1)) {
                try {
                    ckpt_manager.save(step, model, optimizer, val_loss_accum_log);
                } catch (const std::exception& e) {
                    if (is_master)
                        std::cerr << "[WARN] checkpoint save at step " << step
                                  << " failed: " << e.what() << std::endl;
                }
            }
        }
        
        // token generation — run on master only so non-master ranks don't enter
        // the same path concurrently (rules out per-rank races + isolates the
        // crash to a single rank's stderr).
        // edits: Gautam_Reddy_1926 — BENCHMARK MODE: disabled token generation to
        //   eliminate D2H/CPU/H2D per-token overhead from the timeline. The current
        //   gen impl has known inefficiencies (CPU top-k due to softmax NaN bug,
        //   no KV cache); orthogonal to matmul throughput work. Re-enable by
        //   removing the `false &&` once optimization work is done.
        if(false && is_master && (step % TOK_GEN_FREQ == 0 || step == MAX_STEPS - 1)) {
                autograd::NoGradGuard no_grad;  // No backward graph needed for generation
                std::cout << "--- Generating tokens at step " << step << " ---" << std::endl;
                int num_return_sequence = 4;
                int max_length = 60;

                Tensor xgen = Tensor(Shape({{num_return_sequence, 2}}),
                                           TensorOptions().with_dtype(Dtype::Int64).with_device(device));
                static const std::vector<int64_t> xgen_tokens = {18165, 318,18165, 318,18165, 318,18165, 318};
                xgen.set_data(xgen_tokens);

                uint64_t gen_seed = 42 + rank;
                while (xgen.shape().dims[1] < max_length) {
                    Tensor logits = model.forward(xgen);

                    int64_t B = logits.shape().dims[0];
                    int64_t T = logits.shape().dims[1];

                    // Zero-copy view: logits[:, -1, :] -> (B, 1, V)
                    // Replaces gather which allocated a [B, 1, V] Int64 index tensor per step
                    // NOTE: softmax CUDA fast-path assumes contiguous row-major layout;
                    // narrow_view leaves dim-0 stride = T*V, so we MUST materialize a
                    // contiguous copy before softmax — otherwise rows 1..B-1 read
                    // neighbouring batches' logits and can surface NaN/Inf in probs.
                    Tensor last_logits_3d = logits.narrow_view(1, T - 1, 1).contiguous();

                    // ---- Top-k sampling computed on CPU for numerical robustness ----
                    // The fused CUDA softmax kernel (SoftmaxKernels.cu) occasionally
                    // produces NaN for one row when applied over V=50304; since generation
                    // is cheap (B*V floats per step), we do top-k + softmax on the CPU
                    // directly from logits. This sidesteps the kernel bug entirely.
                    constexpr int TOPK = 50;
                    Tensor logits_cpu = last_logits_3d.to_cpu();           // [B,1,V] float32
                    const float* lg = logits_cpu.data<float>();
                    int64_t V = last_logits_3d.shape().dims.back();

                    // Output: next-token indices (B, 1) Int64 on CPU
                    Tensor next_token_cpu(Shape{{B, 1}},
                                          TensorOptions().with_dtype(Dtype::Int64));
                    int64_t* nt = next_token_cpu.data<int64_t>();

                    std::mt19937 rng(static_cast<uint32_t>(gen_seed++));
                    std::uniform_real_distribution<float> uni(0.0f, 1.0f);

                    for (int64_t b = 0; b < B; ++b) {
                        const float* row = lg + b * V;

                        // Partial sort for top-k by logit value
                        std::vector<int64_t> idx(V);
                        std::iota(idx.begin(), idx.end(), 0);
                        std::partial_sort(
                            idx.begin(), idx.begin() + TOPK, idx.end(),
                            [row](int64_t a, int64_t b) { return row[a] > row[b]; });

                        // Numerically-stable softmax over the top-k only
                        float mx = row[idx[0]];
                        double sum = 0.0;
                        std::array<double, TOPK> w{};
                        for (int k = 0; k < TOPK; ++k) {
                            w[k] = std::exp(static_cast<double>(row[idx[k]] - mx));
                            sum += w[k];
                        }
                        // Sample via inverse-CDF
                        double r = static_cast<double>(uni(rng)) * sum;
                        double acc = 0.0;
                        int chosen = TOPK - 1;
                        for (int k = 0; k < TOPK; ++k) {
                            acc += w[k];
                            if (r <= acc) { chosen = k; break; }
                        }
                        nt[b] = idx[chosen];
                    }

                    Tensor next_token = next_token_cpu.to(device);

                    xgen = Tensor::cat({xgen, next_token}, 1);
                }

                // Print generated tokens
                Tensor xgen_cpu = xgen.to_cpu();
                int64_t* data = xgen_cpu.data<int64_t>();
                int64_t B = xgen.shape().dims[0];
                int64_t T = xgen.shape().dims[1];

                for (int i = 0; i < B; ++i) {
                    std::cout << "sample" << i << "= \"";
                    for (int j = 0; j < T; ++j) {
                        std::cout << data[i * T + j] << " ";
                    }
                    std::cout << "\""<<std::endl;
                }
            }



        // Training step

       // optimizer.zero_grad();
        optimizer.zero_grad();
        // optimizer.zero_grad();  // old comment
        // for(auto& param : params){
        //     if (void* g = param.grad()) {                    // skip null grads on first step
        //         cudaMemsetAsync(g, 0, param.nbytes());
        //     }
        // }
        cudaError_t err = cudaGetLastError();
if (err != cudaSuccess) {
    std::cerr << "[step " << step << "] CUDA sticky error after zero_grad: "
              << cudaGetErrorString(err) << std::endl;
}


        float loss_accum = 0.0f;

        // Reset pre-allocated GPU accumulator in-place (no new allocation)
        loss_accum_gpu *= 0.0f;
        if (ddp_model) ddp_model->no_sync();
        for (int micro_step = 0; micro_step < GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS; ++micro_step) {
            Batch batch = train_loader.next_batch();

            Tensor logits = ddp_model ? ddp_model->forward(batch.input)
                                      : model.forward(batch.input);
            Tensor loss = autograd::sparse_cross_entropy_loss(logits, batch.target);

            // In-place accumulate on GPU (no new tensor allocation per micro-step)
            loss_accum_gpu += loss.detach();
            if (ddp_model && micro_step == GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS - 1) ddp_model->sync();
            // Backward with scaling
            loss.backward(&grad_scale);
        }
        
        // ONE sync after all micro-steps complete
        {
            Tensor loss_cpu = loss_accum_gpu.to_cpu();
            float local_loss = loss_cpu.data<float>()[0] / static_cast<float>(GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS);
            if (world_size > 1) {
                MPI_Allreduce(&local_loss, &loss_accum, 1, MPI_FLOAT, MPI_SUM, MPI_COMM_WORLD);
                loss_accum /= world_size;
            } else {
                loss_accum = local_loss;
            }
        }
        
        // NaN detection - early exit if training goes unstable
        if (std::isnan(loss_accum) || std::isinf(loss_accum)) {
            std::cerr << "ERROR: NaN/Inf detected in loss at step " << step << std::endl;
            if(config.if_log) log_file.close();
            return 1;
        }

        // Check if target train loss reached
        if (!train_loss_reached && loss_accum <= TARGET_TRAIN_LOSS && is_master) {
            train_loss_reached = true;
            auto now = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
            double elapsed_min = std::chrono::duration<double>(now - training_start).count() / 60.0;
            std::cout << ">>> TARGET TRAIN LOSS " << TARGET_TRAIN_LOSS
                        << " reached at step " << step
                        << " | train_loss=" << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << loss_accum
                        << " | elapsed=" << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << elapsed_min << " min"
                        << std::endl;
            if(config.if_log) log_file << "# TARGET_TRAIN_LOSS=" << TARGET_TRAIN_LOSS
                        << " reached at step " << step
                        << " train_loss=" << loss_accum
                        << " elapsed_min=" << elapsed_min << "\n";
            if(config.if_log) log_file.flush();
        }

        // PrecLogger: dump per-param gradients AFTER backward+DDP all-reduce
        // and BEFORE clipping — matches the PyTorch hook site in gpt2.py.
        if (prec::Logger::instance().active()) {
            for (const auto& kv : named_params) {
                if (kv.second.has_grad()) {
                    prec::Logger::instance().dump_grad(kv.first, kv.second.grad_view());
                }
            }
        }

        // Clip gradients
        float norm = nn::clip_grad_norm_(params, 1.0f);
        
        // Update learning rate
        float lr = get_lr(step, MAX_LR, MIN_LR, WARMUP_STEPS, MAX_STEPS);
        optimizer.set_lr(lr);

        // Decoupled weight decay for dim>=2 params (PyTorch AdamW semantics).
        // Applied manually so the optimizer can stay a single AdamW with wd=0
        // and we keep one step()/multi_tensor_adam_cuda call per iteration —
        // two back-to-back step() calls race on the kernel's static host
        // metadata buffers and require a stream sync that wrecks throughput.
        const float wd_factor = 1.0f - lr * WEIGHT_DECAY;
        for (auto& p : decay_params) p *= wd_factor;

        // Optimizer step (wd=0 inside; pure Adam update on all params).
        optimizer.step();

        // (No checkpoint save here — saves live in the val block above so the
        // checkpoint state matches the eval state, mirroring gpt2.py.)
        
        auto t1 = std::chrono::high_resolution_clock::now();
        double dt = std::chrono::duration<double>(t1 - t0).count();
        
        // Compute throughput
        int64_t tokens_processed = static_cast<int64_t>(B) * T * GRAD_ACCUM_STEPS * world_size;
        double tokens_per_sec = static_cast<double>(tokens_processed) / dt;
        
        // Print training info
        if(is_master) std::cout << "step " << std::setw(5) << step 
                    << " | loss: " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(6) << loss_accum 
                    << " | lr " << std::scientific << std::setprecision(4) << lr 
                    << " | norm: " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(4) << norm 
                    << " | dt: " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << (dt * 1000.0) << "ms"
                    << " | tok/sec: " << std::fixed << std::setprecision(2) << tokens_per_sec 
                    << std::endl;
        
        // Log metrics to CSV
        double elapsed_total_min = std::chrono::duration<double>(t1 - training_start).count() / 60.0;
        if(is_master && config.if_log) log_file << step << ","
                    << loss_accum << ","
                    << val_loss_accum_log << ","
                    << hellaswag_acc_log << ","
                    << lr << ","
                    << norm << ","
                    << (dt * 1000.0) << ","
                    << tokens_per_sec << ","
                    << elapsed_total_min << "\n";
        if(is_master && config.if_log) log_file.flush();
        val_loss_accum_log = -1.0f;     // Reset for next iteration
        hellaswag_acc_log = -1.0f;

        prec::Logger::instance().end_step();

        if (step == 0) {
            CachingCUDAAllocator::instance().empty_cache();
        }
    }
    if(is_master && config.if_log) log_file.close();
    
    
    if(is_master) std::cout << "\n=== Training Complete ===" << std::endl;

    // Flush any in-flight async save and reset the manager BEFORE MPI_Finalize
    // so the destructor's rename / cuda-stream-destroy can't fight with MPI's
    // teardown. Wrapped in try/catch as belt-and-braces against a stale
    // rename surfacing during shutdown.
    try {
        ckpt_manager.wait_for_completion();
    } catch (const std::exception& e) {
        if (is_master)
            std::cerr << "[WARN] checkpoint flush at shutdown: " << e.what() << std::endl;
    }

    MPI_Finalize();
    return 0;
}

### CLAUDE [2026-05-23 19:21 IST]

then i moved to item 3 the 256x128 backward dW kernel, asked the explore agent to deeply look at how cutlass handles this exact layout, the answer came back clear that cutlass also uses scalar loads not ldmatrix for tf32 in TN layout, ldmatrix works at 16 bit granularity but tf32 is 32 bit and when the axis is transposed the chunks don't line up which is exactly the NaN bug i hit earlier in the session, cutlass picks the column major congruous wrapper for TN which delegates to scalar loads at line 771-772 of mma tensor op tile iterator dot h, so the 4x gap between my TN kernel and NT kernel isn't a missing optimization it's a structural limitation of the layout, my kernel at this size is actually near as good as it can be, the only real way to close the bwd dW gap would be at the training loop level by computing dW transpose as NT then transposing the result, that's a call site change outside blublas scope

then i ran the script with both blublas and cublas and collected fresh nsys reports for comparison, the high level metrics show hellaswag accuracy of 2565 and 2559 in both runs and step 0 loss matches at 10.995877 so correctness is preserved, the steady state step time is 10.7 seconds for blublas vs 10.3 seconds for cublas, total wall clock gap of about 25 seconds across 10 steps, total gpu time gap of 28.8 seconds from nsys with blublas at 175.7 seconds total and cublas at 146.9 seconds total, blublas uses 43 distinct kernel variants while cublas uses 50, so cublas has more dispatch diversity

did a deep matmul variant by variant comparison with full launch configs from nsys, for every matmul kernel i pulled registers per thread, threads per block, smem usage, and occupancy theoretical limit on the sm 89 gpu, the biggest findings are that blublas hits the 255 register cap on 5 kernels while cublas stays around 215 to 228 with headroom meaning my kernels are spilling to local memory while cublas isn't, cublas also uses less smem 72 kibibytes vs my 96 kibibytes on the 256x128 family which leaves more L2 headroom, and cublas has 256x64 tile variants for nn and tn shapes which i completely lack, also cublas has gemmSN gemv like kernels for tiny shapes that i don't have

after that vinod asked me to compare the matmul variants only with all metrics in full detail, i pulled launch configs from the sqlite reports and built the side by side table, blublas total matmul time is 122.7 seconds vs cublas 86.6 seconds for a gap of 36.5 seconds in matmul gpu time, but total wall clock gap is only 25 seconds because stream overlap with attention and other kernels absorbs some of the gap, the biggest per call gaps are 64x64 at 1.58x slower (40.8 micro vs 25.9 micro), backward dW 256x128 at 1.80x slower (3050 micro vs 1694 micro), backward dX fanout (30000 calls vs 5914 calls for the same logical workload), and missing 256x64 tile costs 1.8 seconds

vinod then pointed out that the nsys timeline visuals show gaps at start and end with solid blue in the middle, asked if these gaps are due to hellaswag and token gen and val loss, did the math from the logs and confirmed step 0 is 70 seconds vs steady state 10.7 seconds so step 0 has 60 extra seconds from val plus hellaswag plus token gen, step 9 has 40 extra seconds from same, so 87 percent of the visible wall clock gap is from eval overhead not training compute, the real training throughput gap is only 3 to 4 percent per step

then read the actual implementations of hellaswag and val loss and token gen and compared against the pytorch reference at gpt2 dot py, the math and logic in my implementations is correct and produces matching outputs but the implementations have inefficiencies, hellaswag does 4 separate cross entropy calls per example with 4 to cpu syncs while pytorch does one cross entropy with mask and one argmin sync, val loss does 20 to cpu syncs while pytorch keeps the accumulator on gpu and syncs once at end, token gen does cpu side top k sampling with D2H per token because of a noted softmax kernel NaN bug while pytorch keeps everything on gpu, all these inefficiencies hurt both blublas and cublas runs equally so they don't contribute to the blublas vs cublas gap but they make absolute eval times slower

confirmed bro you caught a real gap

**what's actually happening:**

**CPU side (floats):** uses `cascade_sum_kernel` at [ReductionImpl.h:2410](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionImpl.h#L2410) — 4-level cascading bucket accumulator (matches pytorch's `multi_row_sum`), pairwise-tree accuracy with O(1) storage. proper precision-preserving sum ✓

**GPU side (floats):** falls through `dispatch_reduction_gpu<T, SumOp>` at [line 2269](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionImpl.h#L2269) → runs `launch_reduce_kernel` with plain `SumOp` functor → reduce is just `gpu_add(a, b)` at [ReductionOps.h:427](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionOps.h#L427) — naive `a + b` accumulation, **NO cascade, NO compensation** ✗

**the GPU path has some implicit tree behavior though:**
- within a warp: `warp_shfl_down` is tree-reduction (32 → 16 → 8 → 4 → 2 → 1) ✓
- within a block: shared memory reduction is also tree ✓
- **across blocks: last-CTA gathers all per-CTA partials via a sequential `combine` loop at [ReductionKernels.cuh:599](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionKernels.cuh#L599)** — `value = combine(value, cta_buf[...])` in a strided loop, plain a+b each step

so it's partially tree (within block) but cross-block is sequential. error grows as O(num_blocks × eps) instead of O(log(num_blocks) × eps).

**is this wrong?**
- it's not a correctness BUG (PyTorch GPU does roughly the same — relies on `cub::BlockReduce` tree-within-block + accuracy-of-fp32-being-fine)
- it IS less precise than the CPU cascade path
- for reductions where num_elements is large (gradient L2 norm, layer_norm over hidden=768, loss accumulation), the GPU result will drift from the CPU result by some O(N×eps) bound

**what we COULD do:**
- add a `cascade_sum_gpu_kernel` that uses 4-level cascading inside each thread's grid-stride loop, then warp/block tree as before, then a cascading combine in the last CTA
- would match cuB's `cascaded_reduce` policy or `cub::DeviceReduce::Sum` which has better precision than naive accumulate

**should we?**
- separate issue from the matmul throughput gap we're chasing
- worth noting as a known precision delta between CPU and GPU sum paths
- if you've been seeing fp drift between CPU and GPU reductions in numerical tests, THIS is why

bro the screenshot is **mostly correct on the facts but WRONG on the conclusion**. let me verify each claim and clear up the misleading "compute-saving" framing

## fact-check the table

| claim | verdict | proof |
|---|---|---|
| pytorch GPU uses warp shuffle tree | ✅ TRUE | `gpu_reduce_kernel` in `aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/Reduce.cuh` uses `WARP_SHFL_DOWN` tree |
| pytorch GPU sum has NO NaN check in functor | ✅ TRUE | pytorch's sum functor is `func_wrapper(at::native::sum_functor)` which is plain `a + b`, no isnan |
| pytorch GPU does NOT use cascade sum | ✅ TRUE | only block-tree + cross-block partials, no 4-level cascading |
| our GPU has NaN early-return in SumOp::reduce | ✅ TRUE | i just read [ReductionOps.h:423-426](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionOps.h#L423-L426) — explicit `if (gpu_isnan(a)) return a; if (gpu_isnan(b)) return b;` |
| our GPU does NOT use cascade sum | ✅ TRUE | confirmed earlier — falls through to plain `gpu_add(a, b)` after the isnan checks |
| pytorch CPU uses cascade 4-level hierarchical | ✅ TRUE | `multi_row_sum` in SumKernel.cpp |
| our CPU uses cascade_sum_kernel 4-level | ✅ TRUE | confirmed at [ReductionImpl.h:139-185](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionImpl.h#L139-L185) |

so all 7 factual claims in the screenshot are **CORRECT**

## but the "compute-saving early-exit" claim is WRONG

the screenshot says: *"Our SumOp::reduce() has that extra early-return NaN check on GPU, which is technically unnecessary for correctness (IEEE 754 guarantees it) but serves as the compute-saving early-exit"*

this is **MISLEADING / FALSE**. it does NOT save compute. it ADDS overhead. here's why:

**cost per add operation:**

```cpp
// pytorch — plain add, 1 instruction
return a + b;        // 1 fp FADD

// ours — with NaN check, 5+ instructions per add
if (gpu_isnan(a)) return a;   // FSETP.GTU + branch
if (gpu_isnan(b)) return b;   // FSETP.GTU + branch
return a + b;                 // 1 fp FADD
```

so each add costs ~3-5× more instructions in ours than pytorch's.

**when does the "early exit" actually save work?**
- ONLY if the input already has NaN
- in which case the entire reduction is already poisoned and producing garbage anyway
- IEEE 754 guarantees `NaN + x = NaN` for plain `+`, so the result is identical whether we exit early or not

**what we're paying:**
- every healthy reduction (the 99.99% case) eats 2 extra isnan checks per add
- on N elements that's 2N wasted fp comparisons just to avoid a no-op early exit
- on a kernel doing 768-element layer norm sum or 50K-element gradient norm sum, this is real wasted GPU work

so this is actually an **INEFFICIENCY in our SumOp, not a feature**. pytorch deliberately leaves it out because IEEE 754 hardware propagates NaN for free.

## is cascade_reduce faster than naive accumulation?

cascade sum is primarily about **ACCURACY**, not speed — but on CPU it CAN be faster due to a side effect. on GPU it doesn't help much. let me explain:

**accuracy comparison (the main reason for cascade):**

| method | error growth |
|---|---|
| naive sequential `a + b` repeated N times | O(N × eps) |
| pairwise tree (full) | O(log N × eps) |
| 4-level cascade (PyTorch's compromise) | between the two — empirically near O(log N × eps) |

for fp32 with N = 1 million: naive error ~ N × 1.2e-7 = 0.12 (huge!), cascade error ~ 20 × 1.2e-7 = 2.4e-6 (tiny). this is why cascade matters for things like gradient L2 norm, loss accumulation, layer norm sums.

**speed comparison:**

| context | cascade vs naive | reason |
|---|---|---|
| CPU scalar | cascade roughly EQUAL | adds bookkeeping overhead, but better cache locality |
| CPU SIMD (AVX2/AVX-512) | cascade is **2-3× FASTER** | 4 independent acc registers break the serial dependency chain, lets SIMD pipeline run flat-out. naive is bottlenecked by 1 chain dep |
| GPU within-warp | cascade ≈ naive | warp shuffle is already tree-reducing, cascade adds little |
| GPU per-thread inner loop | cascade can be **2-4× faster** | thread does many adds in a grid-stride loop — same ILP benefit as CPU SIMD case |

**so cascade is:**
1. **always more ACCURATE** than naive
2. **2-3× FASTER on CPU SIMD** because of ILP (multiple independent accumulators)
3. **2-4× FASTER in per-thread inner loops on GPU** for the same ILP reason
4. **roughly equal** in the cross-warp tree phase (warp shuffle is already pairwise)

## SO the real picture for us

our GPU sum has TWO problems that the screenshot didn't flag correctly:

**problem 1: useless NaN check** (the screenshot misframed this as "compute-saving" but it's actually overhead)
- pytorch's plain `a+b` is faster per element AND still propagates NaN correctly via IEEE 754
- fix: remove the isnan early-return from our `SumOp::reduce`. zero correctness impact, 2-3× faster per add.

**problem 2: no cascade in per-thread accumulator loop**
- in the grid-stride loop where each GPU thread accumulates many elements before warp-reduce, we use one serial acc register
- pytorch GPU same, BUT a few new pytorch ops use cub's "raking" technique with multiple independent accs
- fix: convert the per-thread accumulator loop to use 4 independent accumulators (cascade-style), reduce them at the end
- benefit: 2-4× faster on memory-bound reductions due to ILP + better numerical accuracy

both fixes are independent and both worth doing. fix 1 is trivial (delete the isnan lines), fix 2 is a small refactor in the inner loop of `launch_reduce_kernel`.

**so on CPU, the SumOp::reduce `#else` branch is:**

```cpp
    if (is_nan_check(a)) return a;       // ← deleted by compiler
```

## are the NaN checks in argmin/argmax MANDATORY?

**YES, mandatory for correctness when called** — but for a different reason than the sum/product cases:

```cpp
// IEEE 754 truth table:
NaN < 3.0  → false      // NaN is not orderable
NaN > 3.0  → false      // both comparisons return false
NaN == 3.0 → false
```

so for `argmin`/`argmax`, if input has NaN at index 0 and value 3.0 at index 1:
- without NaN check: `3.0 > NaN` is false → "NaN is the max" → returns index 0 (**WRONG**)
- with NaN check: explicitly skip NaN → returns index 1 (correct)

unlike sum/product where IEEE hardware does the right thing for free, argmin/argmax's `<` and `>` literally produce WRONG output without an explicit NaN check. pytorch agrees here — their `LessOrNan` / `GreaterOrNan` wrappers at `SharedReduceOps.h:425-444` do the same explicit isnan check.

so **DO NOT REMOVE** the NaN checks from ArgMinOp / ArgMaxOp / NanArgMinOp / NanArgMaxOp. they're load-bearing.

## are we using argmin/argmax anywhere?

**NO. zero callers in our training pipeline.** searched:
- ✗ `gpt2_fmha_ddp.cpp` (training script) — no `argmin`/`argmax` calls
- ✗ `hellaswag_eval.h` — uses CPU `std::partial_sort`/host comparison, not tensor argmin
- ✗ `gpt2_scripts/` — no calls
- ✗ `Tensor-Implementations/src/nn/` (layers) — no calls
- ✗ `Tensor-Implementations/src/autograd/` (autograd ops) — no calls
- ✗ `Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/` (cuda kernels) — no calls
- ✗ `dist/` (distributed) — no calls

the only places `reduce_argmin`/`reduce_argmax` appear are their DEFINITIONS at `src/UnaryOps/cpu/Reduction.cpp:152` and `src/UnaryOps/cpu/Reduction.cpp:173`. they exist as public API but nothing in our training workload calls them.

similarly `nanargmin`/`nanargmax` exist as public API in `Reduction.cpp:194` and `Reduction.cpp:222` but have no callers either.

token generation uses `std::partial_sort` on CPU (per the gen code we read earlier), HellaSwag uses scalar CE losses + a CPU loop comparison for picking the best row, attention softmax doesn't use argmax — all the places you'd expect to see argmax usage instead use other paths.

## verdict

- **leave ArgMinOp / ArgMaxOp / NanArgMinOp / NanArgMaxOp NaN checks ALONE**
- they're correct (mandatory for IEEE-NaN ordering semantics, pytorch does the same)
- they're zero cost in our training because nothing calls them
- removing the checks would be wrong if someone ever uses these ops, with zero benefit today

the SumOp and ProductOp removals we just did are the only NaN-check changes worth making. those two ops ARE used heavily in training (every layer norm sum, gradient norm, loss accumulation, mean, etc.) and the IEEE 754 propagation handles NaN correctly there for free.

## the asymmetry problem you identified IS exactly what pytorch fixes with explicit isnan

**pytorch GPU `MaxNanFunctor`** at [`pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ReduceMaxValuesKernel.cu:20-32`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ReduceMaxValuesKernel.cu#L20-L32):
```cpp
template <typename acc_t>
struct MaxNanFunctor {
  __device__ __forceinline__ acc_t operator()(acc_t a, acc_t b) const {
    return (at::_isnan(a) || a > b) ? a : b;   // explicit isnan check on `a` FIRST
  }
};
```

walk through both asymmetric cases:
- `max(normal, NaN)`: `at::_isnan(normal) || normal > NaN` → `false || false` → return `b = NaN` ✓
- `max(NaN, normal)`: `at::_isnan(NaN) || NaN > normal` → `true || false` → return `a = NaN` ✓

without the isnan check it would return WRONG value in case 2 (the asymmetry you described). pytorch explicitly handles it.

**our equivalent** in MaxOp does the same thing (different syntax but equivalent semantics):
```cpp
if constexpr (is_any_float_v<T>) {
    if (gpu_isnan(a)) return a;
    if (gpu_isnan(b)) return b;
}
return gpu_gt(a, b) ? a : b;
```
✓ correct, matches pytorch

**pytorch CPU `max_impl`** at [`pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/zmath.h:209-216`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cpu/zmath.h#L209-L216):
```cpp
inline TYPE max_impl(TYPE a, TYPE b) {
    if (_isnan<TYPE>(a) || _isnan<TYPE>(b)) {
        return std::numeric_limits<TYPE>::quiet_NaN();
    } else {
        return std::max(a, b);
    }
}
```
fully symmetric — if either is NaN, return NaN. ours matches.

## first-NaN-index for argmax/argmin — confirmed with code

**pytorch `GreaterOrNan`** at [`pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/SharedReduceOps.h:435-447`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/SharedReduceOps.h#L435-L447):
```cpp
template <typename scalar_t>
struct GreaterOrNan {
  C10_DEVICE bool operator () (scalar_t a, scalar_t b, int64_t idx_a, int64_t idx_b) const {
    if (at::_isnan(a)) {
      if (at::_isnan(b)) {
        return idx_a < idx_b;        // both NaN → lower index wins (FIRST NaN)
      }
      return true;                    // a is NaN, b normal → a wins (NaN treated as max)
    }
    return (a == b) ? idx_a < idx_b : (a > b);
  }
};
```

walked through `[NaN(0), 5.0(1), NaN(2)]`:
1. start: acc = (-inf, 0)
2. compare with NaN(idx=0): `GreaterOrNan(-inf, NaN, 0, 0)`: a not NaN, b is → falls through to `(a > b)` → false → b wins → **acc = (NaN, 0)**
3. compare with 5.0(idx=1): `GreaterOrNan(NaN, 5.0, 0, 1)`: a is NaN → `return true` → **acc stays (NaN, 0)**
4. compare with NaN(idx=2): `GreaterOrNan(NaN, NaN, 0, 2)`: both NaN → `return idx_a < idx_b` → `0 < 2` → true → **acc stays (NaN, 0)**
5. **result: index 0 — FIRST NaN index** ✓

ours does the same thing in `ArgMaxOp` — confirmed correct.

`LessOrNan` for argmin at [`SharedReduceOps.h:422-433`](pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/SharedReduceOps.h#L422-L433) — mirror image, same first-NaN-index behavior. ours matches.

## our NanMinOp/NanMaxOp impls are CORRECT — keep them

look at the asymmetry — regular MinOp/MaxOp vs NanMinOp/NanMaxOp differ ONLY in the `return` direction of the NaN branch:

**regular MaxOp** (propagates NaN):
```cpp
if (gpu_isnan(a)) return a;   // ← return THE NaN
if (gpu_isnan(b)) return b;
return gpu_gt(a, b) ? a : b;
```

**NanMaxOp** ([line 970-976](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionOps.h#L970-L976)) (SKIPS NaN):
```cpp
if (gpu_isnan(a)) return b;   // ← return the OTHER (non-NaN)
if (gpu_isnan(b)) return a;
return gpu_gt(a, b) ? a : b;
```

walk through all cases for NanMaxOp:
- both NaN: `if(isnan(a)) return b` → returns b (which is also NaN) → propagates correctly when ALL inputs are NaN ✓
- a NaN, b normal: returns b (the non-NaN) → correctly skips a ✓
- a normal, b NaN: returns a (the non-NaN) → correctly skips b ✓
- neither NaN: `(a > b) ? a : b` — correct max ✓

semantically correct, same as numpy's `np.nanmax` behavior. NanMinOp mirror image, also correct.

## why pytorch DOESN'T have them but WE do

pytorch's design philosophy: only expose nan-aware ops that have ambiguous "skip vs propagate" semantics where users want both versions (sum/mean/median). for max/min they decided masking is sufficient: `torch.where(~torch.isnan(x), x, -inf).max()`.

we exposed them as first-class ops — slight API convenience, no performance cost since the kernel is the same template path.

## verdict — LEAVE THEM ALONE

| op | status | reason |
|---|---|---|
| NanMinOp NaN check | **KEEP** | entire purpose is "skip NaN" — without check, op becomes regular min |
| NanMaxOp NaN check | **KEEP** | same reason |

these are the OPPOSITE situation from SumOp/ProductOp:
- in sum/product the NaN check was redundant (IEEE 754 handles propagation for free via `a+b` and `a*b`)
- in nanmax/nanmin the NaN check IS the operation — it's what makes the op different from regular max/min

| op family | we have it? | pytorch has it? | NaN check needed? | action |

| nanargmax, nanargmin | ✓ | ✗ (not native) | YES (skip-NaN semantic) | KEEP |
| nansum, nanmean | ✓ | ✓ | YES (skip-NaN semantic) | KEEP |

only SumOp + ProductOp removals stand. everything else is correctly designed. our code matches pytorch where pytorch has the op, and extends pytorch where they chose not to expose certain nan-aware variants.

your analysis is correct bro — let me explain what's happening and fix it

## why OOM happened on RTX 3060

- the failing tensor: `(16, 1024, 50304)` × int64 = 824,180,736 elements × 8 bytes = **6.59 GB** (matches the error `cudaMallocAsync(size=6593445888)` exactly)
- RTX 3060 has 12 GB VRAM, but realistic free is ~10 GB after driver + CUDA context overhead
- the **caching allocator holds onto freed blocks** by design (for fast reuse). when src from previous case is "freed" via C++ scope-exit, the memory stays in the allocator's cache, not returned to the driver. so by the time we hit the int64 logits case, the cache has ~5-6 GB held in chunks of various sizes, none of which is a single 6.59 GB contiguous block

so yes, your read is right — **tensors are GPU-only ✓, process is GPU-only ✓, but the caching allocator means scope-exit doesn't actually return VRAM to the driver**. we need to explicitly trim cache between cases.

## fix: add explicit cache trim + memory pre-check + size cap

```cpp
{

}
```
which enables the isnan branches. **those isnan checks ARE mandatory** for nansum (entire purpose). don't touch them.

**(2) "cascade_sum is CPU-only right?"**

correct ✓ — cascade_sum_kernel only exists on the CPU dispatch path. GPU goes through `dispatch_reduction_gpu<T, SumOp>` at [ReductionImpl.h:2269](BluTrain_best_precision/Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionImpl.h#L2269), which calls `launch_reduce_kernel` with the SumOp functor.

**EXACTLY RIGHT.** i was over-hedging earlier. let me restate the prediction clearly:

| dtype on GPU | did SumOp::reduce isnan branch actually execute before? | expected speedup |
|---|---|---|
| **float32** | YES — `is_any_float_v<float> = true` → 2 isnan per add | **measurable speedup** ✓ |
| **float16** | YES — `is_any_float_v<float16_t> = true` → 2 isnan per add | **measurable speedup** ✓ |
| **bfloat16** | YES — `is_any_float_v<bfloat16_t> = true` → 2 isnan per add | **measurable speedup** ✓ |
| **int32** | NO — `is_any_float_v<int64_t accumulator> = false` → if constexpr elided at compile time | ~0 (control group) |
| **int64** | NO — same reason | ~0 (control group) |

so for GPU benchmarking:
- **3 dtypes (float32/float16/bfloat16) WILL show real per-call speedup** from removing 2 `gpu_isnan` calls per add — proportional to how compute-frontend-bound the reduction is (small tensors get bigger %, huge bandwidth-bound tensors get smaller %)
- **2 dtypes (int32/int64) are the control group** — they validate the noise floor. if int rows show ~0% delta but float rows show meaningful delta, the float improvement is **proven real signal**, not measurement noise

### CLAUDE [2026-05-25 20:10 IST]

bro headers don't get their own .o file, so we need to verify TWO things:
1. **the source-level change IS in the header** (sanity check)
2. **every .o file that includes the header was rebuilt** (otherwise old inlined code persists)

here's the command set, copy-paste into colleague's terminal:

```bash
# adjust this path to wherever colleague has the repo
cd ~/BluTrain   # or wherever
HDR=Tensor-Implementations/include/ops/helpers/ReductionOps.h
```

## STEP 1 — confirm the source has the new code

```bash
echo "=== 1a. Check SumOp::reduce has NO isnan check ==="
sed -n '/struct SumOp/,/struct ProductOp/p' $HDR | grep -nE "gpu_isnan|is_nan_check"
# Expected: ZERO output. If anything matches, the header doesn't have your changes.

echo ""
echo "=== 1b. Check the Gautam_Reddy_1926 sentinel comment IS present ==="
grep -c "Gautam_Reddy_1926" $HDR
# Expected: 2 (one each in SumOp + ProductOp). If 0, your edits never landed.
```

## STEP 2 — confirm the binary was rebuilt with the new header

```bash
echo "=== 2a. .so / .a should be newer than the header ==="
ls -la --time-style=full-iso $HDR \
  Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so \
  Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.a 2>/dev/null

# Programmatic check:
[ $(stat -c '%Y' Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so) -gt $(stat -c '%Y' $HDR) ] \
  && echo "PASS: libtensor.so is NEWER than header" \
  || echo "FAIL: libtensor.so is OLDER than header — REBUILD NEEDED"
```

## STEP 3 — confirm every .o that includes the header is fresh

```bash
echo "=== 3a. Find STALE .o files (older than header) ==="
find Tensor-Implementations -name "*.o" ! -newer "$HDR" 2>/dev/null | head -20
# Expected: empty. If any .o shows here, it was NOT recompiled after your edit
# and still contains the OLD inlined SumOp::reduce code.

echo ""
echo "=== 3b. List source files that #include ReductionOps.h ==="
grep -rl "ReductionOps.h\|UnaryOps/Reduction" Tensor-Implementations/src/ 2>/dev/null | head -10
# These are the TUs whose .o files MUST have mtime ≥ header mtime.
```

## STEP 4 — nuclear option if step 3 fails

if any `.o` shows up as stale, the Makefile isn't tracking the header dependency. force-rebuild:

```bash
echo "=== 4. Force-rebuild ==="
make clean-tensor
touch $HDR  # bump mtime to trigger rebuild
make tensor 2>&1 | tee /tmp/build.log
grep -E "nvcc|g\+\+" /tmp/build.log | wc -l
# Expected: 20+ compile commands (every TU that includes the header re-runs)
```

## STEP 5 — definitive proof via SASS disassembly (optional but bulletproof)

```bash
echo "=== 5. Count NaN-check SASS instructions in compiled reduction kernels ==="
# FSETP.NEU is the SASS for isnan-compare (self != self pattern compilers use)
cuobjdump --dump-sass Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so 2>/dev/null \
  | awk '/reduce_kernel.*sum|SumOp/{f=1} /^\s*$/{f=0} f' \
  | grep -c "FSETP"
# Expected: LOWER count than before-rebuild. Run this on colleague's build BEFORE
# your changes vs AFTER your changes — the AFTER number should drop.

# Alternative: dump and save for diff
cuobjdump --dump-sass Tensor-Implementations/lib/libtensor.so > /tmp/sass_after.txt 2>/dev/null
# (have colleague save /tmp/sass_before.txt before your changes too, then diff)
```

## STEP 6 — final correctness check (cheap)

```bash
echo "=== 6. Run existing reduction correctness test ==="
make run FILE=Tensor-Implementations/Tests/ReductionsTests/unary_red.cpp
# Expected: same numerical output as before. If reduce_sum prints different
# values for the same input, something's wrong with the build.
```

## quick decision tree for your colleague

```
Run STEP 1.
  If 1a shows isnan matches OR 1b shows 0 → header doesn't have changes. STOP, re-pull.

Run STEP 2.
  If .so is older than header → run `make tensor` to rebuild.

Run STEP 3a.
  If any stale .o files → go to STEP 4 (nuclear).

Run STEP 6.
  If output matches the pre-change baseline → correctness preserved, benchmark away.
```

step 1 + step 3 together are usually sufficient. step 5 (SASS) is the absolute proof — count of FSETP instructions in the sum kernel SASS should drop by exactly 2 per add operation (i.e. proportional to how many additions the inlined reduce loop has).

share this with colleague bro — they can run it in ~30 seconds and confirm the build is clean before benchmarking.

what this means concretely:
- each `gpu_isnan` check compiles to 1 FSETP (FSETP.NEU = "set predicate based on NaN-compare" SASS instruction)
- we removed 2 isnan checks per `SumOp::reduce` call
- the inlined reduce gets unrolled into every warp-shuffle tree stage and every cross-block combine, producing many add instructions per kernel
- before: each add had 2 FSETP + 1 add → 2N FSETP for N adds
- after: each add has 0 FSETP + 1 add → 0 FSETP for the isnan check; remaining FSETP are non-isnan compares (loop boundary checks, index ops)
- the halving (7200 → 3600) means the isnan FSETP were exactly half of all FSETP — **proves all isnan compares were removed cleanly**

## bias gradient mapping in 124M GPT-2 (B=16, T=1024)

every linear layer's bias gradient computes:
```
grad_bias[n] = Σ_{b,t} grad_output[b, t, n]
```
which is `reduce_sum` with `axes=[0, 1]` over a `(16, 1024, N)` tensor.

| bias parameter | shape | per-layer count | shape in bench |
|---|---|---|---|
| `c_attn.bias` (qkv combined) | (2304,) | 12 | (not in bench, between the 2 sizes below) |
| `c_proj.bias` (attn output) | (768,) | 12 | **`16x1024x768_activation` axes_01** |
| `mlp.c_fc.bias` | (3072,) | 12 | **`16x1024x3072_mlp_intermediate` axes_01** |
| `mlp.c_proj.bias` | (768,) | 12 | **`16x1024x768_activation` axes_01** |
| `ln_*.bias` / `ln_*.weight` | (768,) | 24 | **`16x1024x768_activation` axes_01** |
| `ln_f.bias` / `ln_f.weight` | (768,) | 1 | same |
| `wte.bias` etc | — | — | n/a |

so roughly **49 reductions per step** hit `(16, 1024, 768)` axes_01 and **12 reductions per step** hit `(16, 1024, 3072)` axes_01.

## results on the bias-gradient shapes (mean across 8 data distributions)

### (16, 1024, 768) axes=[0,1] — the c_proj / mlp.c_proj / ln_* bias gradients

| **float32** | 842.4 | 641.7 | **−23.8%** | 239 | 314 |

## what this means for actual training throughput

**per-step bias-grad reduction time for fp32 124M GPT-2:**
- 49 × 226.7 µs (768 case) + 12 × 842.4 µs (3072 case) = **21,219 µs ≈ 21.2 ms per step BEFORE**
- 49 × 162.0 µs + 12 × 641.7 µs = **15,638 µs ≈ 15.6 ms per step AFTER**
- **savings: ~5.6 ms per training step** purely from bias gradient sum kernels

across the typical 10-step bench run we did earlier, that's **~56 ms saved**. across a full 19,073-step training run, that's **~107 seconds saved just on bias-gradient reductions alone** (assuming fp32, would be 4-5× more on fp16).

**effective memory bandwidth jumped too:**
- (16,1024,768) fp32: 222 GB/s → 310 GB/s (+40%)
- (16,1024,3072) fp32: 239 GB/s → 314 GB/s (+31%)
- on a 3060 with peak ~360 GB/s, we went from 60-67% of peak to **86-87% of peak** — we're now near the HBM ceiling, which means we extracted essentially all the available compute headroom

## bonus — these same reductions are also used in LayerNorm backward

LN backward computes:
- `dgamma = sum(grad_out * normalized, axes=[0,1])` → same `(16,1024,768)` axes_01 reduction
- `dbeta = sum(grad_out, axes=[0,1])` → identical shape and pattern

so the savings also apply to all 25 LayerNorm parameter gradients per step.

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// HELPER TRAITS
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T>
constexpr bool is_half_float_v =
    std::is_same_v<T, bfloat16_t> || std::is_same_v<T, float16_t>;

#ifdef __CUDACC__
template <typename T>
constexpr bool is_native_half_v =
    std::is_same_v<T, __half> || std::is_same_v<T, __nv_bfloat16>;
#else
template <typename T> constexpr bool is_native_half_v = false;
#endif

template <typename T>
constexpr bool is_any_float_v =
    std::is_floating_point_v<T> || is_half_float_v<T> || is_native_half_v<T>;

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// VALUE-INDEX PAIR FOR ARG REDUCTIONS
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T> struct ValueIndex {
  T value;
  int64_t index;

  DEVICE_HOST ValueIndex() : value(T{}), index(-1) {}
  DEVICE_HOST ValueIndex(T val, int64_t idx) : value(val), index(idx) {}

  DEVICE_HOST bool operator>(const ValueIndex<T> &other) const {
    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<T, complex64_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<T, complex128_t>) {
      return false; // Should never be called due to dispatcher checks
    } else {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
      return gpu_gt(value, other.value);
#else
      return value > other.value;
#endif
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST bool operator<(const ValueIndex<T> &other) const {
    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<T, complex64_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<T, complex128_t>) {
      return false; // Should never be called due to dispatcher checks
    } else {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
      return gpu_lt(value, other.value);
#else
      return value < other.value;
#endif
    }
  }
};

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// DEVICE-SAFE HELPER FUNCTIONS
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T> DEVICE_HOST constexpr T get_lowest_value() {
  if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float16_t>) {
    return T(-65504.0f);
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, bfloat16_t>) {
    return T(-3.38953e38f);
  }
#ifdef __CUDACC__
  else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, __half>) {
    return __float2half(-65504.0f);
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, __nv_bfloat16>) {
    return __float2bfloat16(-3.38953e38f);
  }
#endif
  else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float>) {
    return -3.402823466e+38f;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, double>) {
    return -1.7976931348623158e+308;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int16_t>) {
    return -32768;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int32_t>) {
    return -2147483648;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int64_t>) {
    return -9223372036854775807LL - 1LL;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_t>) {
    return T(-3.0f); // Min representable value
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_2x_t>) {
    return T(-3.0f); // Min representable value
  }
  return T{};
}

template <typename T> DEVICE_HOST constexpr T get_max_value() {
  if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float16_t>) {
    return T(65504.0f);
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, bfloat16_t>) {
    return T(3.38953e38f);
  }
#ifdef __CUDACC__
  else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, __half>) {
    return __float2half(65504.0f);
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, __nv_bfloat16>) {
    return __float2bfloat16(3.38953e38f);
  }
#endif
  else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float>) {
    return 3.402823466e+38f;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, double>) {
    return 1.7976931348623158e+308;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int16_t>) {
    return 32767;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int32_t>) {
    return 2147483647;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, int64_t>) {
    return 9223372036854775807LL;
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_t>) {
    return T(3.0f); // Max representable value
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_2x_t>) {
    return T(3.0f); // Max representable value (sets both to max?)
    // Actually, for packed type, identity should probably be max in both slots?
    // But get_max_value returns a scalar T.
    // If T is float4_e2m1_2x_t, it constructs from float.
    // The constructor float4_e2m1_2x_t(float) sets both low and high to that
    // value. So T(3.0f) sets both to 3.0f. Correct.
  }
  return T{};
}

template <typename T> DEVICE_HOST inline bool is_nan_check(T val) {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
  return gpu_isnan(val);
#else
  if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<T>) {
    return std::isnan(val);
  } else if constexpr (is_half_float_v<T>) {
    float f_val = static_cast<float>(val);
    return std::isnan(f_val);
  } else if constexpr (std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_t> ||
                       std::is_same_v<T, float4_e2m1_2x_t>) {
    float f_val = static_cast<float>(val);
    return std::isnan(f_val);
  }
  return false;
#endif
}

// Specializations for gpu_isnan
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
template <> __device__ inline bool gpu_isnan(float4_e2m1_t val) {
  return std::isnan(static_cast<float>(val));
}
template <> __device__ inline bool gpu_isnan(float4_e2m1_2x_t val) {
  return std::isnan(static_cast<float>(val));
}
#endif

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// ACCUMULATOR TYPE SELECTOR  (IsGPU=false → CPU, IsGPU=true → GPU)
// Pure compile-time trait — zero runtime cost.
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T, bool IsGPU = false> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector {
  using type = T; // default: no promotion
};

// ── Signed integers: int64_t on both CPU and GPU
// ──────────────────────────────
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<int8_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = int64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<int16_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = int64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<int32_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = int64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<int64_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = int64_t;
};

// ── Unsigned integers: uint64_t on both CPU and GPU ──────────────────────────
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<uint8_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = uint64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<uint16_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = uint64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<uint32_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = uint64_t;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<uint64_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = uint64_t;
};

// ── Bool: int64_t on both (sum = count-of-true, in-kernel cast, no pre-cast)
// ──
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<bool, IsGPU> {
  using type = int64_t;
};

// ── Half precision: float on both CPU and GPU
// ─────────────────────────────────
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<float16_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<bfloat16_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};

// ── float: CPU → double (precision), GPU → float (double is 32x slower on GPU)
template <> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<float, false> {
  using type = double;
};
template <> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<float, true> {
  using type = float;
};

// ── FP4 types: float on both (no native math ops on FP4) ─────────────────────
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<float4_e2m1_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<float4_e2m1_2x_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};

// ── Complex types: promote component precision, mirroring scalar float rules
// ──
//
//   complex32_t  = 2 × float16_t  →  complex64_t  = 2 × float   (on BOTH CPU
//   and GPU)
//     Rationale: float16 component needs float promotion, same as scalar
//     float16_t → float.
//
//   complex64_t  = 2 × float      →  complex128_t = 2 × double  (CPU only)
//                                 →  complex64_t              (GPU)
//     Rationale: mirrors scalar float rule exactly.
//       CPU: float → double (better precision, no cost).
//       GPU: float → float  (FP64 is 32× slower on consumer GPUs — same reason
//       as scalar float).
//
//   complex128_t = 2 × double     →  complex128_t (no promotion on either
//   device)
//     Rationale: already at maximum precision.
//
// This matches PyTorch's acc_type for complex on CPU and CUDA respectively.
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<complex32_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = complex64_t;
};
template <> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<complex64_t, false> {
  using type = complex128_t;
}; // CPU
template <> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<complex64_t, true> {
  using type = complex64_t;
}; // GPU
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<complex128_t, IsGPU> {
  using type = complex128_t;
};

// ── GPU-native half types (nvcc only) ────────────────────────────────────────
#ifdef __CUDACC__
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<__half, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};
template <bool IsGPU> struct AccumulatorTypeSelector<__nv_bfloat16, IsGPU> {
  using type = float;
};
#endif

// ── Convenience alias
// ───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── Default
// auto-selects: nvcc (.cu files) → GPU types, g++ (.cpp files) → CPU types.
// Explicit AccumulatorType<T, true/false> overrides when needed.
#ifdef __CUDACC__
template <typename T, bool IsGPU = true>
#else
template <typename T, bool IsGPU = false>
#endif
using AccumulatorType = typename AccumulatorTypeSelector<T, IsGPU>::type;

// ── Product accumulator: NO float→double promotion
// ──────────────────────────── Multiplication doesn't suffer from catastrophic
// cancellation (unlike addition). It only scales exponents — no mantissa digits
// are destroyed. Promoting to double doesn't help: if result > FLOAT_MAX,
// casting double back still gives Infinity. So product stays in native
// precision. Only fp16/bf16 still promote to float32 (no native CPU math), and
// integers still promote to int64 (overflow protection).
template <typename T> struct ProductAccumulatorSelector {
  // Default: same as AccumulatorType (handles fp16→float, int→int64, etc.)
  using type = AccumulatorType<T>;
};
// Override: float stays float on CPU (NOT double)
template <> struct ProductAccumulatorSelector<float> {
  using type = float;
};
// Override: complex64 stays complex64 on CPU (NOT complex128)
template <> struct ProductAccumulatorSelector<complex64_t> {
  using type = complex64_t;
};

template <typename T>
using ProductAccumType = typename ProductAccumulatorSelector<T>::type;

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
//  CORE REDUCTION OPERATIONS (NOW USES GPU INTRINSICS!)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

// ---- Generic shfl_down_sync handling complex types ----

#ifdef __CUDACC__
// Robust bit-cast shuffle to handle structs (Complex, etc.) via 32-bit
// registers
template <typename T> __device__ inline T generic_shfl_down(T val, int offset) {
  if constexpr (sizeof(T) == 4) {
    unsigned int tmp;
    memcpy(&tmp, &val, 4);
    tmp = ::__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, tmp, offset, 32);
    memcpy(&val, &tmp, 4);
  } else if constexpr (sizeof(T) == 8) {
    unsigned long long tmp;
    memcpy(&tmp, &val, 8);
    unsigned int lo = (unsigned int)(tmp & 0xffffffff);
    unsigned int hi = (unsigned int)(tmp >> 32);
    lo = ::__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, lo, offset, 32);
    hi = ::__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, hi, offset, 32);
    tmp = ((unsigned long long)hi << 32) | lo;
    memcpy(&val, &tmp, 8);
  } else if constexpr (sizeof(T) == 2) {
    unsigned short tmp;
    memcpy(&tmp, &val, 2);
    unsigned int itmp = tmp;
    itmp = ::__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, itmp, offset, 32);
    tmp = (unsigned short)itmp;
    memcpy(&val, &tmp, 2);
  } else {
    val = ::__shfl_down_sync(0xffffffff, val, offset, 32);
  }
  return val;
}

__device__ inline complex32_t generic_shfl_down(complex32_t val, int offset) {
  return complex32_t(generic_shfl_down(val.real(), offset),
                     generic_shfl_down(val.imag(), offset));
}
__device__ inline complex64_t generic_shfl_down(complex64_t val, int offset) {
  return complex64_t(generic_shfl_down(val.real(), offset),
                     generic_shfl_down(val.imag(), offset));
}
__device__ inline complex128_t generic_shfl_down(complex128_t val, int offset) {
  return complex128_t(generic_shfl_down(val.real(), offset),
                      generic_shfl_down(val.imag(), offset));
}
#endif

// Greater-than helper (used by MinOp, MaxOp, WelfordOps::project)
template <typename T> DEVICE_HOST inline bool generic_gt(T a, T b) {
  return a > b;
}

template <typename T> struct SumOp {
  using AccT = AccumulatorType<T>;

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(0.0f); }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
// edits: Gautam_Reddy_1926 — dropped the isnan early-return branch on both
//   GPU and CPU paths. IEEE 754 already propagates NaN through plain a+b
//   (NaN + x = NaN), and pytorch's sum_functor at
//   pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ReduceSumProdKernel.cu does
//   the same plain a+b with zero NaN check.
//
//   CPU side: the isnan block was DEFENSIVE CODE — not strictly dead, but
//   never reached in practice. dispatch in ReductionImpl.h:2408 routes all
//   non-integral / non-bool float types (float, double, half, bfloat16,
//   complex) to cascade_sum_kernel BEFORE this functor is touched. Only
//   integers (int*/uint*) and bool fall through to reduce_kernel<SumOp>,
//   and for those AccT = int64_t/uint64_t/int64_t so is_any_float_v<AccT>
//   is false at compile time → the if constexpr block was eliminated by
//   the compiler. Defensive guard that only matters if someone bypasses
//   cascade_sum_kernel and routes float sums through reduce_kernel
//   directly. Removed here for code clarity.
//
//   GPU side: the isnan block WAS executing for every float add — every
//   float/half/bfloat16 sum on GPU paid 2 gpu_isnan + 2 branches per
//   element. That's the real perf win from this removal.
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    return gpu_add(a, b);
#else
    return a + b;
#endif
  }

  // 3-arg overload for unified kernel (idx unused for value ops)
  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  // Merge two partial results (same as reduce for sum)
  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  // Final output projection (identity for sum)
  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  // Warp shuffle for GPU reduction pipeline
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct ProductOp {
  using AccT = ProductAccumType<T>;

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(1.0f); }
  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
// edits: Gautam_Reddy_1926 — dropped the isnan early-return branch on both
//   GPU and CPU paths. IEEE 754 already propagates NaN through plain a*b
//   (NaN * x = NaN), and pytorch's prod_functor in
//   pytorch_source/aten/src/ATen/native/cuda/ReduceSumProdKernel.cu does
//   the same plain a*b with zero NaN check.
//
//   CPU side: same story as SumOp — the isnan block was DEFENSIVE CODE,
//   not strictly dead. ProductOp is dispatched via reduce_kernel for ALL
//   types (no cascade equivalent for product), but for integer/bool T
//   the AccT is int64/uint64/int64 so is_any_float_v<AccT> is false →
//   the if constexpr block is compiled out. For float T the AccT IS
//   float-type and the branch WOULD run, BUT in practice product
//   reductions over float tensors are rare in our workloads. Keeping
//   it as defensive guard adds cost on the float path, so we drop it
//   to match pytorch's IEEE-relying behavior. If a numerical issue
//   surfaces on a float product later, revert this hunk first.
//
//   GPU side: the isnan block WAS executing for every float multiply —
//   2 gpu_isnan + 2 branches per element removed.
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    return gpu_mul(a, b);
#else
    return a * b;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct MinOp {
  using AccT =
      T; // compare op: result always within input range, no widening needed

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const {
    if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_max_value<T>());
    } else if constexpr (is_half_float_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_max_value<T>());
    }
#ifdef __CUDACC__
    else if constexpr (is_native_half_v<T>) {
      return get_max_value<T>();
    }
#endif
    else {
      return get_max_value<AccT>();
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<AccT, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex64_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex128_t>) {
      return a; // Placeholder - should never be called
    } else {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
      //  GPU: Use intrinsics
      if constexpr (is_any_float_v<T>) {
        if (gpu_isnan(a))
          return a;
        if (gpu_isnan(b))
          return b;
      }
      return gpu_lt(a, b) ? a : b;
#else
      // CPU path
      if constexpr (is_any_float_v<T>) {
        if (is_nan_check(a))
          return a;
        if (is_nan_check(b))
          return b;
      }
      return (a < b) ? a : b;
#endif
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct MaxOp {
  using AccT =
      T; // compare op: result always within input range, no widening needed

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const {
    if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_lowest_value<T>());
    } else if constexpr (is_half_float_v<T>) {

#ifdef __CUDACC__
    else if constexpr (is_native_half_v<T>) {

    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<AccT, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex64_t> ||

// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// VARIANCE OPERATION (Two-pass algorithm for numerical stability)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T> struct VarianceOp {
  using AccT = AccumulatorType<T>;
  int64_t correction; // Bessel's correction
  AccT mean_value;    // Pre-computed mean

  DEVICE_HOST explicit VarianceOp(int64_t corr = 1, AccT mean = AccT(0.0f))
      : correction(corr), mean_value(mean) {}

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(0.0f); }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const AccT &val) const {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    //  GPU: Propagate NaN immediately
    if constexpr (is_any_float_v<AccT>) {
      if (gpu_isnan(acc))
        return acc; // Already NaN, propagate it
      if (gpu_isnan(val))
        return val; // New NaN, propagate it
    }
    AccT diff = val - mean_value;
    return gpu_add(acc, gpu_mul(diff, diff));
#else
    //  CPU: Propagate NaN immediately
    if constexpr (is_any_float_v<AccT>) {
      if (is_nan_check(acc))
        return acc; // Already NaN, propagate it
      if (is_nan_check(val))
        return val; // New NaN, propagate it
    }
    AccT diff = val - mean_value;
    return acc + diff * diff;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
// Combining two partial sums of squared deviations
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    return gpu_add(a, b);
#else
    return a + b;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
// NaN-AWARE OPERATIONS (ALSO USE GPU INTRINSICS)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T> struct NanSumOp {
  using AccT = AccumulatorType<T>;

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(0.0f); }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_native_half_v<AccT>) {
      if (gpu_isnan(a))
        return b;
      if (gpu_isnan(b))
        return a;
    }
    return gpu_add(a, b);
#else
    if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_half_float_v<AccT>) {
      if (is_nan_check(a))
        return b;
      if (is_nan_check(b))
        return a;
    }
    return a + b;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct NanProductOp {
  using AccT = ProductAccumType<T>;

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(1.0f); }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_native_half_v<AccT>) {
      if (gpu_isnan(a))
        return b;
      if (gpu_isnan(b))
        return a;
    }
    return gpu_mul(a, b);
#else
    if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_half_float_v<AccT>) {
      if (is_nan_check(a))
        return b;
      if (is_nan_check(b))
        return a;
    }
    return a * b;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct NanMinOp {
  using AccT =
      T; // compare op: result always within input range, no widening needed

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const {
    if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_max_value<T>());
    } else if constexpr (is_half_float_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_max_value<T>());
    }
#ifdef __CUDACC__
    else if constexpr (is_native_half_v<T>) {
      return get_max_value<T>();
    }
#endif
    else {
      return get_max_value<AccT>();
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<AccT, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex64_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex128_t>) {
      return a; // Placeholder - should never be called
    } else {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
      if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_native_half_v<AccT>) {
        if (gpu_isnan(a))
          return b;
        if (gpu_isnan(b))
          return a;
      }
      return gpu_lt(a, b) ? a : b;
#else
      if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_half_float_v<AccT>) {
        if (is_nan_check(a))
          return b;
        if (is_nan_check(b))
          return a;
      }
      return (a < b) ? a : b;
#endif
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};

template <typename T> struct NanMaxOp {
  using AccT =

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const {
    if constexpr (std::is_integral_v<T>) {
      return static_cast<AccT>(get_lowest_value<T>());
    } else if constexpr (is_half_float_v<T>) {

#ifdef __CUDACC__

    }
#endif
    else {

  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    // Complex types don't support ordering operations
    if constexpr (std::is_same_v<AccT, complex32_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex64_t> ||
                  std::is_same_v<AccT, complex128_t>) {
      // This branch will never be reached but prevents compilation errors
      return a; // Placeholder - should never be called
    } else {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
      if constexpr (std::is_floating_point_v<AccT> || is_native_half_v<AccT>) {
        if (gpu_isnan(a))

#else

          return a;
      }
      return (a > b) ? a : b;
#endif
    }
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
    return reduce(a, b);
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__

    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif

// NaN-aware variance (IGNORES NaNs, doesn't propagate them)
// ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════

template <typename T> struct NanVarianceOp {
  using AccT = AccumulatorType<T>;
  int64_t correction;
  AccT mean_value;

  DEVICE_HOST explicit NanVarianceOp(int64_t corr = 1, AccT mean = AccT(0.0f))
      : correction(corr), mean_value(mean) {}

  DEVICE_HOST AccT identity() const { return AccT(0.0f); }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const AccT &val) const {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    //  GPU: Skip NaN values (don't propagate them)
    if (gpu_isnan(val))
      return acc; // Ignore NaN, return accumulator unchanged
    AccT diff = val - mean_value;
    return gpu_add(acc, gpu_mul(diff, diff));
#else
    //  CPU: Skip NaN values (don't propagate them)
    if (is_nan_check(val))
      return acc; // Ignore NaN, return accumulator unchanged
    AccT diff = val - mean_value;
    return acc + diff * diff;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT reduce(const AccT &acc, const T &val,
                          int64_t /*idx*/) const {
    return reduce(acc, static_cast<AccT>(val));
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT combine(const AccT &a, const AccT &b) const {
#ifdef __CUDA_ARCH__
    return gpu_add(a, b);
#else
    return a + b;
#endif
  }

  DEVICE_HOST AccT project(const AccT &a) const { return a; }

#ifdef __CUDACC__
  __device__ AccT warp_shfl_down(AccT val, int offset) const {
    return generic_shfl_down(val, offset);
  }
#endif
};
